accounting.grade10.accrued-and-prepaid-i.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.accrued-and-prepaid-i.question: The timing problem exists because:
options: Money moves on its own schedule, but matching demands each year carry exactly its own incomes and expenses
The trial balance cannot handle cash
Expenses may only be recorded when paid

accounting.grade10.accrued-and-prepaid-i.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.accrued-and-prepaid-i.question: The two-by-two grid is built from the two questions:
options: Is it big, and is it recurring?
Expense or income — and did the cash move before or after the use/earning it belongs to?
Debit or credit — and which journal?
Asset or liability — and which ledger?

accounting.grade10.accrued-and-prepaid-i.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.accrued-and-prepaid-i.question: Income already received but not yet earned is called:

accounting.grade10.accrued-and-prepaid-i.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.accrued-and-prepaid-i.question: Every timing adjustment is always:
options: A cash entry in the CPJ
A note with no double entry
One income-statement correction PLUS one balance-sheet creation — the pair

accounting.grade10.accrued-and-prepaid-i.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.accrued-and-prepaid-i.question: Telephone shows R1 100; February's R100 account arrives in March. The adjustment:
options: Debit Telephone R100, credit Accrued Expenses (current liability) — the year used twelve months
Credit Telephone R100 — only paid months count

accounting.grade10.accrued-and-prepaid-i.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.accrued-and-prepaid-i.question: Insurance of R1 200 was paid on 1 September for twelve months (year end 28 February). This year's true expense is:
options: R1 200 — it was all paid this year
R600 — six months used (September to February); the rest is next year's cover

accounting.grade10.accrued-and-prepaid-i.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.accrued-and-prepaid-i.question: The prepaid R600 becomes:
options: Prepaid Expenses — a CURRENT ASSET: value bought and stored for next year

accounting.grade10.accrued-and-prepaid-i.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.accrued-and-prepaid-i.question: What both expense cases share:
options: Both leave the expense at what was PAID
The expense ends at what the YEAR USED, regardless of what the bank account did

accounting.grade10.accrued-and-prepaid-i.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.accrued-and-prepaid-i.question: The tenant (R500/month) has paid only eleven months by year end. Rent Income must be:
options: Credited R500 to the true R6 000, with Accrued Income debited as a current ASSET
Left at R5 500 — cash is cash

accounting.grade10.accrued-and-prepaid-i.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.accrued-and-prepaid-i.question: If instead the tenant paid THIRTEEN months, the extra R500 is:
options: Income received in advance — a current LIABILITY: the business owes a month of occupation

accounting.grade10.accrued-and-prepaid-i.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.accrued-and-prepaid-i.question: "Interest capitalised" on the R10 000 loan at 12% means:
options: The interest was paid in cash monthly
The R1 200 interest was ADDED to the loan — expense debited, loan rising to R11 200
The interest was waived by the bank

accounting.grade10.accrued-and-prepaid-i.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.accrued-and-prepaid-i.question: Missing the capitalised interest causes:
options: TWO errors at once — the expense understated and the liability understated

accounting.grade10.accrued-and-prepaid-i.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.accrued-and-prepaid-i.question: The five afterlives, in order (accrued expense / prepaid expense / accrued income / income in advance / interest capitalised):
options: Current liability / current asset / current asset / current liability / folded into the loan

accounting.grade10.accrued-and-prepaid-i.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.accrued-and-prepaid-i.question: The symmetry check on any timing adjustment:
options: Profit and cash always move together
Whatever it does to profit, its balance-sheet twin moves the equation to match — one without the other means half the entry is missing
Assets and expenses always both rise
The trial balance total must change

accounting.grade10.accrued-and-prepaid-i.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.accrued-and-prepaid-i.question: Every error in this topic is really:
options: A CLASSIFICATION error wearing an arithmetic disguise — so classify by the grid before calculating

accounting.grade10.accrued-and-prepaid-i.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.accrued-and-prepaid-i.question: The verbs "owing", "outstanding", "still to be received" signal:
options: ACCRUALS — amounts belonging to this year whose cash has not yet moved

accounting.grade10.accrued-and-prepaid-i.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.accrued-and-prepaid-i.question: The chalk line on the floor represents:
options: Midnight at year end — everything earned and used on each side belongs to that side's report card
The line between debit and credit

accounting.grade10.accrued-and-prepaid-i.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.accrued-and-prepaid-i.question: The four corners of straddlers are:

accounting.grade10.accrued-and-prepaid-i.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.accrued-and-prepaid-i.question: The fix, the same in every corner:
options: Record the amount in the year the cash moved
Split every amount fifty-fifty between years
Put the amount where the USING or EARNING happened; the balance sheet remembers the loose end
Wait until the money settles itself

accounting.grade10.accrued-and-prepaid-i.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.accrued-and-prepaid-i.question: February's electricity billed in March belongs to February because:
options: The lights burned in February — the report card charges the year that USED it
March is in the new year
Bills count from their printing date
Electricity is always a March expense

accounting.grade10.accrued-and-prepaid-i.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.accrued-and-prepaid-i.question: The "sticky note" the telephone adjustment leaves is:
options: A small DEBT — we still owe February's R100 — torn up when March pays it
A reminder with no accounting effect

accounting.grade10.accrued-and-prepaid-i.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.accrued-and-prepaid-i.question: The R600 of unused insurance cover is like:
options: Six unopened months on the shelf — a parcel of value waiting for the new year

accounting.grade10.accrued-and-prepaid-i.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.accrued-and-prepaid-i.question: The two expense corners differ in what they leave behind:
options: One leaves a sticky note of debt; the other a parcel on the shelf — and neither may distort the report card

accounting.grade10.accrued-and-prepaid-i.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.accrued-and-prepaid-i.question: The tenant a month behind means the shop earned R6 000 but holds:
options: An IOU in its favour — an asset collected in the new year
Nothing — unpaid rent is never income

accounting.grade10.accrued-and-prepaid-i.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.accrued-and-prepaid-i.question: "Money in hand can still be a liability" because:
options: Cash always belongs to the bank
The tenant's thirteenth payment bought occupation not yet delivered — the shop holds the money, the tenant holds the claim
The money is counterfeit until earned

accounting.grade10.accrued-and-prepaid-i.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.accrued-and-prepaid-i.question: The capitalised interest is easily missed because:
options: It is too small to matter
No cash moved — no slip, no reminder; only the loan statement, quietly larger
It only applies to big businesses

accounting.grade10.accrued-and-prepaid-i.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.accrued-and-prepaid-i.question: After capitalisation, the two truths in the books are:
options: Profit rose and the loan fell
The year carried a R1 200 borrowing cost AND the debt now stands at R11 200

accounting.grade10.bookkeeping-cycle-ess.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.bookkeeping-cycle-ess.question: The accounting equation states:
options: ASSETS equal OWNER'S EQUITY plus LIABILITIES — at every moment, after every transaction

accounting.grade10.bookkeeping-cycle-ess.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.bookkeeping-cycle-ess.question: Every transaction has two equal effects because:
options: The equation must stay level — double entry is the arithmetic of the equation defending itself
One entry is always an estimate

accounting.grade10.bookkeeping-cycle-ess.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.bookkeeping-cycle-ess.question: On the debit-credit compass, assets, expenses and drawings:
options: Increase on the debit side; equity, liabilities and income increase on the credit side
Increase on whichever side is empty

accounting.grade10.bookkeeping-cycle-ess.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.bookkeeping-cycle-ess.question: The owner deposits R10 000 capital. The double entry is:
options: Debit Bank R10 000 (asset up), credit Capital R10 000 (equity up)

accounting.grade10.bookkeeping-cycle-ess.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.bookkeeping-cycle-ess.question: A credit sale of R2 400 to Mrs Dube is recorded in:
options: The Debtors Journal, from the duplicate invoice

accounting.grade10.bookkeeping-cycle-ess.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.bookkeeping-cycle-ess.question: Under the perpetual system, the CRJ records a cash sale of R6 900 together with:
options: Cost of sales R4 600 — the sale AND the shelf's loss together

accounting.grade10.bookkeeping-cycle-ess.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.bookkeeping-cycle-ess.question: Goods returned BY a debtor and goods returned TO a supplier go, respectively, to:
options: Debtors Allowances Journal (credit note) and Creditors Allowances Journal (debit note)

accounting.grade10.bookkeeping-cycle-ess.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.bookkeeping-cycle-ess.question: The two facts that choose the correct journal are:
options: The customer's name and the month
The VAT rate and the discount
Cash or credit, and which direction the value moves

accounting.grade10.bookkeeping-cycle-ess.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.bookkeeping-cycle-ess.question: The month's bank balance is:
options: R8 600 debit — receipts R17 900 less payments R9 300

accounting.grade10.bookkeeping-cycle-ess.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.bookkeeping-cycle-ess.question: Trading stock ends the month at:
options: R2 000 debit — in 5 000 plus 3 000 plus the R200 returned; out 4 600 plus 1 600 as cost of sales

accounting.grade10.bookkeeping-cycle-ess.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.bookkeeping-cycle-ess.question: The trial balance totals:
options: R20 000 on each side — bank, stock, debtors, cost of sales, rent and wages against capital, sales and creditors

accounting.grade10.bookkeeping-cycle-ess.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.bookkeeping-cycle-ess.question: Equal trial balance totals CANNOT detect:
options: A casting error in one account
An entry posted to the WRONG account, or a transaction left out on both sides

accounting.grade10.bookkeeping-cycle-ess.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.bookkeeping-cycle-ess.question: The debtors control account and the debtors list differ in source:
options: Control is built from JOURNAL TOTALS; the individual accounts from INDIVIDUAL POSTINGS — same street, counted twice
Control comes from the bank statement
The list comes from the trial balance
Both come from the same postings, so agreement proves nothing

accounting.grade10.bookkeeping-cycle-ess.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.bookkeeping-cycle-ess.question: The month's debtors control balance is:
options: R1 100 — sales 2 400 less allowances 300 less receipts 1 000, agreeing with Mrs Dube's account

accounting.grade10.bookkeeping-cycle-ess.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.bookkeeping-cycle-ess.question: A receipt posted to the wrong customer's page disturbs:
options: The LIST but not the control — the journal total that feeds the control was correct

accounting.grade10.bookkeeping-cycle-ess.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.bookkeeping-cycle-ess.question: The creditors mirror ends the month at:
options: R1 000 credit — purchases 3 000 less payments 2 000, agreeing with the wholesaler's account

accounting.grade10.bookkeeping-cycle-ess.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.bookkeeping-cycle-ess.question: The two questions that sort every slip are:
options: Did cash move or a promise, and which way did the value travel?
How big is the amount, and who signed it?
Is it VAT-inclusive, and is it dated?
Is it a sale, and is it profitable?

accounting.grade10.bookkeeping-cycle-ess.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.bookkeeping-cycle-ess.question: The wholesaler's invoice of R3 000 belongs in:
options: The invoice-in box — a promise, value coming in from the supplier

accounting.grade10.bookkeeping-cycle-ess.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.bookkeeping-cycle-ess.question: The slip that fits none of the six ordinary boxes goes to:
options: The catch-all box — the General Journal for corrections, write-offs and interest

accounting.grade10.bookkeeping-cycle-ess.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.bookkeeping-cycle-ess.question: The ledger answers a question the shoebox cannot:
options: Where do we STAND — one page per thing, each with its balance, instead of slips by date

accounting.grade10.bookkeeping-cycle-ess.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.bookkeeping-cycle-ess.question: The level scale at R20 000 a side proves:
options: The PAIRS were equal — every debit had its matching credit

accounting.grade10.bookkeeping-cycle-ess.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.bookkeeping-cycle-ess.question: A slip stolen BEFORE it reaches the shoebox:
options: Steals invisibly, as far as the scale knows — both sides are short by the same nothing
Is caught by the trial balance

accounting.grade10.bookkeeping-cycle-ess.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.bookkeeping-cycle-ess.question: The two records of the trust-buying street are:
options: The exercise book with a page per customer, and the single total line built from journal totals
The till tape and the bank statement
Two copies of the same list

accounting.grade10.bookkeeping-cycle-ess.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.bookkeeping-cycle-ess.question: When the two counts disagree, the difference:
options: Gives directions — a wrong-page posting damages the book, a miscast journal damages the total line

accounting.grade10.bookkeeping-cycle-ess.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.bookkeeping-cycle-ess.question: Two independent records forced to face each other monthly is valuable because:
options: It doubles the work and halves the errors automatically
Two witnesses who never compared notes telling the same story make the books BELIEVABLE
It is required only in large companies

accounting.grade10.bookkeeping-cycle-ess.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.bookkeeping-cycle-ess.question: The year's whole machine, in order, is:
options: Only journals and a trial balance
Sort the slips; write the diaries; gather the ledger; weigh the trial balance; count the street twice

accounting.grade10.budgeting-concepts-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.budgeting-concepts-an.question: A statement and a budget differ in that:
options: A statement REPORTS the verified past; a budget ESTIMATES the planned future — and variances between them demand explanation
Budgets are drawn after the fact

accounting.grade10.budgeting-concepts-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.budgeting-concepts-an.question: The cash budget answers:
options: The survival question — can we pay our way each month?

accounting.grade10.budgeting-concepts-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.budgeting-concepts-an.question: The capital budget plans:
options: The purchase of long-term assets — machines, vehicles, equipment — separately from daily running

accounting.grade10.budgeting-concepts-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.budgeting-concepts-an.question: Zero-based budgeting requires that:
options: Every budget starts at last year's figure plus a percentage
Every line starts at NOTHING and justifies its whole amount afresh — so dead costs die instead of riding along

accounting.grade10.budgeting-concepts-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.budgeting-concepts-an.question: January's receipts of R20 000 comprise:
options: Cash sales R12 000 plus the collection of December's credit sales R8 000 (40% of R20 000)
January's full sales of R20 000, cash and credit

accounting.grade10.budgeting-concepts-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.budgeting-concepts-an.question: The cash budget records a credit sale:
options: When the money ARRIVES — a month later, at collection; the cash budget thinks in cash only
Never — credit sales are excluded entirely

accounting.grade10.budgeting-concepts-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.budgeting-concepts-an.question: February's closing balance is:
options: R3 000 — opening R5 500 plus surplus R3 500 minus the machine's R6 000

accounting.grade10.budgeting-concepts-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.budgeting-concepts-an.question: The skeleton's fixed order is:
options: Receipts; payments; surplus/deficit; opening balance; closing balance — each closing rolling into the next opening

accounting.grade10.budgeting-concepts-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.budgeting-concepts-an.question: The budget's "first gift" regarding the machine is:
options: TIMING — big purchases go where the balances can carry them, seen in advance
Hiding the cost from the bank

accounting.grade10.budgeting-concepts-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.budgeting-concepts-an.question: If the dip had gone negative, the cheap-while-early choices are:
options: Delay the machine a month, or arrange an overdraft IN ADVANCE — banks price desperation dearly and preparation kindly

accounting.grade10.budgeting-concepts-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.budgeting-concepts-an.question: The credit-sales lag means that when sales GROW:
options: Nothing changes for the cash budget
A bumper month's cash arrives AFTER its costs were paid — growth can feel tight in cash

accounting.grade10.budgeting-concepts-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.budgeting-concepts-an.question: "A budgeted business meets its problems as variances" means:
options: Actual figures stand beside estimates, and every difference becomes an investigation months before it becomes an emergency

accounting.grade10.budgeting-concepts-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.budgeting-concepts-an.question: The capital budget feeds the cash budget by:
options: Supplying the landing dates and amounts of planned asset purchases — assets bought by plan, not appetite
Removing large purchases from the books

accounting.grade10.budgeting-concepts-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.budgeting-concepts-an.question: Medium-term and long-term budgets differ in that:
options: Medium-term plans one to three years (expansion, staffing); long-term carries strategy beyond that, in broader strokes

accounting.grade10.budgeting-concepts-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.budgeting-concepts-an.question: Depreciation never enters a cash budget because:
options: It belongs to the capital budget
No rand LEAVES — the cash budget records only actual money movements

accounting.grade10.budgeting-concepts-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.budgeting-concepts-an.question: The comment habits for budget questions are:
options: A dip is a timing question; a deficit is a financing question; a variance is an investigation question

accounting.grade10.budgeting-concepts-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.budgeting-concepts-an.question: "A report is a mirror; a budget is a headlamp" means:
options: Statements look backward at what happened; the budget looks forward so the month can be steered instead of suffered
Mirrors are more accurate than headlamps

accounting.grade10.budgeting-concepts-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.budgeting-concepts-an.question: The household page with incoming pay and outgoing rent, food and transport IS:
options: A cash budget — the same tool as Thabo's and the government's, differing only in zeros

accounting.grade10.budgeting-concepts-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.budgeting-concepts-an.question: Writing the plan down matters because:
options: Unwritten plans cannot be CHECKED — the written budget turns 'the money just went' into specific, answerable questions

accounting.grade10.budgeting-concepts-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.budgeting-concepts-an.question: The quarter's purse runs:
options: Opens R2 000; January closes R5 500; February dips to R3 000; March recovers to R6 500
Opens R5 500; closes R3 000 in March

accounting.grade10.budgeting-concepts-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.budgeting-concepts-an.question: February was safe for Thabo but dangerous for the cousin because:
options: The cousin paid more for the machine
Thabo SAW the dip on paper in advance and confirmed the purse could carry it; the cousin bought on feeling in a lean month

accounting.grade10.budgeting-concepts-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.budgeting-concepts-an.question: "Earning and receiving keep different calendars" refers to:
options: The credit-sales lag — 40% of each month's sales arrives a month late, so a good month can still feel tight
The difference between wages and salaries

accounting.grade10.budgeting-concepts-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.budgeting-concepts-an.question: "Dead costs love the copy" means:
options: Copied budgets carry forgotten, useless lines forever — the unused subscription, the outdated arrangement

accounting.grade10.budgeting-concepts-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.budgeting-concepts-an.question: Zero-based budgeting "fires the whole list" by asking:
options: Why does this line exist, what does it buy us NOW, and what breaks if we cut it?

accounting.grade10.budgeting-concepts-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.budgeting-concepts-an.question: The trade-off of zero-based budgeting is:
options: More effort than copying — repaid in found rands whenever honestly done

accounting.grade10.budgeting-concepts-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.budgeting-concepts-an.question: The year's complete toolkit closes with:
options: Recording, posting, reconciling, adjusting, closing, reporting, analysing, costing — and budgeting: stewardship from spaza to state

accounting.grade10.cash-payments-and-pet.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.cash-payments-and-pet.question: The Cash Payments Journal records:
options: All payments made from the business bank account, in date order, for one month

accounting.grade10.cash-payments-and-pet.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.cash-payments-and-pet.question: The CPJ's name column records:
options: What the money was spent on

accounting.grade10.cash-payments-and-pet.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.cash-payments-and-pet.question: Under the perpetual system, buying stock for cash is entered in:
options: The Trading Stock column — the asset loads directly at cost

accounting.grade10.cash-payments-and-pet.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.cash-payments-and-pet.question: The new R6 000 display fridge is recorded as:
options: An expense, because money left the bank
Sundries, detail Equipment — an asset kept for use, not an expense

accounting.grade10.cash-payments-and-pet.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.cash-payments-and-pet.question: The owner transfers R2 000 to himself for personal use. The correct entry is:
options: Sundries, detail Drawings — the owner withdrawing equity, never an expense

accounting.grade10.cash-payments-and-pet.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.cash-payments-and-pet.question: The sorting test for every payment is:
options: Was the payment made by EFT or cash?
Did the BUSINESS receive value — a possession, a consumed service — or did the owner?
Is the amount larger than R1 000?

accounting.grade10.cash-payments-and-pet.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.cash-payments-and-pet.question: Burying drawings among expenses causes the books to:
options: Understate the business's true profit and misjudge its performance

accounting.grade10.cash-payments-and-pet.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.cash-payments-and-pet.question: The CPJ cross-cast requires:
options: Trading Stock + Wages + Sundries totals to equal the Bank column total
Sundries to be the largest column

accounting.grade10.cash-payments-and-pet.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.cash-payments-and-pet.question: At month end, the Bank column total of the CPJ is posted as:
options: A credit to Bank — payments reduce the asset

accounting.grade10.cash-payments-and-pet.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.cash-payments-and-pet.question: Which pairing of internal controls belongs with the CPJ?
options: Payments only against approved documents, and monthly bank reconciliation against the journals
Two people counting the till at closing

accounting.grade10.cash-payments-and-pet.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.cash-payments-and-pet.question: Under the imprest system with a R500 float, at any moment:
options: Cash in the tin plus vouchers must equal exactly R500
The tin must hold R500 in cash

accounting.grade10.cash-payments-and-pet.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.cash-payments-and-pet.question: Vouchers total R360 at month end. The restoration payment is:
options: R360 — the restoration always equals the voucher total, returning the float to R500

accounting.grade10.cash-payments-and-pet.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.cash-payments-and-pet.question: The tin holds R95 cash and R340 in vouchers against a R500 float. This means:
options: The float was set too high
R65 is unaccounted for — the tin announces the shortfall immediately

accounting.grade10.cash-payments-and-pet.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.cash-payments-and-pet.question: In the money-out diary, WHO comes before WHAT because:
options: Payments are chased payee-first when questions arise later

accounting.grade10.cash-payments-and-pet.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.cash-payments-and-pet.question: Which payments earned their own lanes in Thabo's money-out diary?
options: Stock and wages — the constant traffic

accounting.grade10.cash-payments-and-pet.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.cash-payments-and-pet.question: The money-out handshake states that:
options: The tin must equal the float
The lanes plus named visitors must add to exactly the Bank column total

accounting.grade10.cash-payments-and-pet.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.cash-payments-and-pet.question: 'What did the SHOP get?' — for the R2 000 Thabo transferred to himself, the answer is:
options: Nothing — so the payment is drawings, the owner dipping into his own stake
A machine for years of use

accounting.grade10.cash-payments-and-pet.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.cash-payments-and-pet.question: If the R2 000 hid among expenses, a bank reading the books would:
options: See the same picture either way
Judge a good shop as weaker than it truly performed

accounting.grade10.cash-payments-and-pet.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.cash-payments-and-pet.question: The fridge is not a 'cost of the month' because:
options: Costs are what the month consumed; the fridge is a possession the shop keeps for years

accounting.grade10.cash-payments-and-pet.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.cash-payments-and-pet.question: An afternoon count shows R245 cash and R255 in slips against a R500 float. The tin is:
options: Perfectly in balance — cash plus slips equals the float
Impossible to judge until month end

accounting.grade10.cash-payments-and-pet.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.cash-payments-and-pet.question: The month's slips read: stamps R60, taxi R85, tea R120, cleaning R95. The refill from the bank is:
options: R360 — the refill IS the voucher total

accounting.grade10.cash-payments-and-pet.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.cash-payments-and-pet.question: Why does ONE named person own the tin?
options: So every question about the tin has an address — accountability with division of duties
Because only managers may touch cash

accounting.grade10.cash-receipts-journal.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.cash-receipts-journal.question: The Cash Receipts Journal records:
options: All money received by the business, in date order, for one month

accounting.grade10.cash-receipts-journal.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.cash-receipts-journal.question: The day's cash sales are proven by which source document?
options: The cash register roll, totalled at the end of the day

accounting.grade10.cash-receipts-journal.subject: accounting

options: It records the stock leaving at cost, keeping the Trading Stock account truthful
It is a spare column for rounding errors
It should in fact be left empty

accounting.grade10.cash-receipts-journal.subject: accounting

options: Bank, Sales, Cost of Sales and Trading Stock

options: Analysis, Bank, and Sundry accounts (detail: Capital)

accounting.grade10.cash-receipts-journal.subject: accounting

options: Capital is not important enough to record
Frequency — daily items earn a column so a month posts as one total; rare items are handled by name in Sundries
Capital is recorded in the CPJ instead

options: Money received from debtors — that column only arrives with credit transactions

accounting.grade10.cash-receipts-journal.subject: accounting

options: Sales total plus Sundries total equals the Bank column total
All columns add to the same figure

accounting.grade10.cash-receipts-journal.subject: accounting

options: It is always posted separately in January

It is too small to matter

options: Exposing any gap between what was received and what reached the bank

accounting.grade10.cash-receipts-journal.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.cash-receipts-journal.question: The diary picture explains the CRJ as:

A list of everything the business owns
A diary of money in and out together

accounting.grade10.cash-receipts-journal.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.cash-receipts-journal.question: Sales earns its own column in the diary because:
options: It is a daily regular — a lane makes the month add up in seconds

accounting.grade10.cash-receipts-journal.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.cash-receipts-journal.question: The tenant's rent payment is handled as:
options: A regular lane of its own, always
An entry in the Sales column
A named visitor — amount in Sundries with 'Rent income' written beside it
No entry, since it is not sales

accounting.grade10.cash-receipts-journal.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.cash-receipts-journal.question: Sales of R1 500 at 25% mark-up on cost: what does the line show Thabo immediately?
options: R1 500 in, R1 200 off the shelf — R300 gross profit today

accounting.grade10.cash-receipts-journal.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.cash-receipts-journal.question: The 'classic slip' when finding the shelf's number is:
options: Taking 25% off the selling price instead of reversing the mark-up by division

accounting.grade10.cash-receipts-journal.subject: accounting

options: The counting-tray — collecting each amount as it arrives until the tray is banked as one deposit

accounting.grade10.cash-receipts-journal.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.cash-receipts-journal.question: The columns 'shake hands' when:
options: Sales total + Sundries total = Bank total
Every column shows the same figure
Cost of Sales equals gross profit
The diary has no blank lines

accounting.grade10.cash-receipts-journal.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.cash-receipts-journal.question: The handshake fails by R300. The bookkeeper should:
options: Post the journal anyway and fix it later
Adjust the Bank total to match
Hunt the R300 inside the journal — usually a line with a number on one side and a blank on the other — before posting anything
Add R300 to Cost of Sales

accounting.grade10.cash-receipts-journal.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.cash-receipts-journal.question: How does the CRJ protect the business's cash?
options: Daily intact banking, numbered receipts and the analysis column point at the exact day any rand goes missing
It replaces the need for a bank account

accounting.grade10.code-of-ethics.subtop.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.code-of-ethics.subtop.question: A code of ethics is best described as:
options: A list of punishments for dishonest staff
A formal statement of the values and standards of behaviour a business commits itself to
The rules for balancing a trial balance

accounting.grade10.code-of-ethics.subtop.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.code-of-ethics.subtop.question: Why does Accounting specifically depend on ethics?
options: Accountants handle more money than other workers
Ethics is examinable, so it must be learned
Financial information only has value if it can be trusted — bent records stop being information
The law requires a code before a business may open

accounting.grade10.code-of-ethics.subtop.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.code-of-ethics.subtop.question: The relationship between internal control and ethics is that:
options: They are the same thing under two names
Ethics replaces the need for controls in honest businesses
Controls matter only in big businesses; ethics only in small ones
Controls make dishonesty difficult; ethics makes it unwanted — a business needs both

accounting.grade10.code-of-ethics.subtop.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.code-of-ethics.subtop.question: Consistent adherence to rules and procedures, even under pressure, is:

accounting.grade10.code-of-ethics.subtop.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.code-of-ethics.subtop.question: A manager who explains a loss to the owner rather than burying it demonstrates:
options: Accountability — answering for decisions and actions

accounting.grade10.code-of-ethics.subtop.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.code-of-ethics.subtop.question: Conducting business so it can endure — refusing profit today that destroys tomorrow's base — defines:

accounting.grade10.code-of-ethics.subtop.question: Why do ethics scenarios often admit more than one characteristic?
options: The characteristics overlap by design — the skill is choosing and defending the best fit
Only one answer is ever marked correct
Because scenarios are written vaguely by mistake

accounting.grade10.code-of-ethics.subtop.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.code-of-ethics.subtop.question: An owner instructs the bookkeeper to omit cash sales 'to reduce tax'. The owner's clearest breaches are:
options: Leadership (dishonesty instructed from the top) and fairness (the tax burden shifts to honest taxpayers)
None — tax planning is always legal

accounting.grade10.code-of-ethics.subtop.subject: accounting

options: Transparency and fairness — the buyer cannot see what is really being sold
No characteristic — pricing is the owner's right

accounting.grade10.code-of-ethics.subtop.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.code-of-ethics.subtop.question: The lesson's pattern behind ethical failures is:
options: They happen only in large companies
A small, certain, immediate gain purchased with a large, delayed loss — and trust does not restock

accounting.grade10.code-of-ethics.subtop.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.code-of-ethics.subtop.question: The four moves of an ethics answer, in order, are:
options: Quote GAAP, name a party, add a law, conclude
Define all seven characteristics, pick two, summarise, moralise
Consequence first, then the issue, then the name
State the issue plainly; name the characteristic(s); argue the link to the scenario; give consequence and correction

accounting.grade10.code-of-ethics.subtop.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.code-of-ethics.subtop.question: 'This behaviour is wrong and very bad for everyone' earns nothing because:
options: It moralises without naming and applying a characteristic
Ethics answers must never judge behaviour

accounting.grade10.code-of-ethics.subtop.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.code-of-ethics.subtop.question: Listing 'transparency, accountability, fairness' without tying each to the scenario fails because:
options: Only one characteristic may ever be named
Naming without applying earns little — each name must connect to a fact of the scenario
The list is in the wrong order
Lists are not allowed in Accounting

accounting.grade10.code-of-ethics.subtop.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.code-of-ethics.subtop.question: The captain who trains hardest and never asks the team for anything they will not do themselves shows:
options: Leadership — the example set from the front

accounting.grade10.code-of-ethics.subtop.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.code-of-ethics.subtop.question: Explaining team selections openly instead of whispering in corners is:

accounting.grade10.code-of-ethics.subtop.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.code-of-ethics.subtop.question: The shop that checks the till, finds your extra R50 and pays it out passes the tests of:

options: Transparency — the deal is built to be invisible, with accountability lost alongside it

accounting.grade10.code-of-ethics.subtop.subject: accounting

The bargain is too small to matter

SARS pays rewards for neat books

A single sentence stating ethics is important

Final accounts → trial balance → ledger → journal

options: The number of COMPLETED years of service
The year of service you are standing in
The months worked divided by six

accounting.grade10.gross-pay-scales-and-.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.gross-pay-scales-and-.question: Annual salary converts to monthly pay by:
options: Dividing by 13 to allow for a bonus
Dividing by twelve, only at the END of the calculation
Dividing by the number of working days

accounting.grade10.gross-pay-scales-and-.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.gross-pay-scales-and-.question: The wage earner's gross versus the salary earner's gross:
options: Both respond to the hours of the week
Both are fixed for the year
The salary responds weekly; the wage is fixed
The wage RESPONDS to the week's hours; the salary is STABLE with growth arriving through the annual notch

accounting.grade10.gross-pay-scales-and-.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.gross-pay-scales-and-.question: "I sell my hours" and "I sell my year" describe:
options: The wage deal (counted by the clock) and the salary deal (one number sliced into twelve)
The employer's and employee's views of the same pay

accounting.grade10.gross-pay-scales-and-.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.gross-pay-scales-and-.question: Why does the "year deal" fit the office job better than the "clock deal"?
options: Office workers may not legally earn wages
The responsibility is continuous — the same in January as in June — so a stable slice fits
Salaries are cheaper for the shop

accounting.grade10.gross-pay-scales-and-.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.gross-pay-scales-and-.question: Both deals produce a number called GROSS, which is:
options: The employer's profit on the worker
What the work earned before anything is taken off

accounting.grade10.gross-pay-scales-and-.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.gross-pay-scales-and-.question: The three rows of the hourly price list (normal R40) are:
options: R40 plain; R60 evenings and Saturdays; R80 Sundays and public holidays
R40 weekdays; R40 Saturdays; R60 Sundays

accounting.grade10.gross-pay-scales-and-.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.gross-pay-scales-and-.question: Unsocial hours are paid more because:
options: The work is physically harder at night
They cost the worker more to give — rest, weekends, family time
The shop earns more on Sundays

accounting.grade10.gross-pay-scales-and-.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.gross-pay-scales-and-.question: The one trap in wage calculations, and the habit that beats it:
options: Forgetting normal hours; count them twice to be safe
Rounding the rate; always round up
Multiplying overtime hours by the PLAIN price; beat it by writing the correct row's price BEFORE touching the hours
Adding gross twice; subtract once at the end

accounting.grade10.gross-pay-scales-and-.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.gross-pay-scales-and-.question: Mokoena's two Sunday stocktake hours (normal rate R36) add to her gross:
options: R144 — two hours at the double price of R72

accounting.grade10.gross-pay-scales-and-.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.gross-pay-scales-and-.question: On the ladder R96 000 × R9 600 — R144 000, each rung represents:
options: One completed year of service, worth R9 600 more per year
A promotion to a new position

accounting.grade10.gross-pay-scales-and-.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.gross-pay-scales-and-.question: The ladder "makes tomorrow visible" because:
options: The worker can read exactly what year four pays before year one is finished — and the shop can budget years ahead
It hides future pay from the worker
It changes with each month's profits

accounting.grade10.gross-pay-scales-and-.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.gross-pay-scales-and-.question: When the ladder tops out at R144 000, further rising comes only from:
options: A new ladder — a promotion to a different scale
Dividing by eleven instead of twelve

accounting.grade10.gross-pay-scales-and-.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.gross-pay-scales-and-.question: The three moves for any ladder question are:
options: Guess the rung; check the answer; move on
Multiply by twelve; add the notch; subtract deductions
Count the hours; find the rate; multiply
Count completed years for the rung; divide by twelve for the month; measure the ladder and divide by the rung for the top

accounting.grade10.informal-vs-formal-bo.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.informal-vs-formal-bo.question: The key difference between the formal and informal sectors, according to the lesson, is:
options: The formal sector understands profit; the informal sector does not
The concepts differ completely between the sectors
The concepts are identical; what differs is the recording of them
The informal sector has no capital

accounting.grade10.informal-vs-formal-bo.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.informal-vs-formal-bo.question: A spaza shop's fridge is classified as:
options: Stock, because it can be sold
A fixed asset — a possession kept for use, not resale

accounting.grade10.informal-vs-formal-bo.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.informal-vs-formal-bo.question: Profit, in both sectors, is defined as:
options: Cash in the tin at month end

accounting.grade10.informal-vs-formal-bo.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.informal-vs-formal-bo.question: The supermarket's R500 000 bank deposit and the spaza owner's R3 000 saved cash are BOTH examples of:
options: Capital — the owner's resources committed to the business

accounting.grade10.informal-vs-formal-bo.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.informal-vs-formal-bo.question: A cooldrink bought for R8 and sold for R12 illustrates:
options: Cost price R8, selling price R12 — a margin of R4
Cost price R12, selling price R8
Income of R8 and an expense of R12

accounting.grade10.informal-vs-formal-bo.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.informal-vs-formal-bo.question: Why does the spaza owner's profit often look better than it truly is?
options: Her stock is cheaper than the supermarket's
Her own unpaid labour is an invisible cost that never reduces the profit figure
Informal profits are always overstated by law

accounting.grade10.informal-vs-formal-bo.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.informal-vs-formal-bo.question: A profitable informal trader is refused a bank loan. The most likely accounting reason is:
options: Informal traders may not open bank accounts
Without records she cannot PROVE her income — unrecorded success is invisible

accounting.grade10.informal-vs-formal-bo.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.informal-vs-formal-bo.question: Taking school fees from the shop's cash tin and 'restocking later' violates which principle?
options: The business entity rule — business and owner's money must be kept apart
No principle — the money belongs to the owner anyway

accounting.grade10.informal-vs-formal-bo.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.informal-vs-formal-bo.question: The lesson's verdict on informal traders is that:
options: They are poor businesspeople rescued by formal accounting
Business skill exists; recording ADDS proof, accuracy, separation and continuity to it
They should avoid records to stay flexible
Their methods have nothing in common with formal accounting

accounting.grade10.informal-vs-formal-bo.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.informal-vs-formal-bo.question: In a stokvel, the treasurer's book of who paid and whose turn is next corresponds to which modern record?
options: A ledger of contributions and claims

accounting.grade10.informal-vs-formal-bo.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.informal-vs-formal-bo.question: Cattle held as countable, visible wealth correspond most closely to:
options: Recorded fixed assets — a store of capital the owner can verify

accounting.grade10.informal-vs-formal-bo.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.informal-vs-formal-bo.question: Communal grazing rules, with elders checking that nobody overgrazes, demonstrate:
options: Internal control — agreed rules over resource use, with someone trusted to monitor

accounting.grade10.informal-vs-formal-bo.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.informal-vs-formal-bo.question: The R3 000 the spaza owner saved to start her shop is her:

accounting.grade10.informal-vs-formal-bo.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.informal-vs-formal-bo.question: The bread and airtime she buys at the wholesaler to sell again are her:

accounting.grade10.informal-vs-formal-bo.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.informal-vs-formal-bo.question: Her taxi fare to the wholesaler and the fridge's electricity are:
options: Expenses — money spent to keep the shop running

accounting.grade10.informal-vs-formal-bo.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.informal-vs-formal-bo.question: Head-count: R4 500 in, R3 000 stock — 'about R1 500 profit'. The notebook adds taxi R160, electricity R90, airtime R50. True profit is:

accounting.grade10.informal-vs-formal-bo.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.informal-vs-formal-bo.question: The R300 gap between the head's answer and the notebook's answer exists because:
options: The notebook made an arithmetic error
Small expenses leak from memory, quietly inflating the profit figure
Profit is always R300 lower on paper

accounting.grade10.informal-vs-formal-bo.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.informal-vs-formal-bo.question: Why should the owner's own unpaid work eventually appear in her figures?
options: Because SARS demands it for spaza shops
It should not — unpaid work is free
Labour is a real cost; counting it lets her compare the shop honestly against earning a wage elsewhere

accounting.grade10.informal-vs-formal-bo.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.informal-vs-formal-bo.question: In stokvel terms, the rule that a member who skips two months cannot claim a payout is:

accounting.grade10.informal-vs-formal-bo.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.informal-vs-formal-bo.question: The December meeting where the treasurer accounts for every rand is the stokvel's version of:

accounting.grade10.informal-vs-formal-bo.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.informal-vs-formal-bo.question: The lesson's closing takeaway is that formal accounting:
options: Replaces community practices that never worked
Formalises familiar practices — sharper tools for instincts communities already trust
Is unrelated to anything before textbooks

accounting.grade10.internal-control-basi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.internal-control-basi.question: Internal control is best defined as:
options: The security guards a business employs
The system of policies, procedures and checks that safeguards assets, ensures accurate records, promotes efficiency and encourages adherence to policies
The owner personally watching every worker

accounting.grade10.internal-control-basi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.internal-control-basi.question: Division of duties means:
options: Every worker gets an equal share of tasks
Managers do the important work themselves
No single person controls a transaction from beginning to end

accounting.grade10.internal-control-basi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.internal-control-basi.question: Internal control assumes that:
options: Errors never happen in a well-run business
People are human — so the structure must surface errors quickly and make dishonesty difficult and detectable

accounting.grade10.internal-control-basi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.internal-control-basi.question: An owner who takes cash from the till for private use damages which component most directly?
options: The control environment — the tone at the top that makes every other control credible

accounting.grade10.internal-control-basi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.internal-control-basi.question: Deliberately asking 'where can stock disappear and which records could be manipulated?' is:

accounting.grade10.internal-control-basi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.internal-control-basi.question: Surprise cash counts and comparing the annual stocktake against the records belong to:
options: Monitoring — checking that controls work in practice, not only on paper

accounting.grade10.internal-control-basi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.internal-control-basi.question: A sensible rule that no staff member was ever told about fails because of weak:

accounting.grade10.internal-control-basi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.internal-control-basi.question: Numbered source documents are a control because:
options: A missing number in the sequence immediately raises a question that demands an answer

accounting.grade10.internal-control-basi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.internal-control-basi.question: Which arrangement shows correct division of duties for cash?
options: The person who receives cash also records and banks it
The cashier receives cash, a different person records it, and banking is checked against the records
Whoever is free at closing counts the till alone

accounting.grade10.internal-control-basi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.internal-control-basi.question: Comparing the bank statement against the cash journals is an example of:
options: An independent check (reconciliation) — two independently created records that must agree

accounting.grade10.internal-control-basi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.internal-control-basi.question: The three-move answer to any internal-control scenario is:
options: Quote the definition, name the owner, suggest a meeting
Identify the weakness, explain the concrete risk, recommend a specific control
List all five components, then choose one
Calculate the loss, blame the employee, add security cameras

accounting.grade10.internal-control-basi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.internal-control-basi.question: Why does 'the owner must be more careful' earn no marks as a recommendation?
options: Recommendations must criticise employees, not owners
It is not specific or actionable — a control must name who does what differently
It is too short for the mark allocation

accounting.grade10.internal-control-basi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.internal-control-basi.question: Takings kept in a drawer and banked 'whenever there is time' should be answered with:
options: Weakness: cash not banked promptly; risk: theft, loss and unverifiable records; control: bank daily and intact, reconciling deposits against the cash journal
Weakness: too much cash; risk: none if staff are trusted; control: a bigger drawer
Weakness: no computer; risk: slow service; control: buy software
Weakness: banking fees; risk: high costs; control: bank monthly

accounting.grade10.internal-control-basi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.internal-control-basi.question: In the one-person tuck shop, why can nobody — including Sipho — prove whether money was taken?
options: The float was too small to count
No separate cash box, no records, no counting: honesty and theft produce identical evidence — none

accounting.grade10.internal-control-basi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.internal-control-basi.question: The three-learner version (money, stock and recording split; box counted by two) mainly demonstrates:
options: Division of duties with independent checking

accounting.grade10.internal-control-basi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.internal-control-basi.question: The lesson says a good control system PROTECTS honest workers because:
options: It hides small mistakes from managers
When the box matches the notebook, their honesty is provable instead of merely hoped
It prevents them being given difficult duties
It guarantees nobody is ever suspected

accounting.grade10.internal-control-basi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.internal-control-basi.question: 'Who sets the example?' is the plain version of which component?

accounting.grade10.internal-control-basi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.internal-control-basi.question: A teacher who borrows from the cash box 'till Monday' teaches learners that:
options: The box is borrowable — the example at the top has made the rules unreal
The box needs a better lock

accounting.grade10.internal-control-basi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.internal-control-basi.question: The treasurer doing a surprise count at break answers which plain question?
options: Who checks that the rules still happen?
Does everyone know what is happening?

accounting.grade10.internal-control-basi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.internal-control-basi.question: The nephew running the spaza alone and paying his own wages from the tin is primarily a failure of:
options: Division of duties and documentation — one person, all roles, self-served wages from unrecorded cash

accounting.grade10.internal-control-basi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.internal-control-basi.question: The storeroom standing open on delivery days is best fixed by:
options: Buying more stock so losses matter less
Keeping it locked, with one named person receiving deliveries and counting them against the delivery note

accounting.grade10.internal-control-basi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.internal-control-basi.question: Unnumbered receipts written 'when the customer asks' are dangerous because:
options: A missing receipt is invisible, so recorded income becomes whatever happened to be written down

accounting.grade10.liquidity-solvency-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.liquidity-solvency-an.question: The current ratio for the year is:
options: 22 700 : 3 800 — about 6 : 1: six rand turning to cash for every rand knocking

accounting.grade10.liquidity-solvency-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.liquidity-solvency-an.question: The acid-test ratio strips out inventories because:
options: Stock must first find a buyer, at full price, in time — it is the least cash-like current asset

accounting.grade10.liquidity-solvency-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.liquidity-solvency-an.question: The guideline norms are:
options: Around 2 : 1 (current) and 1 : 1 (acid test) — held as GUIDES, not laws
There are no guidelines at Grade 10

accounting.grade10.liquidity-solvency-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.liquidity-solvency-an.question: A very high current ratio can be criticised because:
options: It means the business is insolvent
Excess liquidity is idle money — cash sleeping instead of earning the mark-up or paying down the 12% loan

accounting.grade10.liquidity-solvency-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.liquidity-solvency-an.question: The solvency ratio is:

accounting.grade10.liquidity-solvency-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.liquidity-solvency-an.question: The threshold that separates solvent from insolvent is:
options: 1 : 1 — below it, debts exceed assets and trading has legal consequences

accounting.grade10.liquidity-solvency-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.liquidity-solvency-an.question: "Solvent but illiquid" describes:
options: Debts exceeding assets with plenty of cash
A business with no debts at all
Rich in equipment yet unable to pay Friday's wages — the whole game strong, the sprint failing
A failed acid test and a failed solvency test

accounting.grade10.liquidity-solvency-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.liquidity-solvency-an.question: Solvency underpins the going concern assumption because:
options: Carrying assets at useful values presumes a future — a failing ratio questions the whole basis of the statements

accounting.grade10.liquidity-solvency-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.liquidity-solvency-an.question: Return on owner's equity uses the AVERAGE equity because:
options: The equity changed during the year — profit joining, drawings leaving — so the fair base is the mean of opening and closing
The formula sheet prints it that way without reason

accounting.grade10.liquidity-solvency-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.liquidity-solvency-an.question: The calculation for the year is:
options: 7 900 / 21 950 × 100 ≈ 36% — profit over the average of 20 000 and 23 900

accounting.grade10.liquidity-solvency-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.liquidity-solvency-an.question: The return gains meaning when compared against:
options: The safe alternative — a fixed deposit at around 8% — which the business must beat COMFORTABLY

accounting.grade10.liquidity-solvency-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.liquidity-solvency-an.question: A business returning barely more than the bank's rate is a warning because:
options: The owner carries risk and does the work — a return equal to the safe rate leaves the risk unpaid

accounting.grade10.liquidity-solvency-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.liquidity-solvency-an.question: The format habit for these answers is:
options: Ratios AS ratios (6 : 1) and percentages as percentages — format itself carries marks

accounting.grade10.liquidity-solvency-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.liquidity-solvency-an.question: The classic error in return on equity is:
options: Using the UNAVERAGED equity — opening or closing alone — instead of the mean

accounting.grade10.liquidity-solvency-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.liquidity-solvency-an.question: "Both directions score" in liquidity comments means:
options: Too LOW is dangerous (bills at risk) and too HIGH can be idle resources — the mature answer can argue either

accounting.grade10.liquidity-solvency-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.liquidity-solvency-an.question: Every ratio is best learned as:
options: A formula to memorise despite the sheet
A DECISION quantified — the bank deciding to lend, the owner deciding to stay, the supplier deciding to give credit

accounting.grade10.liquidity-solvency-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.liquidity-solvency-an.question: The month-end test asks:
options: Can what's coming in cover what's knocking at the door?
Did the year make a profit?

accounting.grade10.liquidity-solvency-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.liquidity-solvency-an.question: "I can't pay the landlord in rice" is the household version of:
options: The acid test — re-asking the question with the hard-to-sell stock stripped out

accounting.grade10.liquidity-solvency-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.liquidity-solvency-an.question: R15 000 sleeping under the mattress while the loan charges 12% shows:
options: Safety quietly becoming waste — enough should stay ready, the rest should work

accounting.grade10.liquidity-solvency-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.liquidity-solvency-an.question: The whole-race count for the shop gives:
options: R38 900 owned against R15 000 owed — R2,60 for every rand owed: everyone could be paid

accounting.grade10.liquidity-solvency-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.liquidity-solvency-an.question: The sprint and the whole race can disagree, as when:
options: A family owns a valuable house yet misses Friday's rent money — solvent, but illiquid

accounting.grade10.liquidity-solvency-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.liquidity-solvency-an.question: Trading while insolvent means:
options: Spending money that already belongs to the creditors — which is why the bank checks this number first
Having no stock on the shelves

accounting.grade10.liquidity-solvency-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.liquidity-solvency-an.question: The bank's order of questions is:
options: Could you pay AT ALL (solvency) before will you pay ON TIME (liquidity)

accounting.grade10.liquidity-solvency-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.liquidity-solvency-an.question: The owner's return computes as:
options: About 36% — R7 900 earned on an average stake of R21 950

accounting.grade10.liquidity-solvency-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.liquidity-solvency-an.question: The bank's 8% and the shop's 36% differ in nature because:
options: The 8% is PROMISED; the 36% was EARNED — with labour, worry and risk, and no guarantee of repeating
The shop's figure includes the loan
Percentages from banks are calculated differently

accounting.grade10.liquidity-solvency-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.liquidity-solvency-an.question: A shop returning 9% against a safe 8% deserves the advice:
options: RETHINK — a year of work and full risk for one extra rand per hundred leaves the risk unpaid

accounting.grade10.liquidity-solvency-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.liquidity-solvency-an.question: This one ratio "joins the two statements" because:
options: The formula sheet lists it twice
Profit comes from the story page and the owner's stake from the photograph — one fraction answering a life decision

accounting.grade10.manufacturing-concept.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.manufacturing-concept.question: The first sorting question for any production cost is:
options: Can this cost be traced to ONE SPECIFIC unit?
Is this cost large or small?
Was this cost paid in cash?

accounting.grade10.manufacturing-concept.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.manufacturing-concept.question: The fabric (R40 per shirt) and the machinist (R25 per shirt) are:
options: Direct materials and direct labour — each traceable to the specific shirt it made

accounting.grade10.manufacturing-concept.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.manufacturing-concept.question: Thread, needles, the supervisor, workshop rent and machine depreciation gather under:
options: FACTORY OVERHEADS — real production costs, spread over all units, traceable to none

accounting.grade10.manufacturing-concept.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.manufacturing-concept.question: The shop's sales assistant's wage is:
options: OUTSIDE the factory fence — a selling cost, not a production cost at all

accounting.grade10.manufacturing-concept.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.manufacturing-concept.question: Prime cost for the month is:
options: R26 000 — direct materials R16 000 plus direct labour R10 000

accounting.grade10.manufacturing-concept.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.manufacturing-concept.question: Total cost of production is:
options: Prime cost R26 000 plus factory overheads R6 000 = R32 000

accounting.grade10.manufacturing-concept.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.manufacturing-concept.question: The unit cost of a shirt is:
options: R80 — total production cost R32 000 over 400 units

accounting.grade10.manufacturing-concept.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.manufacturing-concept.question: Work-in-progress is:
options: Half-made units — no longer raw material, not yet finished goods — their cost sitting in the factory until completion

accounting.grade10.manufacturing-concept.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.manufacturing-concept.question: Variable costs behave so that:
options: The TOTAL moves in step with output, while the PER-UNIT amount stays constant (R65 per shirt)
The total stays constant while per-unit falls
Both total and per-unit stay constant

accounting.grade10.manufacturing-concept.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.manufacturing-concept.question: Fixed costs behave so that:
options: The TOTAL stands still within the month, while the PER-UNIT share FALLS as output rises
They are always the largest costs

accounting.grade10.manufacturing-concept.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.manufacturing-concept.question: At 500 shirts the unit cost falls from R80 to R77 because:
options: The machinist took a pay cut
The same R6 000 of fixed overheads spread over more units — R12 each instead of R15

accounting.grade10.manufacturing-concept.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.manufacturing-concept.question: A quiet month at 200 shirts pushes the unit cost to R95, warning that:
options: Fixed costs make quiet months hurt more than they seem — R30 of rent-and-standing costs lands on each unit

accounting.grade10.manufacturing-concept.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.manufacturing-concept.question: Every cost carries BOTH labels, as in:
options: Fabric: direct AND variable; workshop rent: overhead AND fixed

accounting.grade10.manufacturing-concept.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.manufacturing-concept.question: The cost statement's fixed order is:
options: Unit cost, then overheads, then prime
Direct materials + direct labour = prime cost; + factory overheads = total cost of production; ÷ units = unit cost
Any order, provided the total is right

accounting.grade10.manufacturing-concept.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.manufacturing-concept.question: The what-if error the marker hunts is:
options: SCALING THE FIXED COSTS with volume — multiplying rent because output rose contradicts fixed's definition

accounting.grade10.manufacturing-concept.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.manufacturing-concept.question: At 500 shirts the what-if computes:
options: Prime R32 500 + overheads R7 500 = R40 000; unit R80
Prime R26 000 + overheads R6 000 = R32 000; unit R64
Prime R32 500 + overheads R6 500 = R39 000; unit R78
Prime R32 500 (20 000 + 12 500) + overheads R6 000 = R38 500; unit R77

accounting.grade10.manufacturing-concept.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.manufacturing-concept.question: In the wedding order, the flour and oil are:
options: Direct material — the aunt can say to the cent what each vetkoek carries

accounting.grade10.manufacturing-concept.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.manufacturing-concept.question: The gas bottle, pot-wear and the pot-watcher are:
options: The overheads — costs of KEEPING THE KITCHEN COOKING, serving all units and none in particular

accounting.grade10.manufacturing-concept.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.manufacturing-concept.question: The taxi fare to deliver the order is:
options: Outside the kitchen fence — delivering is not making

accounting.grade10.manufacturing-concept.subject: accounting
accounting.grade10.manufacturing-concept.question: The order's three layers compute:
options: Prime R1 200 (R3 × 400); + overheads R600 = R1 800; ÷ 400 = R4,50 per vetkoek
Prime R600; + overheads R1 200 = R1 800; ÷ 400 = R4,50
Prime R1 200; + overheads R600 = R1 800; ÷ 200 = R9
Prime R1 800; ÷ 400 = R4,50 with no overheads
