accounting.grade11.cash-budgets-and-proj.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.cash-budgets-and-proj.question: With credit sales of R150 000 in February and 50% settling in the following month less 5% discount, March collects from February:
options: R71 250 — 50% of R150 000, less the 5% discount

accounting.grade11.cash-budgets-and-proj.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.cash-budgets-and-proj.question: March's collections from debtors draw on:
options: THREE different months' credit sales — February, January and December

accounting.grade11.cash-budgets-and-proj.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.cash-budgets-and-proj.question: The settlement discount is applied:
options: To the whole month's credit sales
To all collections in the month
ONLY to the portion that earns it — the group settling in the first month

accounting.grade11.cash-budgets-and-proj.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.cash-budgets-and-proj.question: The 5% of credit sales never collected:
options: Reduces the cash budget's receipts line
Appears as a payment in the cash budget
Is added to next month's collections
Never appears in the cash budget — it appears in the projected income statement as bad debts

accounting.grade11.cash-budgets-and-proj.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.cash-budgets-and-proj.question: The cash budget's arithmetic chain runs:
options: Receipts less payments = surplus or deficit; plus opening balance = closing balance, which becomes next month's opening
Sales less cost of sales = gross profit
Opening stock plus purchases less closing stock

accounting.grade11.cash-budgets-and-proj.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.cash-budgets-and-proj.question: In the projected income statement, sales are recorded:
options: In FULL — cash and credit alike — in the month of sale

accounting.grade11.cash-budgets-and-proj.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.cash-budgets-and-proj.question: A forecast closing bank balance that turns negative is:
options: Impossible if the business is profitable
A forecast OVERDRAFT — the single most useful warning a business can receive
A reason to stop trading immediately

accounting.grade11.cash-budgets-and-proj.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.cash-budgets-and-proj.question: A good answer to "how can a business forecast profit and a cash deficit in the same month?" must:
options: Say one is cash and one is profit
State that the budget is wrong
NAME the timing difference and the specific items causing it — credit sales collected later, stock paid earlier, an asset bought for cash

accounting.grade11.cash-budgets-and-proj.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.cash-budgets-and-proj.question: A variance is stated properly by giving:
options: The item, both figures, the difference in rand and percentage, and whether it is favourable or unfavourable
The budgeted figure and nothing else

accounting.grade11.cash-budgets-and-proj.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.cash-budgets-and-proj.question: A FAVOURABLE expense variance is not automatically good news because:
options: Advertising far below budget may explain the sales shortfall beside it, and maintenance not done becomes next year's breakdown
It means the budget was too low

accounting.grade11.cash-budgets-and-proj.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.cash-budgets-and-proj.question: Presenting a projected income statement known to be unachievable, to obtain a loan, is:
options: MISREPRESENTATION — a fraud on the lender

accounting.grade11.cash-budgets-and-proj.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.cash-budgets-and-proj.question: What makes a budget a control rather than a wish is:
options: The COMPARISON afterwards — actual against budget every month, with material variances explained

accounting.grade11.cash-budgets-and-proj.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.cash-budgets-and-proj.question: The cousin who did R8 000 of hair but holds R4 000 shows that:
options: Earning well and having money are two different, both-honest answers about the same month

accounting.grade11.cash-budgets-and-proj.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.cash-budgets-and-proj.question: Drawings, buying a bakkie and repaying a loan appear:
options: In the CASH BUDGET — they move money even though they are not profit or loss items

accounting.grade11.cash-budgets-and-proj.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.cash-budgets-and-proj.question: Depreciation goes only in the profit forecast because:
options: It is too small to budget
The bakkie is wearing out this month, but no rand left the account for that wearing
It is a form of drawings

accounting.grade11.cash-budgets-and-proj.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.cash-budgets-and-proj.question: Money arriving in March comes from:
options: Half of February's credit sales, thirty percent of January's, fifteen percent of December's — three months landing in one
An equal share of every month

accounting.grade11.cash-budgets-and-proj.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.cash-budgets-and-proj.question: With December, January and February credit sales of R108 000, R120 000 and R150 000, March's collection from debtors is:

accounting.grade11.cash-budgets-and-proj.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.cash-budgets-and-proj.question: The grid — sales down the side, arrival months across — exists because:
options: Three different months' sales land in one month's bank account, and holding that in your head crosses lines

accounting.grade11.cash-budgets-and-proj.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.cash-budgets-and-proj.question: You cannot budget to receive the five percent that never comes because:
options: It is collected the following year
It is paid by the supplier
You cannot budget to receive money you will never get — it belongs in the profit forecast as bad debts

accounting.grade11.cash-budgets-and-proj.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.cash-budgets-and-proj.question: The shop's best-ever month can empty its bank account because:
options: Stock was paid for last month, wages went out this month, a bakkie was bought for cash, and the credit customers have not paid yet

accounting.grade11.cash-budgets-and-proj.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.cash-budgets-and-proj.question: "Profit tells you whether the business deserves to survive; cash tells you..."
options: Whether it WILL — a business can survive a bad profit month but not a payday with an empty account

accounting.grade11.cash-budgets-and-proj.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.cash-budgets-and-proj.question: Seeing the shortfall in advance gives the owner cheap options such as:
options: Delaying the bakkie, arranging an overdraft calmly, tightening collection terms, or negotiating longer supplier payment

accounting.grade11.cash-budgets-and-proj.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.cash-budgets-and-proj.question: Budgets get "dressed up" when:
options: Sales forecasts are inflated to obtain finance, or expenses padded to hide later overspending

accounting.grade11.creditors-reconciliat.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.creditors-reconciliat.question: A supplier's monthly statement is an extract from:
options: The supplier's own DEBTORS ledger — to the supplier, we are a debtor

accounting.grade11.creditors-reconciliat.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.creditors-reconciliat.question: What makes the creditors reconciliation different in principle from the bank reconciliation?
options: The outsider — another ordinary business with an ordinary bookkeeper — may itself be wrong
No entries are ever made in our books
It is done annually rather than monthly

accounting.grade11.creditors-reconciliat.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.creditors-reconciliat.question: The discipline the lesson sets for reading a supplier's statement is:
options: Adjust our books to match it exactly
Read it as a claim to be tested, not an instruction to be obeyed
File it until the auditor asks

accounting.grade11.creditors-reconciliat.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.creditors-reconciliat.question: An invoice dated 26 February that reaches our office on 3 March is an example of:
options: A timing difference that becomes our omission — the goods were received before year end

accounting.grade11.creditors-reconciliat.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.creditors-reconciliat.question: Invoice 2214 for R6 400, for boards delivered on 26 February but invoiced to us in March, is recorded as:
options: Debit Trading stock, credit Creditors control
Debit Creditors control, credit Trading stock
Debit Interest expense, credit Creditors control
Nothing — it belongs on the reconciliation statement

accounting.grade11.creditors-reconciliat.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.creditors-reconciliat.question: Credit note 118 for R3 600 was entered as R2 340. The correction of R1 260 is:
options: Debit Trading stock, credit Creditors control
Debit Creditors control, credit Trading stock — we reduced the debt by too little
Debit Discount received, credit Creditors control
No entry — the supplier will fix it

accounting.grade11.creditors-reconciliat.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.creditors-reconciliat.question: R1 850 of ironmongery charged to us but delivered to another customer must be:
options: Left out of our books entirely and shown on the reconciliation statement, with the supplier queried
Deducted from our next payment without telling anyone

accounting.grade11.creditors-reconciliat.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.creditors-reconciliat.question: Starting at R40 440 and processing the corrections (+R6 400, −R1 260, +R620, −R800), the corrected creditors ledger balance is:

accounting.grade11.creditors-reconciliat.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.creditors-reconciliat.question: The Creditors Reconciliation Statement runs:
options: From the balance per the statement received to the balance per our corrected creditors ledger account
From the Creditors Control account to the creditors list
From the bank statement to the Bank account
From the trial balance to the ledger

accounting.grade11.creditors-reconciliat.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.creditors-reconciliat.question: Statement balance R59 250, less payment in transit R12 000, less R1 850 invoiced in error, gives:

accounting.grade11.creditors-reconciliat.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.creditors-reconciliat.question: Invoice 2214, once recorded in our own books, appears on the reconciliation statement:
options: As an addition to the statement balance
As a deduction from the statement balance
Not at all — the reconciliation statement carries only what remains for the SUPPLIER to do

accounting.grade11.creditors-reconciliat.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.creditors-reconciliat.question: How does this reconciliation differ from the Grade 10 control-account reconciliation?
options: It uses percentages instead of rands
It is done only at year end
It covers all creditors at once
Control-against-list is an INTERNAL check; statement-against-ledger-account is EXTERNAL, one supplier at a time

accounting.grade11.creditors-reconciliat.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.creditors-reconciliat.question: Journalising the supplier's R1 850 error in our books would mean:
options: Quietly paying for goods another business received
Nothing, since the totals still agree

accounting.grade11.creditors-reconciliat.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.creditors-reconciliat.question: Reversing the direction of the understated credit note puts the answer out by:

accounting.grade11.creditors-reconciliat.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.creditors-reconciliat.question: Interest of R620 charged by the supplier on the overdue account should be:
options: Ignored, because we never agreed to it
Recorded — debit Interest expense, credit Creditors control — and then queried if it looks wrong

accounting.grade11.creditors-reconciliat.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.creditors-reconciliat.question: Which practice best protects a business against supplier overcharging?
options: Paying every statement in full on the day it arrives
Letting the person who authorises payments also do the reconciliation
Carrying old differences forward until they disappear
Reconciling every statement in the month it arrives and paying from our own corrected ledger account

accounting.grade11.creditors-reconciliat.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.creditors-reconciliat.question: The lesson's golden rule about a supplier's bill is:
options: It is a claim, not a command
It should be paid before it is read

accounting.grade11.creditors-reconciliat.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.creditors-reconciliat.question: The "twist" that makes this different from the bank reconciliation is that:
options: The wholesaler's clerk is a person, and people put one customer's delivery on another customer's account

accounting.grade11.creditors-reconciliat.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.creditors-reconciliat.question: The spaza owner's correct response to a bill of R59 250 against an exercise book showing R40 440 is to:
options: Insist on the exercise book's figure
Sit down with both records and go line by line until every difference is understood

accounting.grade11.creditors-reconciliat.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.creditors-reconciliat.question: The boards delivered on the twenty-sixth with the invoice arriving in March mean:
options: Your book is short — you have the goods, so add R6 400
Their book is wrong — deduct R6 400 from the statement

accounting.grade11.creditors-reconciliat.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.creditors-reconciliat.question: The R800 discount allowed for early payment, never written down, means:
options: Your balance is too low; add R800
Your balance is too high; take R800 off
The supplier owes you R800 in cash
It belongs on the reconciliation statement

accounting.grade11.creditors-reconciliat.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.creditors-reconciliat.question: Which two items are "not your problem" and change nothing in your book?
options: The invoice and the credit note
The R1 850 invoiced in error and the R12 000 transfer not yet processed
The credit note and the R12 000 transfer

accounting.grade11.creditors-reconciliat.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.creditors-reconciliat.question: The single question to ask about every difference is:
options: Which month does it belong to?
Is it a debit or a credit?

accounting.grade11.creditors-reconciliat.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.creditors-reconciliat.question: Paying the R59 250 statement instead of the reconciled R45 400 would mean:
options: Handing a stranger almost fourteen thousand rand you did not owe
Nothing — the difference washes out later

accounting.grade11.creditors-reconciliat.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.creditors-reconciliat.question: The question that steers every line of the bridge is:
options: What does the OTHER side still have to do to this balance?
Is it an asset or a liability?

accounting.grade11.creditors-reconciliat.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.creditors-reconciliat.question: Why can nobody inside a small business catch a supplier overcharging?
options: Because the control account hides it
Because nobody inside the business sees the supplier's books — except through this statement
Because overcharging is illegal and therefore rare

accounting.grade11.creditors-reconciliat.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.creditors-reconciliat.question: The lesson's closing warning is that businesses usually:
options: Lose money mainly through bank charges
Bleed slowly from bills nobody checked

accounting.grade11.disposal-of-fixed-ass.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.disposal-of-fixed-ass.question: The asset disposal account gathers:
options: The asset's COST, its accumulated depreciation, and the proceeds — weighed against each other in one place
The asset's market value and insurance value

accounting.grade11.disposal-of-fixed-ass.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.disposal-of-fixed-ass.question: Posting the proceeds directly against the asset's cost is wrong because:
options: It is slower than using a disposal account
Selling price and cost are different amounts — the difference is a profit or loss belonging on the income statement, and both figures get corrupted
Proceeds belong in the capital account

accounting.grade11.disposal-of-fixed-ass.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.disposal-of-fixed-ass.question: If the credits in the disposal account exceed the debits, the result is:
options: A PROFIT on disposal — the asset sold for more than its carrying value

accounting.grade11.disposal-of-fixed-ass.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.disposal-of-fixed-ass.question: A profit or loss on disposal really represents:
options: A cash gain to the owner
An error in the original purchase price
A CORRECTION — the accumulated verdict on every depreciation estimate made across the asset's life

accounting.grade11.disposal-of-fixed-ass.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.disposal-of-fixed-ass.question: Step one of every disposal is:
options: Bring DEPRECIATION UP TO DATE to the date of sale — the most commonly forgotten step and the one carrying the most marks

accounting.grade11.disposal-of-fixed-ass.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.disposal-of-fixed-ass.question: A vehicle cost R180 000, depreciated 20% on diminishing balance, sold six months into year three. The part-year depreciation is:
options: R11 520 — 20% of the R115 200 carrying value, for six of twelve months

accounting.grade11.disposal-of-fixed-ass.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.disposal-of-fixed-ass.question: Transferring the cost to the disposal account is recorded as:
options: Debit the asset account, credit Asset Disposal
DEBIT Asset Disposal, CREDIT the asset account with the full original cost
Debit Accumulated Depreciation, credit the asset account

accounting.grade11.disposal-of-fixed-ass.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.disposal-of-fixed-ass.question: With cost R180 000, accumulated depreciation R76 320 and proceeds R95 000, the result is:
options: A LOSS of R8 680 — proceeds R95 000 against a carrying value of R103 680

accounting.grade11.disposal-of-fixed-ass.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.disposal-of-fixed-ass.question: An asset sold on the FIRST day of the financial year:
options: Needs NO additional depreciation — the accumulated figure is simply the balance brought forward

accounting.grade11.disposal-of-fixed-ass.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.disposal-of-fixed-ass.question: An asset sold on credit creates:
options: A trade debtor recorded in Debtors Control
A SUNDRY or other debtor — the business does not trade in vehicles, so it belongs under other receivables

accounting.grade11.disposal-of-fixed-ass.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.disposal-of-fixed-ass.question: Old bakkie traded in at R95 000 against a new one priced at R250 000, with R155 000 paid in cash. The new asset is recorded at:
options: R250 000 — the full cost; the trade-in was real value forming part of the payment

accounting.grade11.disposal-of-fixed-ass.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.disposal-of-fixed-ass.question: An owner taking a vehicle worth R95 000 but recording drawings of R20 000 has:
options: Understated their withdrawals and overstated the business's equity — a misstatement an auditor traces against carrying value and market evidence

accounting.grade11.disposal-of-fixed-ass.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.disposal-of-fixed-ass.question: After a disposal, the asset register's totals:
options: Must still agree with the ledger's asset and accumulated depreciation balances — a mismatch signals a control failure
Are updated only at year end

accounting.grade11.disposal-of-fixed-ass.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.disposal-of-fixed-ass.question: Requiring quotes or a valuation before disposal exists to:
options: Show the price was REASONABLE rather than a favour to a friend or relative — the point where nepotism enters

accounting.grade11.disposal-of-fixed-ass.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.disposal-of-fixed-ass.question: Segregation of duties at disposal means:
options: Assets are sold only for cash
The person who AUTHORISES the disposal should not be the person who receives the money or updates the records
One person handles the whole transaction for accountability

accounting.grade11.disposal-of-fixed-ass.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.disposal-of-fixed-ass.question: The classic disposal fraud is:
options: Recording a trade-in at full cost
Selling an asset at a profit
Selling the asset, pocketing the proceeds, and writing it off as scrapped — defeated by independent authorisation plus a register reconciled to the ledger

accounting.grade11.disposal-of-fixed-ass.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.disposal-of-fixed-ass.question: The books' answer to "what is the bakkie worth?" is:
options: The carrying value — cost minus everything written off for wear, R103 680

accounting.grade11.disposal-of-fixed-ass.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.disposal-of-fixed-ass.question: The temporary "desk" opened for the transaction:
options: Is the ASSET DISPOSAL account — opened for one deal, weighed, and cleared away the same day

accounting.grade11.disposal-of-fixed-ass.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.disposal-of-fixed-ass.question: The R8 680 loss means:
options: The business traded badly this year
The books' depreciation guess was slightly off — reality checked the estimate on the day of sale

accounting.grade11.disposal-of-fixed-ass.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.disposal-of-fixed-ass.question: The move everybody forgets is:
options: CATCH UP THE WEAR — the months driven in the final year, written off before anything else
Putting the cost on the desk

accounting.grade11.disposal-of-fixed-ass.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.disposal-of-fixed-ass.question: The amount of wear placed on the desk is:
options: R76 320 — everything ever written off, including the caught-up R11 520

accounting.grade11.disposal-of-fixed-ass.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.disposal-of-fixed-ass.question: The five-second check that catches nearly every mistake is:
options: Comparing what the books said it was worth against what was actually received — the gap must equal your answer

accounting.grade11.disposal-of-fixed-ass.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.disposal-of-fixed-ass.question: If the long method and the quick check disagree, the usual culprit is:
options: An error in the accumulated total brought forward
The forgotten part-year wear from move one

accounting.grade11.disposal-of-fixed-ass.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.disposal-of-fixed-ass.question: The buyer of the bakkie from a building-materials business is:
options: A once-off debtor, filed separately from customers who buy stock
A trade debtor in Debtors Control

accounting.grade11.disposal-of-fixed-ass.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.disposal-of-fixed-ass.question: Recording the new bakkie at the R155 000 cash handed over:
options: Is correct, since that is what left the bank
UNDERSTATES the asset by R95 000 — and makes every depreciation charge for the next five years wrong too

accounting.grade11.disposal-of-fixed-ass.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.disposal-of-fixed-ass.question: When the owner keeps the bakkie for the family, the entry is:
options: A cash sale at market value
DRAWINGS at an honest value — the owner helping himself to business property

accounting.grade11.disposal-of-fixed-ass.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.disposal-of-fixed-ass.question: An asset scrapped or given away produces:
options: A profit equal to the accumulated depreciation
A loss equal to the WHOLE remaining book value, since nothing was received

accounting.grade11.final-accounts-and-th.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.final-accounts-and-th.question: The trading account of Molefe and de Waal Traders shows sales of R2 460 000 and cost of sales of R1 640 000. Gross profit is:
options: R820 000 — exactly 50 percent on cost, matching the mark-up policy

accounting.grade11.final-accounts-and-th.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.final-accounts-and-th.question: The profit and loss account gathers, on its credit side:
options: Gross profit R820 000 plus operating incomes of R60 000

accounting.grade11.final-accounts-and-th.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.final-accounts-and-th.question: With operating expenses of R441 000 and interest on loan of R18 000 against R880 000 of credits, net profit is:

accounting.grade11.final-accounts-and-th.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.final-accounts-and-th.question: In a partnership, net profit closes off to:
options: The appropriation account, where the agreement divides it

accounting.grade11.final-accounts-and-th.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.final-accounts-and-th.question: The order in which the agreement is executed in the appropriation account is:
options: Interest on capital, then salaries and bonus, then the remaining profit in the ratio four to three
Whatever order the partners prefer each year

accounting.grade11.final-accounts-and-th.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.final-accounts-and-th.question: After appropriating R337 000 of the R421 000 net profit, the remaining R84 000 is shared four to three, giving:
options: R48 000 to Molefe and R36 000 to de Waal
R63 000 to Molefe and R21 000 to de Waal
R36 000 to Molefe and R48 000 to de Waal

accounting.grade11.final-accounts-and-th.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.final-accounts-and-th.question: De Waal's total earnings for the year — interest R27 000, salary R144 000, bonus R10 000, profit share R36 000 — come to:

accounting.grade11.final-accounts-and-th.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.final-accounts-and-th.question: A partner's salary belongs in:
options: Operating expenses in the profit and loss account
The appropriation account — it is a distribution of profit, never an expense

accounting.grade11.final-accounts-and-th.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.final-accounts-and-th.question: Molefe's current account: opening credit R8 200, earnings R204 000, drawings R176 000. The closing balance is:
options: R36 200 credit — the business owes Molefe R36 200

accounting.grade11.final-accounts-and-th.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.final-accounts-and-th.question: De Waal's current account opens with R5 400 on the debit side. This means:
options: Last year he drew more than he earned, so he owed the business R5 400
His capital was reduced by R5 400
An error was made last year

accounting.grade11.final-accounts-and-th.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.final-accounts-and-th.question: De Waal's closing balance, after credits of R217 000 against the old R5 400 plus drawings of R182 000, is:

accounting.grade11.final-accounts-and-th.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.final-accounts-and-th.question: Which item never appears in a current account?
options: A capital contribution — that belongs in the fixed capital account

accounting.grade11.final-accounts-and-th.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.final-accounts-and-th.question: Molefe takes trading stock of R3 000 for personal use. The effects are:
options: Assets down R3 000; equity down R3 000 through drawings at cost; liabilities unchanged
Assets up R3 000; equity up R3 000
Assets down R3 000; liabilities down R3 000
Equity down R3 000; liabilities up R3 000

accounting.grade11.final-accounts-and-th.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.final-accounts-and-th.question: Interest on capital allowed to a partner changes total equity by:
options: A decrease equal to the interest
Nothing — it redistributes equity from the profit pool to the partner's current account claim
An increase equal to the interest

accounting.grade11.final-accounts-and-th.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.final-accounts-and-th.question: Interest of R18 000 capitalised on the loan affects the equation as:
options: Assets down R18 000, liabilities down R18 000
Assets up R18 000, equity up R18 000
Liabilities up R18 000, equity down R18 000, assets untouched
No effect anywhere, since no cash moved

accounting.grade11.final-accounts-and-th.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.final-accounts-and-th.question: The reliable method for equation analysis is:
options: Guess the effects from the story
Write the double entry first, classify each account, then read the effects off the debits and credits

accounting.grade11.final-accounts-and-th.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.final-accounts-and-th.question: The three ladles serve the profit pot in the order:
options: Interest for the money that waited, salaries and bonus for the hands that worked, then the leftovers split for risk
Leftovers first, then interest, then salaries
Equal shares to each partner, three times

accounting.grade11.final-accounts-and-th.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.final-accounts-and-th.question: Paying bigger partner salaries changes the size of the profit pot by:
options: Nothing — the ladles serve profit after it is measured; they never shrink it
Shrinking it only if paid in cash

accounting.grade11.final-accounts-and-th.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.final-accounts-and-th.question: The recipe that ends the argument at the pot is:
options: The partnership agreement, written before the cooking started

accounting.grade11.final-accounts-and-th.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.final-accounts-and-th.question: The servings from the appropriation account land on:
options: Each partner's tab — the current account — not in an envelope of cash
The capital account on the wall

accounting.grade11.final-accounts-and-th.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.final-accounts-and-th.question: A tab that goes red during a year tells you:

options: Sits UNTOUCHED at its opening balance — nobody knows the stock figure between counts

accounting.grade11.perpetual-and-periodi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.perpetual-and-periodi.question: The design difference in one sentence:
options: Both systems record cost at every movement
The periodic system is more accurate at all times
Perpetual records COST AT EVERY MOVEMENT; periodic records PURCHASES and works cost of sales out backwards at period end

accounting.grade11.perpetual-and-periodi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.perpetual-and-periodi.question: Sales are R450 000 with a mark-up of 50% ON COST. Cost of sales is:

accounting.grade11.perpetual-and-periodi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.perpetual-and-periodi.question: The periodic formula runs:
options: Sales less gross profit less closing stock
Opening stock + purchases + carriage on purchases − purchases returns − drawings of stock = goods available for sale; less closing stock = cost of sales

accounting.grade11.perpetual-and-periodi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.perpetual-and-periodi.question: Carriage on purchases is included, but carriage OUTWARD is excluded, because:
options: Carriage outward is never paid in cash
Freight inward is part of the cost of getting stock onto the shelf; delivering to customers is a SELLING expense
Carriage outward belongs in opening stock

accounting.grade11.perpetual-and-periodi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.perpetual-and-periodi.question: The periodic system's silent flaw is that:
options: Stock lost to theft, breakage or error is INSIDE cost of sales — the formula assumes everything not counted was sold, so losses are never named

accounting.grade11.perpetual-and-periodi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.perpetual-and-periodi.question: The perpetual system's decisive advantage is that:
options: The account's claim can be TESTED against a physical count, so losses are identified and sized as a deficit
It always shows a higher profit

accounting.grade11.perpetual-and-periodi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.perpetual-and-periodi.question: The periodic system's serious disadvantage is:
options: NO CONTROL — losses are invisible, absorbed silently into cost of sales, so theft can run unnoticed for a year
It cannot calculate gross profit at all

accounting.grade11.perpetual-and-periodi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.perpetual-and-periodi.question: High-value, individually identifiable items (vehicles, appliances, jewellery) argue for:
options: The PERPETUAL system — the value of knowing and the cost of losing are both high, and the items are few enough to record

accounting.grade11.perpetual-and-periodi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.perpetual-and-periodi.question: The technology argument that distinguishes a strong comparison answer:
options: Computers made the periodic system standard
Barcodes removed the need for stocktakes
Technology has no bearing on the choice
Point-of-sale systems that scan and post cost automatically have made perpetual practical even for supermarkets — periodic now survives mainly where no such system exists

accounting.grade11.perpetual-and-periodi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.perpetual-and-periodi.question: Physical stock controls include:
options: A locked, restricted storeroom with named responsibility; goods checked against order and delivery note before signature; separation of ordering, receiving, recording and paying
Allowing all staff storeroom access for efficiency

accounting.grade11.perpetual-and-periodi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.perpetual-and-periodi.question: Stocktakes should be conducted by:
options: The storeroom manager alone, who knows the stock best
People INDEPENDENT of the storeroom, with every difference investigated rather than merely recorded
The external auditor only, once every five years
Whoever is available on the day

accounting.grade11.perpetual-and-periodi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.perpetual-and-periodi.question: Overstating the closing stock figure has the effect of:
options: Raising cost of sales and lowering profit
LOWERING cost of sales, so gross and net profit RISE — flattering results and shifting the loss into the following year

accounting.grade11.perpetual-and-periodi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.perpetual-and-periodi.question: An unexplained gap between the achieved gross profit percentage and the policy mark-up is:
options: Proof of an arithmetic error only
Often the first fingerprint of stock loss — which is why the internal auditor compares them

accounting.grade11.perpetual-and-periodi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.perpetual-and-periodi.question: The notebook owner writes down, for every loaf sold:
options: The R18 taken AND that a loaf costing R13 left the shelf
Only the delivery it came from

accounting.grade11.perpetual-and-periodi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.perpetual-and-periodi.question: The counting owner's year-end sum is:
options: What I sold, times my mark-up
Everything I started with, plus everything I bought, minus what's still standing — that must be what I sold

accounting.grade11.perpetual-and-periodi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.perpetual-and-periodi.question: The assumption the counting owner is making is that:
options: Everything not on his shelf was SOLD — so a case stolen in June is quietly called a sale

accounting.grade11.perpetual-and-periodi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.perpetual-and-periodi.question: Opening R80 000, purchases R520 000, carriage in R18 000, returns R12 000, drawings of stock R6 000. Goods available for sale:

accounting.grade11.perpetual-and-periodi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.perpetual-and-periodi.question: With closing stock counted at R95 000, cost of sales is:

accounting.grade11.perpetual-and-periodi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.perpetual-and-periodi.question: Stock the owner took home for his family is subtracted because:
options: It was returned to the supplier
It is DRAWINGS, not a sale — it left the pile without being sold

accounting.grade11.perpetual-and-periodi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.perpetual-and-periodi.question: With sales of R700 000 and cost of sales of R505 000, gross profit is:

accounting.grade11.perpetual-and-periodi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.perpetual-and-periodi.question: A shop selling thousands of cheap items historically chose the counting system because:
options: Writing the cost of every item as it leaves is a full-time job that earns nothing — simple and cheap was good enough
Counting is more accurate than recording

accounting.grade11.perpetual-and-periodi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.perpetual-and-periodi.question: "The notebook keeps itself" refers to:
options: A barcode-scanning till that takes the money AND writes the cost entry automatically

accounting.grade11.perpetual-and-periodi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.perpetual-and-periodi.question: The notebook system "lets you catch things" because:
options: Counting the shelf against what the notebook claims gives the gap a SIZE and a NAME

accounting.grade11.perpetual-and-periodi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.perpetual-and-periodi.question: Padding the closing stock count is nasty because:
options: It takes a long time to do
It is easily detected by customers
The shelves are just as empty while the report looks better — misleading owner and bank, and the loss lands anyway next year

accounting.grade11.reconciliations-costi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.reconciliations-costi.question: The bank reconciliation method begins by:
options: Updating YOUR OWN books with what the statement knows and you did not — charges, debit orders, interest

accounting.grade11.reconciliations-costi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.reconciliations-costi.question: The true book balance after updates is:
options: R10 400 — 10 940 less charges 150, less debit order 450, plus interest 60

accounting.grade11.reconciliations-costi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.reconciliations-costi.question: The reconciliation statement proves agreement by:
options: Statement balance 9 800 plus outstanding deposit 3 200 less outstanding payments 2 600 landing on the same R10 400

accounting.grade11.reconciliations-costi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.reconciliations-costi.question: The creditors reconciliation lands both records on:
options: R7 550 — our 6 600 plus the unrecorded invoice 950; their 8 750 less our payment in transit 1 200

accounting.grade11.reconciliations-costi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.reconciliations-costi.question: Contribution per unit is:
options: Selling price R25 less variable cost R10 — R15, first toward fixed costs, then to profit

accounting.grade11.reconciliations-costi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.reconciliations-costi.question: Break-even for the month is:

accounting.grade11.reconciliations-costi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.reconciliations-costi.question: Profit at 620 units is:
options: R1 800 — 120 units past the line times R15, confirmed by contribution 9 300 less fixed 7 500

accounting.grade11.reconciliations-costi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.reconciliations-costi.question: If the price drops to R22, break-even:
options: Jumps to 625 units — contribution falls to R12, so 7 500 over 12

accounting.grade11.reconciliations-costi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.reconciliations-costi.question: Periodic cost of sales is calculated as:
options: Opening stock 12 000 plus purchases 40 000 plus carriage 3 000 less closing stock 15 000 — R40 000

accounting.grade11.reconciliations-costi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.reconciliations-costi.question: The periodic system is "blinder" because:
options: Its calculation cannot tell SOLD from STOLEN between counts

accounting.grade11.reconciliations-costi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.reconciliations-costi.question: September's budgeted collections are:
options: R27 400 — 40% of September's 30 000 plus 55% of August's 28 000

accounting.grade11.reconciliations-costi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.reconciliations-costi.question: The 5% never collected teaches that:
options: The projected income statement equals the cash budget
Budgeted receipts are always LESS than budgeted sales — planning on the full 100% plans on money that never arrives

accounting.grade11.reconciliations-costi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.reconciliations-costi.question: The question separating zero-rated from exempt is:
options: May the seller reclaim its own VAT? Zero-rated yes; exempt no
Is the seller registered for income tax?

accounting.grade11.reconciliations-costi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.reconciliations-costi.question: The VAT inside an inclusive R4 600 is:
options: R690 — fifteen percent of the total
R600 — 4 600 times 15 over 115, on an exclusive R4 000

accounting.grade11.reconciliations-costi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.reconciliations-costi.question: With output tax R9 000 and input tax R6 300, the return shows:
options: R2 700 payable to SARS — and inputs above outputs would mean a refund

accounting.grade11.reconciliations-costi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.reconciliations-costi.question: VAT collected is "trust money" because:
options: It earns interest for the vendor
It belongs to the state, collected on its behalf — spending it is spending money that was never the vendor's

accounting.grade11.reconciliations-costi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.reconciliations-costi.question: Month-end disagreement between your notebook and the bank's is:
options: NORMAL — each side knows things the other has not seen yet

accounting.grade11.reconciliations-costi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.reconciliations-costi.question: Your notebook is corrected with:
options: What the bank knew first — its fee, the debit order, the interest

accounting.grade11.reconciliations-costi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.reconciliations-costi.question: With the wholesaler, the habit in one line is:
options: Never argue balances — correct both records toward each other and pay the meeting point, R7 550

accounting.grade11.reconciliations-costi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.reconciliations-costi.question: Vetkoek number five hundred and one matters because:
options: It is the first one working for YOU — the line is crossed and every further R15 is profit

accounting.grade11.reconciliations-costi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.reconciliations-costi.question: Selling 620 vetkoek gives profit of:
options: R1 800 — 120 past the line, each dropping its whole R15

accounting.grade11.reconciliations-costi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.reconciliations-costi.question: Cutting the price to R22 moves the line because:
options: Each vetkoek now carries only R12, so the line jumps to 625 — cheaper is not automatically smarter

accounting.grade11.reconciliations-costi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.reconciliations-costi.question: The VAT inside a R4 600 inclusive slip is found by:
options: Fifteen parts of one hundred and fifteen — R600, never fifteen percent of the total

accounting.grade11.reconciliations-costi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.reconciliations-costi.question: The counting way of finding cost of sales is blinder because:
options: Whatever left the shelf is assumed sold — theft hides inside the R40 000

accounting.grade11.reconciliations-costi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.reconciliations-costi.question: Planning collections at 40% now, 55% later and 5% never means:
options: Writing the month's money honestly before living it — earning and receiving are different calendars

accounting.grade11.reconciliations-costi.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.reconciliations-costi.question: The grade 11 toolkit, in five words, is:

accounting.grade11.the-asset-register-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.the-asset-register-an.question: The fixed asset register exists because the general ledger:
options: Holds only class totals — it cannot say which asset, how old, how much is left, or whether it still exists

accounting.grade11.the-asset-register-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.the-asset-register-an.question: A register page carries:
options: Description and identifying detail, purchase date and supplier, cost, method and rate, yearly depreciation, accumulated total, carrying value, location and responsible person

accounting.grade11.the-asset-register-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.the-asset-register-an.question: The register relates to the ledger the way:
options: The trial balance relates to the journals
The cash budget relates to the income statement
The DEBTORS LIST relates to Debtors Control — detail whose totals must agree with the summary

accounting.grade11.the-asset-register-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.the-asset-register-an.question: The three uses examiners ask for are:
options: CONTROL (assets produced on inspection), DECISIONS (replace or repair), and AUDIT (every figure traced to a page)

accounting.grade11.the-asset-register-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.the-asset-register-an.question: A machine invoiced at R80 000 with R4 000 delivery and R6 000 installation is recorded at:
options: R90 000 — cost includes everything necessary to bring the asset into use

accounting.grade11.the-asset-register-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.the-asset-register-an.question: The test separating capital from revenue expenditure is:
options: Does the spending EXTEND the asset's life or capacity beyond its original condition, or merely maintain it?
Whether it was paid in cash
Whether the supplier is registered for VAT

accounting.grade11.the-asset-register-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.the-asset-register-an.question: Adding routine servicing to a vehicle's cost:
options: Has no effect on the statements
OVERSTATES profit and the asset — and depreciates money that bought nothing lasting
Is required by the matching principle

accounting.grade11.the-asset-register-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.the-asset-register-an.question: A registered VAT vendor records a fixed asset at:
options: The price plus estimated future repairs
Cost EXCLUDING VAT — the VAT is claimed as input tax and never formed part of the asset's cost

accounting.grade11.the-asset-register-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.the-asset-register-an.question: Grade 11's part-year rule is that depreciation runs:
options: From the MONTH THE ASSET WAS BOUGHT, pro rata for the months owned in that first year
From the start of the financial year regardless
Only from the second year of ownership
From the date of first repair

accounting.grade11.the-asset-register-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.the-asset-register-an.question: A vehicle costing R240 000 bought 1 June, year end 28 February, at 15% diminishing balance, charges in year one:
options: R27 000 — R36 000 × 9/12 for the nine months owned

accounting.grade11.the-asset-register-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.the-asset-register-an.question: In the SECOND year, that same vehicle charges:
options: R36 000, back to the original cost
R31 950 — a full year at 15% of the R213 000 carrying value

accounting.grade11.the-asset-register-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.the-asset-register-an.question: An asset written down to zero but still in use:
options: Continues to be depreciated at a reduced rate
Has no further depreciation — often a nominal R1 is left standing, and it stays on the register and under control

accounting.grade11.the-asset-register-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.the-asset-register-an.question: Acquisition controls include:
options: Authorisation appropriate to the amount, quotations obtained, the asset checked against order and delivery note, and the register updated at once
Allowing any employee to order assets
Recording assets only at year end

accounting.grade11.the-asset-register-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.the-asset-register-an.question: Verification controls require the physical inspection to be performed by:
options: The person responsible for the assets, who knows them best
Someone INDEPENDENT of the person responsible for them, with every difference investigated
The external auditor only, every five years

accounting.grade11.the-asset-register-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.the-asset-register-an.question: A company vehicle used for family trips is:
options: DRAWINGS whether or not it is recorded as such — the honest treatment is a drawings entry at fair value, or a disclosed private-use policy

accounting.grade11.the-asset-register-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.the-asset-register-an.question: The pattern running through every asset control is:
options: A document trail, a separation of duties, or a physical count reconciled to a record — all made possible by the register

accounting.grade11.the-asset-register-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.the-asset-register-an.question: "Vehicles, four hundred and something thousand rand" is useless to the person running the place because:
options: It cannot say which vehicles, how old, which is nearly finished, or whether one has already left

accounting.grade11.the-asset-register-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.the-asset-register-an.question: The notebook works exactly like:
options: The DEBTORS LIST and the creditors list — one book has the total, the other has the faces, and they must agree

accounting.grade11.the-asset-register-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.the-asset-register-an.question: If the pages' totals do not match the ledger:
options: Something is recorded in one book and not the other — worth chasing down today rather than next year
The register must be rewritten annually

accounting.grade11.the-asset-register-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.the-asset-register-an.question: Delivery and installation belong in the machine's cost because:
options: Until it was delivered and installed it could not make a cent — everything needed to get it WORKING is part of what it cost
They are paid at the same time

accounting.grade11.the-asset-register-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.the-asset-register-an.question: A new engine giving the bakkie another five years is:
options: Buying more asset — it goes onto the bakkie's page and is written down over time

accounting.grade11.the-asset-register-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.the-asset-register-an.question: The sorting question is:
options: Does this make the thing BETTER or LONGER-LIVED than it was, or just keep it where it was?
Was it bought from a registered vendor?

accounting.grade11.the-asset-register-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.the-asset-register-an.question: Calling routine servicing "part of the bakkie":
options: Is the safer of the two errors
Makes profit look BETTER than it was, and writes off servicing money for years as if it bought something lasting

accounting.grade11.the-asset-register-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.the-asset-register-an.question: A vehicle bought 1 June with a year ending 28 February was owned for:

accounting.grade11.the-asset-register-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.the-asset-register-an.question: The method is to:
options: Charge a full year and adjust next year
Work out a FULL year first, then take the slice owned — R36 000 becoming R27 000 for nine twelfths
Charge nothing in the first year
Divide the cost by the months owned

accounting.grade11.the-asset-register-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.the-asset-register-an.question: Slicing only ever happens:
options: In the year something ARRIVES — or the year it leaves
When the method is diminishing balance

accounting.grade11.the-asset-register-an.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.the-asset-register-an.question: A machine fully written down but still working:
options: Stays on the register, locked up and somebody's responsibility — a machine finished on paper is still worth stealing

accounting.grade11.unit-costs-and-break-.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.unit-costs-and-break-.question: Variable costs are:
options: Constant per unit but growing in total as output grows
Constant in total at any output

accounting.grade11.unit-costs-and-break-.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.unit-costs-and-break-.question: Fixed costs of R658 000 at an output of 10 000 pairs work out per pair to:
options: R65,80 — and the per-unit figure shrinks as output spreads the fixed total

accounting.grade11.unit-costs-and-break-.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.unit-costs-and-break-.question: Kagiso's total variable cost of R48 per pair consists of:
options: Materials R23, labour R17, factory rent R8
Materials R23, labour R17, depreciation R8
Direct materials R23, direct labour R17, and selling and distribution R8

accounting.grade11.unit-costs-and-break-.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.unit-costs-and-break-.question: A unit cost that includes fixed costs is only true:
options: At the specific output it was computed for — fixed cost per unit changes with volume

accounting.grade11.unit-costs-and-break-.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.unit-costs-and-break-.question: Contribution per unit is calculated as:
options: Selling price per unit less variable cost per unit — R95 less R48 gives R47

accounting.grade11.unit-costs-and-break-.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.unit-costs-and-break-.question: Contribution is NOT profit because:
options: It must first pay toward the pile of fixed costs — only after they are covered does it fall through as profit
It is calculated before variable costs

accounting.grade11.unit-costs-and-break-.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.unit-costs-and-break-.question: Total contribution at 24 000 pairs is:

accounting.grade11.unit-costs-and-break-.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.unit-costs-and-break-.question: The four-line factory income statement runs:
options: Sales, less fixed costs, contribution, less variable costs, profit
Sales, less cost of sales, gross profit, net profit
Sales, less variable costs, contribution, less fixed costs, profit

accounting.grade11.unit-costs-and-break-.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.unit-costs-and-break-.question: The break-even formula in words is:
options: Total fixed costs divided by contribution per unit
Total costs divided by selling price
Fixed costs divided by selling price

accounting.grade11.unit-costs-and-break-.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.unit-costs-and-break-.question: Kagiso's break-even point is:
options: 14 000 pairs — R658 000 over R47 — with a break-even value of R1 330 000

accounting.grade11.unit-costs-and-break-.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.unit-costs-and-break-.question: Interpreted against planned production of 24 000 pairs, break-even at 14 000 means:
options: The survival line sits at 58,3 percent of the plan — a healthy cushion, with 10 000 pairs earning pure profit

accounting.grade11.unit-costs-and-break-.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.unit-costs-and-break-.question: If the division gives 14 002 comma 1 units, the break-even point is:
options: 14 003 units — always round UP, because at 14 002 a sliver of loss remains

accounting.grade11.unit-costs-and-break-.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.unit-costs-and-break-.question: The margin of safety on the budget is:
options: 10 000 pairs — 41,7 percent of planned sales can be lost before the loss line

accounting.grade11.unit-costs-and-break-.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.unit-costs-and-break-.question: Cutting the price to R89 moves break-even to:
options: 16 049 pairs — a R6 cut attacks contribution directly and moves the line violently

accounting.grade11.unit-costs-and-break-.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.unit-costs-and-break-.question: Fixed costs rising by R47 000 moves break-even to:
options: Exactly 15 000 pairs — R705 000 over the unchanged R47

accounting.grade11.unit-costs-and-break-.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.unit-costs-and-break-.question: The break-even model assumes:
options: Fixed costs change with every unit
Constant price and unit variable cost, fixed costs that never step, and that everything made is sold

accounting.grade11.unit-costs-and-break-.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.unit-costs-and-break-.question: The R658 pile of stones stands for:
options: The fixed costs — spent before roll one, the same whether you sell nothing or a mountain

accounting.grade11.unit-costs-and-break-.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.unit-costs-and-break-.question: The R48 that travels with every roll is:
options: The variable cost per unit — wors, bread, sauce, serviette

accounting.grade11.unit-costs-and-break-.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.unit-costs-and-break-.question: Each roll sold at R95 lifts how much off the pile?
options: R47 — the contribution: one stone per roll

accounting.grade11.unit-costs-and-break-.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.unit-costs-and-break-.question: Busy sellers win twice because:
options: More contributions arrive AND the fixed cost per unit thins as volume spreads it

accounting.grade11.unit-costs-and-break-.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.unit-costs-and-break-.question: With a pile of R658 and R47 lifted per roll, the pile is gone at:
options: Roll fourteen — and roll fifteen is the first sold purely for yourself

accounting.grade11.unit-costs-and-break-.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.unit-costs-and-break-.question: If the division gives fourteen comma two rolls, you break even on:
options: Roll fifteen — round the survival line UP; at fourteen you are still one stone short

accounting.grade11.unit-costs-and-break-.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.unit-costs-and-break-.question: Expecting to sell fifteen rolls with break-even at fourteen means:
options: One bad hour from a loss — the line only means something next to what you expect to sell

accounting.grade11.unit-costs-and-break-.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.unit-costs-and-break-.question: The factory's version of roll fourteen is:

accounting.grade11.unit-costs-and-break-.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.unit-costs-and-break-.question: Wors up R3 a roll changes the survival line by:
options: Contribution drops to R44, so the line moves from fourteen to fifteen rolls
Nothing — wors is a fixed cost
The price must rise to R98

accounting.grade11.unit-costs-and-break-.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.unit-costs-and-break-.question: A R6 discount on a R95 roll feels small but:
options: It only matters for big orders
It takes nearly thirteen percent of the contribution — price cuts bite the contribution, not the price
It changes nothing below ten percent

accounting.grade11.unit-costs-and-break-.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.unit-costs-and-break-.question: A fixed-cost rise and a variable-cost rise move the line by different routes:
options: One grows the pile to be buried; the other shrinks every unit's stone-lifting power

accounting.grade11.unit-costs-and-break-.subject: accounting
accounting.grade11.unit-costs-and-break-.question: Break-even analysis is called a headlight because:
options: It prices decisions BEFORE they are made — leather, contracts and rent are tested before anyone signs

accounting.grade11.vat-principles-and-ca.subject: accounting

Preparing the budget after the period

Every downstream figure — collections, purchases, cash — inherits the fiction, so money is lent into a lie

A bad-debts line on the profit list, and on the cash list simply money that never shows up

accounting.grade12.cash-budgets-and-proj.subject: accounting

options: The honest way to plan — the failure is expected, not a surprise

Gross profit, operating profit, net profit before tax, net profit after tax

Nothing — only share capital is affected

R162 000 — always equal to the charge

Financing activities — together with buy-backs and loan movements

The comparison is irrelevant to gearing

options: Fifteen cents in every rand, like VAT
A fixed twenty-seven cents in every rand of profit

options: Stayed in the bakery as retained profit, making every slice worth more
Must be paid out next year by law

Cash always equals profit eventually in the same year

Depreciation is a non-cash expense — the cash left when the van was bought
The van belongs to the bank

Declare the dividend for the year

Own at least half the company's shares
Repay the company's debts personally if it fails

Always follow the wishes of the largest shareholder

options: Money held in trust for SARS from the moment of sale — never the vendor's own
Business income until the return is filed
A loan from SARS to the vendor

options: Output tax — stealing from the fiscus sale by sale

options: Inflating input tax — a direct extraction of money from SARS
Only a problem for the supplier

File it but keep a private note
Adjust it slightly to reduce the lie

Is shared between the shop and SARS

Fifteen percent applies only to luxury goods

Both are outside the VAT system
Bread is zero-rated — in the system at a rate of nothing; residential rent is exempt — it never entered the building

options: The value she added — bought for 32 000, sold for 46 000

accounting.grade12.vat-control-and-the-a.subject: accounting
accounting.grade12.vat-control-and-the-a.question: The three nudges move the bill as follows:

Returns down, drawings up, bad debts down

accounting.grade12.vat-control-and-the-a.subject: accounting

options: The shop must close the period early
The fridge's VAT may not be claimed
SARS owes the refund — the slate points both ways

accounting.grade12.vat-control-and-the-a.question: The two-till trick is called stealing twice because it takes:
options: From SARS, and from everyone who depends on what VAT funds — clinics, schools and grants
From the customer and the supplier
From the bank and the wholesaler
From the till and the safe

accounting.grade12.vat-control-and-the-a.subject: accounting

options: Collecting a tax with no intention of delivering it — the aggravated version of the fraud
Legal if prices are rounded down

accounting.grade12.vat-control-and-the-a.subject: accounting

options: The supplier's own VAT return shows every invoice issued to the shop — the mismatch is a red light on a screen
SARS counts the stock physically each month

accounting.grade12.vat-control-and-the-a.subject: accounting
accounting.grade12.vat-control-and-the-a.question: The examination-ready summary of VAT ethics is:
options: VAT is a cost of doing business, minimised where possible
Evasion is acceptable below the audit threshold
Only registered vendors owe ethical duties

A problem of poor countries only

The value of the NEXT BEST alternative given up — the single best thing, not everything forgone
The total of all alternatives given up
The tax paid on a purchase

GDP, GNI and per capita income

A shift of the whole demand curve
A shift of the whole supply curve

options: EXCESS SUPPLY — quantity supplied minus quantity demanded in that row

options: UTILITY and SCARCITY together — abundance keeps water's price low despite its usefulness

economics.grade10.basic-concepts-and-mar.subject: economics
economics.grade10.basic-concepts-and-mar.question: A PERFECT market requires:

economics.grade10.basic-concepts-and-mar.question: The four phases of the business cycle in order are:

economics.grade10.basic-concepts-and-mar.question: Building plans passed are a LEADING indicator because they:
options: Change BEFORE the economy turns — the headlights showing the road ahead

economics.grade10.basic-concepts-and-mar.subject: economics
economics.grade10.basic-concepts-and-mar.question: The four-hundred-rand wallet against the six-hundred-rand list illustrates:
options: The economic problem — a PERMANENT gap between unlimited wants and limited means, forcing choice
A bad month that will pass

economics.grade10.basic-concepts-and-mar.subject: economics
economics.grade10.basic-concepts-and-mar.question: "The price tag behind the price tag" is:
options: The OPPORTUNITY COST — the best alternative the rands would otherwise have done
The total of everything not bought

options: Firms pay wages to households, households spend at firms, and the wages come back over the counters
Money flows only from shops to workers

economics.grade10.basic-concepts-and-mar.question: The street's three TAPS are:

options: They are decisions about next year's activity — bending before the economy does

Leakage and injection describe the direction of flow, not virtue — savings, for example, finance future investment

Because money earned inside the country is paid to firms outside the country

Drains: exports, investment, spending. Taps: savings, taxes, imports

Nothing; any price can last forever

economics.grade10.demand-supply-and-equi.subject: economics
economics.grade10.demand-supply-and-equi.question: A price below equilibrium creates:
options: A shortage — buyers bid the price up toward equilibrium

economics.grade10.demand-supply-and-equi.subject: economics
economics.grade10.demand-supply-and-equi.question: In the drought example, why does the demand curve stay where it is?
options: Because consumer income and other demand conditions are unchanged
Because the drought reduced demand too

economics.grade10.demand-supply-and-equi.subject: economics
economics.grade10.demand-supply-and-equi.question: Comparing the new equilibrium to the old one after the supply shift, we find:

economics.grade10.demand-supply-and-equi.subject: economics
economics.grade10.demand-supply-and-equi.question: At the OLD price, immediately after the drought shifts supply left, the market experiences:
options: A shortage — quantity demanded exceeds the reduced quantity supplied

economics.grade10.demand-supply-and-equi.subject: economics
economics.grade10.demand-supply-and-equi.question: As the maize price rises toward the new equilibrium, buyers reducing their purchases is shown as:
options: A leftward shift of the demand curve
A movement along the demand curve
A new demand curve being drawn

economics.grade10.demand-supply-and-equi.subject: economics
economics.grade10.demand-supply-and-equi.question: The schoolboy with empty pockets who badly wants a cold drink:
options: Is not part of demand — demand is wanting WITH money ready: willing AND able
Counts as demand because wanting is enough

economics.grade10.demand-supply-and-equi.subject: economics
economics.grade10.demand-supply-and-equi.question: At R20 the vendor phones his cousin for extra stock because:
options: Price is the seller's REWARD — better prices pull more supply to the rank

economics.grade10.demand-supply-and-equi.subject: economics
economics.grade10.demand-supply-and-equi.question: The two laws "lean against each other" because:
options: Buyers and sellers hate each other
Both curves slope the same way
Cheaper pulls MORE buyers while dearer pulls MORE sellers — opposite directions that must meet somewhere

economics.grade10.demand-supply-and-equi.subject: economics
economics.grade10.demand-supply-and-equi.question: At R20, the melting pile of unsold cans is the street version of:
options: A SURPLUS — quantity supplied exceeding quantity demanded, pushing the price down

economics.grade10.demand-supply-and-equi.subject: economics
economics.grade10.demand-supply-and-equi.question: At R8, the fighting queue and empty cooler mean:
options: A SHORTAGE — quantity demanded exceeding supplied, pulling the price up tomorrow

economics.grade10.demand-supply-and-equi.subject: economics
economics.grade10.demand-supply-and-equi.question: Equilibrium is the day that "works perfectly" because:
options: The last can sells to the last willing buyer — nothing left over, nobody turned away

economics.grade10.demand-supply-and-equi.subject: economics
economics.grade10.demand-supply-and-equi.question: "Nobody set it" refers to:
options: Price formation through market forces — millions of small arguments ending, no official in charge

economics.grade10.demand-supply-and-equi.subject: economics
economics.grade10.demand-supply-and-equi.question: The two diagnostic questions for any shock are:
options: WHOSE side of the market got hit, and did the good's OWN price cause it?
How big is it, and who is to blame?
Is it seasonal, and is it fair?
What did government do, and when?

economics.grade10.demand-supply-and-equi.subject: economics
economics.grade10.demand-supply-and-equi.question: The drought shifts the whole supply curve left because:
options: The maize price caused the change
At EVERY price there is less maize to offer — the sky changed the sellers' world, not the price

economics.grade10.demand-supply-and-equi.subject: economics
economics.grade10.demand-supply-and-equi.question: As the price climbs after the drought, the two simultaneous movements are:
options: Demand shifting left and supply shifting right
Buyers sliding along their unchanged demand curve (switching, smaller bags) and sellers stretching along the NEW supply curve
No movements — the price is stuck

economics.grade10.demand-supply-and-equi.subject: economics
economics.grade10.demand-supply-and-equi.question: The new resting place after the drought shows:
options: HIGHER price, LESS maize traded — matching what families see at the shops in drought years

economics.grade10.drawing-and-reading-ma.subject: economics
economics.grade10.drawing-and-reading-ma.question: In the schedule, quantity demanded falls from 100 to 20 as price rises from R2 to R10. This pattern reflects:

economics.grade10.drawing-and-reading-ma.subject: economics
economics.grade10.drawing-and-reading-ma.question: Why should you inspect the table before drawing anything?
options: To find which column has bigger numbers
To predict each curve's slope, spot the equal row, and choose sensible axis scales
Because tables are marked separately from graphs

economics.grade10.drawing-and-reading-ma.subject: economics
economics.grade10.drawing-and-reading-ma.question: At which price do the demand and supply columns show the same quantity?

economics.grade10.drawing-and-reading-ma.subject: economics
economics.grade10.drawing-and-reading-ma.question: By convention, economics graphs place:
options: Price on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal axis
Quantity on the vertical axis and price on the horizontal axis
Both variables on the same axis
Whichever variable is larger on the vertical axis

economics.grade10.drawing-and-reading-ma.subject: economics
economics.grade10.drawing-and-reading-ma.question: What is wrong with an axis where the gap from 20 to 60 takes one block but 60 to 80 takes three blocks?
options: Nothing, as long as all values appear
The uneven scale bends the curves and makes every reading unreliable
It only matters for the demand curve

economics.grade10.drawing-and-reading-ma.subject: economics
economics.grade10.drawing-and-reading-ma.question: The point for the demand row 'price R4, quantity 80' is plotted by:
options: Going up to 4 on the price axis and across to 80 on the quantity axis
Going up to 80 on the price axis and across to 4
Marking 4 and 80 both on the horizontal axis

economics.grade10.drawing-and-reading-ma.subject: economics
economics.grade10.drawing-and-reading-ma.question: Which labels must appear for full presentation marks?
options: Only the curve names D and S
Axis labels with units, curve labels, and a heading
Labels are optional if the drawing is neat

economics.grade10.drawing-and-reading-ma.subject: economics
economics.grade10.drawing-and-reading-ma.question: The equilibrium in our example is at:

economics.grade10.drawing-and-reading-ma.subject: economics
economics.grade10.drawing-and-reading-ma.question: Your curves cross at a price where the table's demand and supply columns are NOT equal. What does this mean?
options: At least one point was plotted incorrectly — check each point against its row

economics.grade10.drawing-and-reading-ma.subject: economics
economics.grade10.drawing-and-reading-ma.question: What do the dotted lines from the intersection to each axis show?
options: The equilibrium price and quantity being read off the axes

economics.grade10.drawing-and-reading-ma.subject: economics
economics.grade10.drawing-and-reading-ma.question: At R8, quantity demanded is 40 and quantity supplied is 80. The excess supply is:

economics.grade10.drawing-and-reading-ma.subject: economics
economics.grade10.drawing-and-reading-ma.question: On the graph, excess supply at R8 appears as:
options: The vertical distance between the curves at quantity 40
The horizontal distance between the demand and supply curves at the height of R8
The area under the supply curve
The distance from R6 to R8 on the price axis

economics.grade10.drawing-and-reading-ma.subject: economics
economics.grade10.drawing-and-reading-ma.question: Why does a surplus occur at R8 specifically?
options: Because R8 is above the equilibrium price of R6, encouraging sellers while pricing out buyers
Because demand shifted left at R8

economics.grade10.drawing-and-reading-ma.subject: economics
economics.grade10.drawing-and-reading-ma.question: The most common error when reading excess supply or demand off a graph is:
options: Reading the two quantities at different prices instead of along one horizontal line
Choosing a price on the vertical axis

economics.grade10.drawing-and-reading-ma.subject: economics
economics.grade10.drawing-and-reading-ma.question: "The table is the boss" means:
options: When graph and table disagree, the table decides — the graph is just its portrait and invents nothing

economics.grade10.drawing-and-reading-ma.subject: economics
economics.grade10.drawing-and-reading-ma.question: Interrogating the columns BEFORE drawing lets you:
options: Know what the finished picture MUST look like — and catch your own errors, like a demand line coming out uphill

economics.grade10.drawing-and-reading-ma.subject: economics
economics.grade10.drawing-and-reading-ma.question: The special row to circle in your head is:
options: The first row of the table
The row with the biggest quantity
R6, where both columns say 60 — the lines must cross exactly there
The row with the highest price

economics.grade10.drawing-and-reading-ma.subject: economics
economics.grade10.drawing-and-reading-ma.question: The subject's "handshake" for axes is:
options: Price UP the side, quantity ALONG the bottom — always
Quantity up the side, price along the bottom
Either way, as long as it's labelled

economics.grade10.drawing-and-reading-ma.subject: economics
economics.grade10.drawing-and-reading-ma.question: Uneven scale steps are forbidden because:
options: They BEND lines that should be straight — and a bent line lies when you read from it, like a ruler with squashed centimetres
They make the graph too large

economics.grade10.drawing-and-reading-ma.subject: economics
economics.grade10.drawing-and-reading-ma.question: Plotting as "postal work" means:
options: Posting the graph to the marker
Drawing the lines before the dots
Each table row is an address — up to the price, across to the quantity, drop a dot; the laws then draw the picture themselves

economics.grade10.drawing-and-reading-ma.subject: economics
economics.grade10.drawing-and-reading-ma.question: Labels — Price (R), Quantity, title, D and S — are:
options: Free marks sitting on the table — markers award them directly

economics.grade10.drawing-and-reading-ma.subject: economics
economics.grade10.drawing-and-reading-ma.question: The "level flight" at R8 touches:
options: Demand at 40 and supply at 80 — same height, two readings, gap of 40 units of excess supply

economics.grade10.drawing-and-reading-ma.subject: economics
economics.grade10.drawing-and-reading-ma.question: The classic reading error is:
options: A crooked finger — reading the two curves at DIFFERENT heights instead of both readings on one price level

economics.grade10.drawing-and-reading-ma.subject: economics
economics.grade10.drawing-and-reading-ma.question: At R4 the machine reads:
options: Supply 40, demand 80 — excess DEMAND of 40 units: below the resting place, buyers outrun sellers

economics.grade10.drawing-and-reading-ma.subject: economics
economics.grade10.drawing-and-reading-ma.question: The skill is "routine, not talent" because:
options: Table interrogated, frame built, dots posted, level flights flown — every step is learnable by anyone willing to draw five graphs

economics.grade10.economic-redress-and-d.subject: economics
economics.grade10.economic-redress-and-d.question: "Marginalised" in economics means:
options: Pushed to the edge of economic life — excluded from ownership, employment, skills, credit and decision-making

economics.grade10.economic-redress-and-d.subject: economics
economics.grade10.economic-redress-and-d.question: Disadvantage persists after the laws are repealed because:
options: The laws were never actually changed
It transmits across generations — through assets, education, networks and address

economics.grade10.economic-redress-and-d.subject: economics
economics.grade10.economic-redress-and-d.question: Rural communities were marginalised principally through:
options: Areas deliberately starved of infrastructure and investment — the spatial pattern behind today's geography of unemployment

economics.grade10.economic-redress-and-d.subject: economics
economics.grade10.economic-redress-and-d.question: The "compounding" point means:
options: Marginalisation ended simultaneously for all groups
The categories OVERLAP — a young rural Black woman with a disability faces one compounded exclusion, not five separate ones

economics.grade10.economic-redress-and-d.subject: economics
economics.grade10.economic-redress-and-d.question: Land reform's three programmes are:
options: RESTITUTION (return or compensation for post-1913 dispossession), REDISTRIBUTION (transfer to those without access), TENURE reform (securing insecure occupation)

economics.grade10.economic-redress-and-d.subject: economics
economics.grade10.economic-redress-and-d.question: "Land without support fails" means redress in this factor requires:
options: Finance, training, equipment and market access alongside the title deed — or the transfer produces neither livelihood nor output

economics.grade10.economic-redress-and-d.subject: economics
economics.grade10.economic-redress-and-d.question: Employment equity deliberately targets management and skilled occupations because:
options: That is where exclusion was sharpest — and where decisions get made
The law only applies to senior staff

economics.grade10.economic-redress-and-d.subject: economics
economics.grade10.economic-redress-and-d.question: Redress in the CAPITAL factor addresses:
options: WHO OWNS productive capital — ownership stakes, management control, enterprise and supplier development, preferential procurement — plus credit access for those without collateral

economics.grade10.economic-redress-and-d.subject: economics
economics.grade10.economic-redress-and-d.question: Labour legislation is itself democratisation because:
options: The rights to organise, bargain and be consulted convert workers from subjects of decisions into parties to them
It sets all wages by statute

economics.grade10.economic-redress-and-d.subject: economics
economics.grade10.economic-redress-and-d.question: NEDLAC's four constituencies are:
options: Parliament, the courts, the Reserve Bank and Treasury
GOVERNMENT, organised BUSINESS, organised LABOUR and organised COMMUNITY

economics.grade10.economic-redress-and-d.subject: economics
economics.grade10.economic-redress-and-d.question: NEDLAC's function is that:
