economics.grade12.paper-2-microeconomics.question: Tourism is called an export that never leaves home because:
options: Foreign visitors spend foreign money inside South Africa
It is not counted in GDP

economics.grade12.paper-2-microeconomics.subject: economics
economics.grade12.paper-2-microeconomics.question: The plastic bag levy is an example of:
options: Making the polluter pay through an environmental tax

economics.grade12.paper-2-practice-run.s.subject: economics
economics.grade12.paper-2-practice-run.s.question: Oligopolies that collude in a formal, written manner are called:

economics.grade12.paper-2-practice-run.s.subject: economics
economics.grade12.paper-2-practice-run.s.question: Many sellers, differentiated products and easy entry describe:

economics.grade12.paper-2-practice-run.s.subject: economics
economics.grade12.paper-2-practice-run.s.question: Prices rising while output falls and unemployment climbs is matched to the term:

economics.grade12.paper-2-practice-run.s.subject: economics
economics.grade12.paper-2-practice-run.s.question: Give the term: the point where price equals the minimum of average variable cost, below which production stops. The full-mark answer is:
options: The shutdown point, written out in words

economics.grade12.paper-2-practice-run.s.subject: economics
economics.grade12.paper-2-practice-run.s.question: Name TWO characteristics of perfect competition. A full-mark pair is:
options: Homogeneous products and free entry and exit

economics.grade12.paper-2-practice-run.s.subject: economics
economics.grade12.paper-2-practice-run.s.question: Why can a monopolist not charge any price it likes?
options: Because the Competition Commission sets its prices daily
Because the demand curve still rules — at higher prices consumers buy less, so price and quantity are chosen ON the demand curve

economics.grade12.paper-2-practice-run.s.subject: economics
economics.grade12.paper-2-practice-run.s.question: When a short item says 'name' or 'list', the right response is:
options: A paragraph of explanation for each item
The items alone — explanation spends effort the marks have not paid for

economics.grade12.paper-2-practice-run.s.subject: economics
economics.grade12.paper-2-practice-run.s.question: On the described graph, the selling price of R150 is read from:
options: The demand curve directly above the equilibrium quantity
The intersection of MC and MR itself
The lowest point of average cost
The vertical axis at zero output

economics.grade12.paper-2-practice-run.s.subject: economics
economics.grade12.paper-2-practice-run.s.question: Marginal revenue lies below the monopolist's demand curve because:
options: The monopolist has no marginal costs
Selling one more unit requires lowering the price on ALL units, so the last unit adds less than its price

economics.grade12.paper-2-practice-run.s.subject: economics
economics.grade12.paper-2-practice-run.s.question: With price R150, average cost R125 and output 100 units, total economic profit is:
options: R2 500 — R25 per unit times 100 units

economics.grade12.paper-2-practice-run.s.subject: economics
economics.grade12.paper-2-practice-run.s.question: If instead average cost were R150 and price R125, the same procedure would show:

economics.grade12.paper-2-practice-run.s.subject: economics
economics.grade12.paper-2-practice-run.s.question: The CPI moves from 120,0 to 127,2. The inflation rate is:
options: 6,0 percent — 7,2 divided by the OLD index of 120,0, times 100

economics.grade12.paper-2-practice-run.s.subject: economics
economics.grade12.paper-2-practice-run.s.question: Food weighted 40% up 8%, transport 35% up 6%, education 25% up 4%. The weighted increase is:

economics.grade12.paper-2-practice-run.s.subject: economics
economics.grade12.paper-2-practice-run.s.question: Low-income households often experience worse-than-headline inflation because:
options: Their real baskets are food-heavy, so food price surges hit them at greater weight

economics.grade12.paper-2-practice-run.s.subject: economics
economics.grade12.paper-2-practice-run.s.question: If fuel and electricity led the increases, the inflation is best classified as:
options: Demand-pull, cured by the repo rate alone
Cost-push — and the repo rate cools spending without cheapening fuel

economics.grade12.paper-2-practice-run.s.subject: economics
economics.grade12.paper-2-practice-run.s.question: In the kinked demand curve, a lone price INCREASE loses many customers because:
options: Demand above the kink is elastic — rivals hold their prices and shoppers switch
Demand above the kink is inelastic

economics.grade12.paper-2-practice-run.s.subject: economics
economics.grade12.paper-2-practice-run.s.question: The kink pushes oligopolists toward:
options: Non-price competition — advertising, branding and service — because price moves lose revenue both ways

economics.grade12.paper-2-practice-run.s.subject: economics
economics.grade12.paper-2-practice-run.s.question: A balanced minimum wage evaluation concludes that:
options: All workers lose from wage floors
The outcome depends on the level set and enforcement — a modest floor helps more than it harms; an aggressive one costs jobs
Employers set wages fairly without any floor

economics.grade12.paper-2-practice-run.s.subject: economics
economics.grade12.paper-2-practice-run.s.question: Tradeable pollution permits control river pollution by:
options: Capping total discharge and letting firms trade the right to pollute within the cap

economics.grade12.paper-2-practice-run.s.subject: economics
economics.grade12.paper-2-practice-run.s.question: The essay's forty marks divide as:
options: Introduction 2, main body 26, additional part 10, conclusion 2

economics.grade12.paper-2-practice-run.s.subject: economics
economics.grade12.paper-2-practice-run.s.question: In the comparison body, each developed contrast — such as horizontal against downward-sloping demand — earns:
options: Two marks when fully explained in context
Marks only if a diagram is drawn

economics.grade12.paper-2-practice-run.s.subject: economics
economics.grade12.paper-2-practice-run.s.question: The monopoly's long-run economic profit, described verbally, is:
options: The area under the marginal cost curve
The rectangle between price and average cost across the equilibrium quantity, persisting because barriers block entry

economics.grade12.paper-2-practice-run.s.subject: economics
economics.grade12.paper-2-practice-run.s.question: A strong additional part on monopoly argues that:
options: Monopolies are always evil in every case
Monopolies never exist in South Africa
Economies of scale can justify regulated natural monopolies, while unregulated dominance harms consumers — hence the Competition Act

economics.grade12.paper-2-practice-run.s.subject: economics
economics.grade12.paper-2-practice-run.s.question: The measure that attacks DEMAND-PULL inflation most directly is:
options: Raising the repo rate to make credit dearer and cool spending

economics.grade12.paper-2-practice-run.s.subject: economics
economics.grade12.paper-2-practice-run.s.question: Discipline over administered prices such as electricity tariffs fights inflation on:
options: The cost-push side — it removes a supply-side price engine directly

economics.grade12.paper-2-practice-run.s.subject: economics
economics.grade12.paper-2-practice-run.s.question: A fair evaluation of South African inflation targeting credits it with:
options: Anchoring expectations and predictability since 2000, while noting its weakness against cost-push shocks

economics.grade12.paper-2-practice-run.s.subject: economics
economics.grade12.paper-2-practice-run.s.question: The conclusion 'the cure must match the cause' earns its two marks because it is:
options: A summary of every body fact
A fresh closing judgement the body supports but has not already stated

economics.grade12.perfect-competition-ou.subject: economics
economics.grade12.perfect-competition-ou.question: Which list gives assumptions of perfect competition?
options: Very many small buyers and sellers, a homogeneous product, free entry and exit, perfect knowledge, mobile factors
One seller, unique product, blocked entry
A few large sellers, branded products, heavy advertising

economics.grade12.perfect-competition-ou.subject: economics
economics.grade12.perfect-competition-ou.question: The individual business in perfect competition is a PRICE TAKER, meaning:
options: It sets whatever price maximises profit
It accepts the price set by industry demand and supply, and decides only its quantity
It negotiates prices with each customer
It always charges below the market price

economics.grade12.perfect-competition-ou.subject: economics
economics.grade12.perfect-competition-ou.question: The demand curve facing the individual business is:
options: Downward sloping like the industry curve
A horizontal line at the market price — it can sell any quantity at that price and nothing above it

economics.grade12.perfect-competition-ou.subject: economics
economics.grade12.perfect-competition-ou.question: In perfect competition, the flat line at the market price is simultaneously:
options: Total cost, total revenue and profit
The industry demand and supply curves
Marginal cost, average cost and average variable cost
The demand curve, average revenue and marginal revenue — D equals AR equals MR equals P

economics.grade12.perfect-competition-ou.subject: economics
economics.grade12.perfect-competition-ou.question: The marginal cost curve cuts the average cost curve:
options: At AC's lowest point — while the marginal unit costs less than the average it drags the average down; once it costs more, it pulls the average up
Only when the firm makes a loss

economics.grade12.perfect-competition-ou.subject: economics
economics.grade12.perfect-competition-ou.question: The universal profit-maximising rule is to produce where:
options: Average cost is at its minimum
Marginal revenue equals marginal cost, with MC rising
Total revenue is at its maximum

economics.grade12.perfect-competition-ou.subject: economics
economics.grade12.perfect-competition-ou.question: NORMAL profit is:
options: The minimum earnings needed to keep the entrepreneur in the industry — an opportunity cost already included in the cost curves

economics.grade12.perfect-competition-ou.subject: economics
economics.grade12.perfect-competition-ou.question: Price is R15, average cost at the best output is R12, and output is 200 units. Economic profit is:
options: R600 — the R3 per-unit surplus times 200 units, the rectangle between the price line and the AC curve

economics.grade12.perfect-competition-ou.subject: economics
economics.grade12.perfect-competition-ou.question: A loss-making firm should keep producing in the short run when:
options: Price covers average variable cost — each unit then contributes something toward the fixed costs owed anyway
Price is below average variable cost

economics.grade12.perfect-competition-ou.subject: economics
economics.grade12.perfect-competition-ou.question: The firm's short-run supply curve is:
options: Its rising marginal cost curve above minimum average variable cost

economics.grade12.perfect-competition-ou.subject: economics
economics.grade12.perfect-competition-ou.question: When firms in the industry earn economic profit, the long-run sequence is:
options: Firms exit, supply falls, price rises
Newcomers enter, industry supply shifts right, price falls until it touches minimum average cost and economic profit disappears
Nothing changes because profit is permanent

economics.grade12.perfect-competition-ou.subject: economics
economics.grade12.perfect-competition-ou.question: Long-run equilibrium in perfect competition achieves both efficiencies because:
options: The state sets prices at cost
Price equals marginal cost (allocative efficiency) and output occurs at minimum average cost (productive efficiency)

economics.grade12.perfect-competition-ou.subject: economics
economics.grade12.perfect-competition-ou.question: The three institutions of the Competition Act 1998, in order of function, are:
options: The Commission investigates, the Tribunal adjudicates, and the Competition Appeal Court hears appeals
The Reserve Bank, the Treasury and SARS
The Tribunal investigates, the Commission fines, the High Court appeals
The JSE, the FSCA and the Ombudsman

economics.grade12.perfect-competition-ou.subject: economics
economics.grade12.perfect-competition-ou.question: The bread cartel and the World Cup construction cases are examples of:
options: Horizontal restrictive practices — collusion between rivals through price fixing and bid rigging

economics.grade12.perfect-competition-ou.subject: economics
economics.grade12.perfect-competition-ou.question: South African merger control is distinctive because it also weighs:
options: Public interest — employment, small-business access and the spread of ownership

economics.grade12.perfect-competition-ou.subject: economics
economics.grade12.perfect-competition-ou.question: In terms of the model, collusion is attacked because it:
options: Converts many competing price takers into one price maker — output restricted, price above marginal cost, the efficiencies lost

economics.grade12.perfect-competition-ou.subject: economics
economics.grade12.perfect-competition-ou.question: Charging R12 when the street price is R10 fails because:
options: Buyers step two tables over and buy identical tomatoes for R10

economics.grade12.perfect-competition-ou.subject: economics
economics.grade12.perfect-competition-ou.question: Cutting to R8 is foolish because:
options: She could already sell everything she brought at R10 — she throws away R2 on every kilo
The other sellers will match R8
Selling fast is bad for business

economics.grade12.perfect-competition-ou.subject: economics
economics.grade12.perfect-competition-ou.question: The seller's only real decision on the street is:
options: How many kilos to bring — quantity, because the street sets the price

economics.grade12.perfect-competition-ou.subject: economics
economics.grade12.perfect-competition-ou.question: "Each wall keeps the price honest" refers to:
options: The municipal fences around the market
The assumptions — many sellers, identical goods, visible prices, free entry — whose removal would give a seller price power

economics.grade12.perfect-competition-ou.subject: economics
economics.grade12.perfect-competition-ou.question: The cost of one more kilo rises as she brings more because:
options: Beyond her own garden she must buy from neighbours at rising prices, hire a bakkie and pay her cousin
Tomato prices fall in the afternoon

economics.grade12.perfect-competition-ou.subject: economics
economics.grade12.perfect-competition-ou.question: The street version of MR equals MC is:
options: Bring as many kilos as the bakkie holds
Keep adding kilos while one more earns more than it costs; stop when the next kilo would cost more than it earns
Stop when total cost equals total revenue
Sell until noon and then go home

economics.grade12.perfect-competition-ou.subject: economics
economics.grade12.perfect-competition-ou.question: Her own forgone factory wage belongs in the costs because:
options: A morning at the table is a morning's wages lost — opportunity cost, which is why normal profit sits inside the cost curves

economics.grade12.perfect-competition-ou.subject: economics
economics.grade12.perfect-competition-ou.question: All-in cost R10 per kilo, street price R10. The verdict is:
options: Economic loss — she should quit today
Economic profit of R10 per kilo
She cannot cover her variable costs
Normal profit — she earns exactly what her time and money could earn anywhere, and staying makes sense

economics.grade12.perfect-competition-ou.subject: economics
economics.grade12.perfect-competition-ou.question: "Profit was the invitation; entry was the RSVP" describes:
options: Economic profit attracting newcomers through free entry until extra supply pushes the price down and the surplus disappears
Sellers inviting buyers to the market

economics.grade12.perfect-competition-ou.subject: economics
economics.grade12.perfect-competition-ou.question: In the drought year, losses lead to:
options: Exit — some sellers quit, supply falls, price climbs until the survivors break even

economics.grade12.perfect-competition-ou.subject: economics
economics.grade12.perfect-competition-ou.question: The street's resting point, in model language, is:
options: Price above marginal cost with restricted output
Price equal to marginal cost and to minimum average cost — normal profit only, both efficiencies achieved

economics.grade12.perfect-competition-ou.subject: economics
economics.grade12.perfect-competition-ou.question: The Sunday meeting where forty sellers agree on a R15 floor is:
options: Legal if the price is fair
Illegal collusion — price fixing that the Commission investigates and the Tribunal can fine at up to ten percent of turnover

economics.grade12.protectionism-free-tra.subject: economics
economics.grade12.protectionism-free-tra.question: A tariff protects home producers by:
options: Taxing imports at the border, raising their shelf price so local products compete more easily — with revenue as a bonus
Limiting the quantity of imports allowed

economics.grade12.protectionism-free-tra.subject: economics
economics.grade12.protectionism-free-tra.question: Economists dislike quotas more than tariffs because quotas:
options: Hand valuable import licences to favoured firms and yield the state no revenue

economics.grade12.protectionism-free-tra.subject: economics
economics.grade12.protectionism-free-tra.question: DUMPING is:
options: Any export sold at a profit
Selling exports below cost or below the home-market price, often to kill competitors before raising prices

economics.grade12.protectionism-free-tra.subject: economics
economics.grade12.protectionism-free-tra.question: Protection is "politically easy and economically expensive" because:
options: Its costs fall only on foreigners
Losses are spread thinly over many consumers while gains concentrate on few visible producers and workers

economics.grade12.protectionism-free-tra.subject: economics
economics.grade12.protectionism-free-tra.question: The standard rebuttal to the infant-industry argument is that:
options: Infants rarely admit to growing up — protection that never lapses breeds permanent inefficiency

economics.grade12.protectionism-free-tra.subject: economics
economics.grade12.protectionism-free-tra.question: The employment argument for protection is weakened because:
options: It saves visible jobs while destroying invisible ones — dearer inputs burden downstream producers, and retaliation kills export jobs
Imports create no competition for jobs

economics.grade12.protectionism-free-tra.subject: economics
economics.grade12.protectionism-free-tra.question: Which argument for protection do even free traders generally accept?
options: Permanent tariffs on all consumer goods
Anti-dumping action against predatory pricing from abroad

economics.grade12.protectionism-free-tra.subject: economics
economics.grade12.protectionism-free-tra.question: The DESIRABLE MIX of trade policy is:
options: Pure free trade with no exceptions
Broadly open trade plus targeted, temporary, conditional protection with sunset clauses — the scalpel, never the blanket

economics.grade12.protectionism-free-tra.subject: economics
economics.grade12.protectionism-free-tra.question: Import substitution industrialises by:
options: Replacing imports with home production behind tariff walls — the inward path

economics.grade12.protectionism-free-tra.subject: economics
economics.grade12.protectionism-free-tra.question: The recorded weakness of import substitution is that industries built behind walls:
options: Stay small — capped by the home market — and inefficient, since the wall removes pressure to match world costs

economics.grade12.protectionism-free-tra.subject: economics
economics.grade12.protectionism-free-tra.question: Export promotion succeeded in East Asia because:
options: Selling to a ceiling-free world market opened scale economies while global competition forced efficiency

economics.grade12.protectionism-free-tra.subject: economics
economics.grade12.protectionism-free-tra.question: South Africa's current trade-policy mix is best described as:
options: Full import substitution behind high walls
Pure free trade with zero tariffs

Officially export-led — with automotive incentives the flagship — plus selective protection in contested sectors like poultry, clothing and steel, throttled mainly by logistics and electricity constraints

economics.grade12.protectionism-free-tra.subject: economics
economics.grade12.protectionism-free-tra.question: The WTO was created:
options: In 1995 by the Uruguay Round, succeeding the GATT of 1947 after eight rounds of tariff cutting
In 1947 as a United Nations agency

economics.grade12.protectionism-free-tra.subject: economics
economics.grade12.protectionism-free-tra.question: The most-favoured-nation principle requires that:
options: A trade benefit granted to one partner extends to all members — non-discrimination
Each country favours one chosen nation
Imports be taxed above local goods

economics.grade12.protectionism-free-tra.subject: economics
economics.grade12.protectionism-free-tra.question: A standing critique of trade liberalisation is that:
options: Tariffs are higher now than in 1947
Rich countries kept protecting agriculture — the very sector where developing countries hold advantage
The WTO has no dispute system

economics.grade12.protectionism-free-tra.subject: economics
economics.grade12.protectionism-free-tra.question: The ladder of integration, in order, is:
options: Economic union, common market, customs union, free trade area
Customs union, free trade area, economic union, common market
Common market, customs union, free trade area, economic union
Free trade area (AfCFTA), customs union (SACU), common market, economic union (the EU with the euro)

economics.grade12.protectionism-free-tra.subject: economics
economics.grade12.protectionism-free-tra.question: Charging each gate vendor R20 a day to trade corresponds to:
options: A tariff — raising the outsiders' costs so the insider competes more easily

economics.grade12.protectionism-free-tra.subject: economics
economics.grade12.protectionism-free-tra.question: The three licensed vendors "suddenly love the rule" because:
options: The licence itself becomes valuable — quotas create privileged insiders who then defend the restriction

economics.grade12.protectionism-free-tra.subject: economics
economics.grade12.protectionism-free-tra.question: Free kitchen use for the tuckshop is a subsidy that is:
options: Invisible to learners but real — protection hidden in the school's budget rather than at the gate

economics.grade12.protectionism-free-tra.subject: economics
economics.grade12.protectionism-free-tra.question: Protecting the tuckshop is politically attractive because:
options: The saved jobs are visible and grateful while eight hundred learners each lose too little to march — concentrated gains, thin-spread losses

economics.grade12.protectionism-free-tra.subject: economics
economics.grade12.protectionism-free-tra.question: The infant-industry argument is respectable because:
options: A genuinely new producer buying small and dear can reach competitive costs once grown to scale — you cannot learn to swim while drowning

economics.grade12.protectionism-free-tra.subject: economics
economics.grade12.protectionism-free-tra.question: "The ladder becomes a hammock" when:
options: Protection removes the pressure to improve, and the shop still calls itself an infant at ten years old

economics.grade12.protectionism-free-tra.subject: economics
economics.grade12.protectionism-free-tra.question: Honest infant protection requires:
options: A written expiry date, performance pressure through targets, and shelter for genuine infants only
Protection for the oldest firms first

economics.grade12.protectionism-free-tra.subject: economics
economics.grade12.protectionism-free-tra.question: The tuckshop's two futures — selling to its own school forever, or getting good enough to sell to other schools — represent:
options: Import substitution with its home-market ceiling, and export promotion with no ceiling but real competition — and the school van as the logistics that must work

economics.grade12.protectionism-free-tra.subject: economics
economics.grade12.protectionism-free-tra.question: The district agreement letting any learner buy from any school's vendors, with no gate fees, is:
options: A free trade area — the AfCFTA at continental scale

economics.grade12.protectionism-free-tra.subject: economics
economics.grade12.protectionism-free-tra.question: Adding one common gate fee for OUTSIDERS turns the arrangement into:
options: A customs union — like SACU, the world's oldest, which shares the takings by formula

economics.grade12.protectionism-free-tra.subject: economics
economics.grade12.protectionism-free-tra.question: The deal's "real cost" stands at the empty tables because:
options: Squeezed mediocre stands close, and their owners bear concentrated losses while everyone else's lunches improve — losers who deserve real help
The kota stand raises prices fivefold

economics.grade12.protectionism-free-tra.subject: economics
economics.grade12.protectionism-free-tra.question: The four-part honest summary of globalisation is:
options: Smaller playgrounds, dearer lunches, no losers, no rules
A rulebook that never changes and never argues
Bigger playgrounds, better and cheaper lunches, real losers deserving real help, and a rulebook forever arguing with itself

economics.grade12.sustainability-measure.subject: economics
economics.grade12.sustainability-measure.question: The Brundtland definition of sustainable development is development that:
options: Meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs
Maximises GDP growth in every year
Bans all use of natural resources
Prioritises the environment over jobs in all cases

economics.grade12.sustainability-measure.subject: economics
economics.grade12.sustainability-measure.question: A factory's effluent kills fish and sickens downstream users who get no compensation. Economically this is:
options: A negative externality — real costs landing on people outside the factory's transactions, so private cost sits below social cost

economics.grade12.sustainability-measure.subject: economics
economics.grade12.sustainability-measure.question: Clean air is a public good because it is:
options: Non-excludable and non-rival — nobody can be fenced out, and one person's breathing does not use up another's

economics.grade12.sustainability-measure.subject: economics
economics.grade12.sustainability-measure.question: The tragedy of the commons predicts that an ownerless fish stock will be:
options: Raced to exhaustion — each fisher correctly reasons that a spared fish will simply be caught by someone else

economics.grade12.sustainability-measure.subject: economics
economics.grade12.sustainability-measure.question: South Africa is DOUBLY exposed to climate change because:
options: Its coal-heavy economy is among the world's most carbon-intensive, AND the region is warming at nearly twice the global average
It has no renewable resources and no coastline

economics.grade12.sustainability-measure.subject: economics
economics.grade12.sustainability-measure.question: South Africa's water situation is precarious because:
options: Rainfall is double the world average but polluted
Rainfall is about half the world average, while rivers carry acid mine drainage, sewage from failing works and farm runoff

economics.grade12.sustainability-measure.subject: economics
economics.grade12.sustainability-measure.question: Biodiversity is described as economic capital because:
options: It is the genetic library for medicine and crops, and the asset base of the tourism industry

economics.grade12.sustainability-measure.subject: economics
economics.grade12.sustainability-measure.question: The economic reading of environmental damage is that it is:
options: A moral issue with no economic content
A cost only to rich countries
Future GDP quietly draining away — lost harvests, deterred tourists, sickened workers, rebuilt cities

economics.grade12.sustainability-measure.subject: economics
economics.grade12.sustainability-measure.question: Which list contains ONLY command-and-control measures?
options: Emission standards, environmental impact assessments, fishing quotas, water-use licences
Carbon tax, plastic-bag levy, tyre levy

economics.grade12.sustainability-measure.subject: economics
economics.grade12.sustainability-measure.question: South Africa's carbon tax, in force since 2019:
options: Prices each ton of carbon dioxide, making the social cost private so every producer saves by polluting less — Africa's first such tax

economics.grade12.sustainability-measure.subject: economics
economics.grade12.sustainability-measure.question: Tradable permits work by:
options: Letting each firm choose its own cap
Fixing prices and letting pollution vary freely
Capping total pollution and letting firms trade allowances — the cap secures the outcome, trading finds the cheapest cutters

economics.grade12.sustainability-measure.subject: economics
economics.grade12.sustainability-measure.question: Community ownership of conservancies cures a commons problem because:
options: It removes wildlife from the economy
Wildlife becomes a village asset with a defending owner instead of a poaching target owned by nobody

economics.grade12.sustainability-measure.subject: economics
economics.grade12.sustainability-measure.question: The Montreal Protocol of 1987 matters as:
options: The most successful environmental treaty — CFCs phased out, the ozone layer healing — proof that cooperation can work
The treaty that created carbon markets
A failed attempt to ban coal

economics.grade12.sustainability-measure.subject: economics
economics.grade12.sustainability-measure.question: The Rio Earth Summit of 1992 produced:
options: The Kyoto targets and the Paris rulebook
Agenda 21, the Convention on Biological Diversity, and the UNFCCC with its common-but-differentiated-responsibilities principle

economics.grade12.sustainability-measure.subject: economics
economics.grade12.sustainability-measure.question: Paris 2015 differs from Kyoto 1997 in that Paris is:
options: Universal but voluntary — every nation sets its own progressively tightened contributions, aiming well below two degrees
An agreement between the US and China alone

economics.grade12.sustainability-measure.subject: economics
economics.grade12.sustainability-measure.question: South Africa's Just Energy Transition Partnership involves:
options: The IMF lending for new coal stations
A ban on all mining by 2030
Wealthy nations pledging 8,5 billion dollars to help decarbonise without abandoning coal workers and coal towns

economics.grade12.sustainability-measure.subject: economics
economics.grade12.sustainability-measure.question: The factory's books look excellent while the village suffers because:
options: The biggest cost of production — medicine, lost catches, boiled water — lands outside the factory's fence and appears in nobody's invoice

economics.grade12.sustainability-measure.subject: economics
economics.grade12.sustainability-measure.question: Nobody dumps sludge in their own yard, yet the river gets dumped in, because:
options: The yard has a defending owner and the river has no owner to send the bill — what everybody owns, nobody protects
Dumping in rivers is legal everywhere

geography.grade10.atmosphere-geomorpholo.subject: geography
geography.grade10.atmosphere-geomorpholo.question: Where contour lines cross a river valley, they form a V that points:

geography.grade10.atmosphere-geomorpholo.subject: geography
geography.grade10.atmosphere-geomorpholo.question: Two points differ by 200 metres in height and lie 4 000 metres apart. The gradient is:

geography.grade10.atmosphere-geomorpholo.subject: geography
geography.grade10.atmosphere-geomorpholo.question: As a cold front passes over Cape Town, the weather changes to:
options: A temperature drop, wind swinging south-westerly, rising pressure and showers
Warmer air, northerly wind and falling pressure
Clear skies and calm winds immediately

geography.grade10.atmosphere-geomorpholo.subject: geography
geography.grade10.atmosphere-geomorpholo.question: Mountaintops are cold although they are nearer the sun because:
options: The atmosphere is heated from below, and summits are further from the warmed surface air
Wind removes all heat at altitude

geography.grade10.atmosphere-geomorpholo.subject: geography
geography.grade10.atmosphere-geomorpholo.question: The three lifts that force air to rise and make rain are:
options: Hot ground convection, mountain barriers, and cold fronts wedging under warm air
Ozone, carbon dioxide and water vapour

geography.grade10.atmosphere-geomorpholo.subject: geography
geography.grade10.atmosphere-geomorpholo.question: Blanket against sunscreen distinguishes:
options: Greenhouse gases trapping outgoing heat from the ozone layer blocking incoming ultraviolet

geography.grade10.atmosphere-geomorpholo.subject: geography
geography.grade10.atmosphere-geomorpholo.question: In the eggshell picture, the jostling of the shell pieces is driven by:
options: Slow convection currents in the mantle dragging the plates
The moon's gravity pulling the crust

geography.grade10.atmosphere-geomorpholo.subject: geography
geography.grade10.atmosphere-geomorpholo.question: The East African Rift Valley is best described as:
options: A fold mountain range being squeezed upward
A widening trench where the continent is pulling apart between faults

geography.grade10.atmosphere-geomorpholo.subject: geography
geography.grade10.atmosphere-geomorpholo.question: The Cape Fold Mountains formed when:
options: A volcano built them layer by layer
Rock layers were slowly squeezed and buckled into folds around 300 million years ago
A rift valley dropped between two faults
Glaciers carved them from a plateau

geography.grade10.atmosphere-geomorpholo.subject: geography
geography.grade10.atmosphere-geomorpholo.question: The epicentre of an earthquake is:
options: The underground point where the rock snaps
The instrument that records the shaking
The zone that feels no shaking at all
The point on the surface directly above the focus

geography.grade10.atmosphere-geomorpholo.subject: geography
geography.grade10.atmosphere-geomorpholo.question: In the bathtub picture, tightly packed rings on the toy mountain mean:
options: A steep slope, because height changes quickly over a short distance
A gentle slope, because the water drained slowly

geography.grade10.atmosphere-geomorpholo.subject: geography
geography.grade10.atmosphere-geomorpholo.question: The spoken gradient routine is:
options: Multiply the two heights and halve the answer
Add height difference to distance and divide by two
Find the height difference, convert the map distance with the scale, divide distance by height, and state it as 1 in the answer
Count the contour lines and multiply by the scale

geography.grade10.atmosphere-geomorpholo.subject: geography
geography.grade10.atmosphere-geomorpholo.question: On a station model, temperature and dew point sitting close together warn that:
options: The air is nearly saturated and rain is close
Pressure is about to rise sharply

geography.grade10.atmosphere-geomorpholo.subject: geography
geography.grade10.atmosphere-geomorpholo.question: The feathers on a station model's wind shaft show:
options: The chance of rain as a percentage

geography.grade10.atmosphere-layers-and-.subject: geography
geography.grade10.atmosphere-layers-and-.question: By volume, dry air is approximately:

geography.grade10.atmosphere-layers-and-.subject: geography
geography.grade10.atmosphere-layers-and-.question: Why are the standard percentages always quoted for DRY air?
options: Because water vapour is a VARIABLE component, ranging from almost nothing to about 4%, so including it would make the figures unstable
Because instruments cannot measure moist air
Because water vapour is not a gas

geography.grade10.atmosphere-layers-and-.subject: geography
geography.grade10.atmosphere-layers-and-.question: The main role of nitrogen in the atmosphere is to:
options: DILUTE oxygen so combustion proceeds at a controllable rate, and supply the raw material that fixing bacteria convert for plant proteins

geography.grade10.atmosphere-layers-and-.subject: geography
geography.grade10.atmosphere-layers-and-.question: Dust and other aerosols matter to weather mainly because they:
options: Act as CONDENSATION NUCLEI — surfaces for water vapour to condense onto, without which raindrops struggle to form

geography.grade10.atmosphere-layers-and-.subject: geography
geography.grade10.atmosphere-layers-and-.question: The atmosphere is divided into layers on the basis of:
options: The direction in which temperature changes with height

geography.grade10.atmosphere-layers-and-.subject: geography
geography.grade10.atmosphere-layers-and-.question: Temperature FALLS with height in the troposphere at about 6,5 °C per 1 000 m because:
options: The sun is further away higher up
The atmosphere is heated FROM BELOW by long-wave radiation from the earth's surface, so distance from that source means cooler air

geography.grade10.atmosphere-layers-and-.subject: geography
geography.grade10.atmosphere-layers-and-.question: Temperature RISES with height in the stratosphere because:
options: It is closer to the thermosphere
The ozone layer at 20–30 km absorbs ultraviolet radiation and converts it to heat

geography.grade10.atmosphere-layers-and-.subject: geography
geography.grade10.atmosphere-layers-and-.question: The coldest part of the entire atmosphere, at about −90 °C, is the:
options: MESOPAUSE — the ceiling of the mesosphere, which has no ozone to warm it

geography.grade10.atmosphere-layers-and-.subject: geography
geography.grade10.atmosphere-layers-and-.question: The ozone layer's function is to:
options: Absorb most incoming ultraviolet-B and ultraviolet-C radiation before it reaches the surface
Trap long-wave radiation leaving the earth

geography.grade10.atmosphere-layers-and-.subject: geography
geography.grade10.atmosphere-layers-and-.question: CFCs are so damaging because they:
options: Are heavier than air and sink
Are chemically stable, so rain cannot wash them out and they drift into the stratosphere, where UV frees chlorine that destroys ozone CATALYTICALLY — one atom wrecking thousands of molecules

geography.grade10.atmosphere-layers-and-.subject: geography
geography.grade10.atmosphere-layers-and-.question: Which effect of ozone depletion damages the base of the marine food web?
options: Damage to phytoplankton from extra ultraviolet radiation, with knock-on effects for fisheries

geography.grade10.atmosphere-layers-and-.subject: geography
geography.grade10.atmosphere-layers-and-.question: The essential distinction the lesson insists on is that:
options: Both problems occur in the mesosphere
Ozone depletion is caused by carbon dioxide
The greenhouse effect thins the ozone layer
Ozone depletion lets radiation IN through the stratosphere; the greenhouse effect traps heat in the troposphere — different gases, layer and mechanism

geography.grade10.atmosphere-layers-and-.subject: geography
geography.grade10.atmosphere-layers-and-.question: Without the natural greenhouse effect, the earth's average surface temperature would be about:

geography.grade10.atmosphere-layers-and-.subject: geography
geography.grade10.atmosphere-layers-and-.question: When a temperature-versus-height graph is supplied, the fastest way to identify every layer is to:
options: Work from the TURNING POINTS — each reversal is a pause (tropopause, stratopause, mesopause) and locates the layers
Measure the length of the line

geography.grade10.atmosphere-layers-and-.subject: geography
geography.grade10.atmosphere-layers-and-.question: A complete description of any single layer must give:
options: Height range, direction of temperature change, the REASON for that change, and a distinguishing feature

geography.grade10.atmosphere-layers-and-.subject: geography
geography.grade10.atmosphere-layers-and-.question: Ozone at ground level, produced by traffic and industry, is:
options: Part of the protective ozone layer
A POLLUTANT — the same molecule, opposite verdict, decided entirely by altitude

geography.grade10.atmosphere-layers-and-.subject: geography
geography.grade10.atmosphere-layers-and-.question: In the bag of one hundred marbles standing for dry air:
options: 78 are nitrogen, 21 are oxygen, and one marble covers everything else

geography.grade10.atmosphere-layers-and-.subject: geography
geography.grade10.atmosphere-layers-and-.question: Nitrogen is compared to the water you add to Oros concentrate because it:
options: DILUTES the oxygen, so fire burns steadily instead of tearing away

geography.grade10.atmosphere-layers-and-.subject: geography
geography.grade10.atmosphere-layers-and-.question: Why does Durban air in February differ so much from Upington air in winter?
options: Different amounts of WATER VAPOUR — the ingredient that refuses to stay still, which is why the textbook figures say 'dry air'

geography.grade10.atmosphere-layers-and-.subject: geography
geography.grade10.atmosphere-layers-and-.question: On the ground floor — the troposphere — the 'heater' is:
options: The FLOOR itself: the ground absorbs sunshine and radiates warmth upward, so it gets colder as you climb

geography.grade10.atmosphere-layers-and-.subject: geography
geography.grade10.atmosphere-layers-and-.question: Aeroplanes cruise in the bottom of the first floor — the stratosphere — because:
options: Warm air sitting on top of cool air acts as a lid: nothing rises, nothing churns, no clouds form — smooth flying above the weather

geography.grade10.atmosphere-layers-and-.subject: geography
geography.grade10.atmosphere-layers-and-.question: The top floor — the thermosphere — reads thousands of degrees yet would freeze you because:
options: The thermometer is broken up there
There is almost no air there to touch you and pass the heat on

geography.grade10.atmosphere-layers-and-.subject: geography
geography.grade10.atmosphere-layers-and-.question: Climbing the four storeys in order, the temperature pattern goes:
options: DOWN, UP, DOWN, UP — troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, thermosphere

geography.grade10.atmosphere-layers-and-.subject: geography
geography.grade10.atmosphere-layers-and-.question: Squeezed down to sea-level pressure, the whole ozone layer would be a film about:
options: Three millimetres thick — roughly the edge of a two-rand coin

geography.grade10.atmosphere-layers-and-.subject: geography
geography.grade10.atmosphere-layers-and-.question: The 'master key' image describes chlorine because one chlorine atom:
options: Destroys thousands of ozone molecules one after another, because it is not used up in the reaction

geography.grade10.atmosphere-layers-and-.subject: geography
geography.grade10.atmosphere-layers-and-.question: The practical habit named for ordinary households is to:
options: Have old fridges and air-conditioners DEGASSED by a technician rather than dumped on a scrapheap

geography.grade10.atmosphere-layers-and-.subject: geography
geography.grade10.atmosphere-layers-and-.question: The Montreal Protocol is described as rare because:
options: It is the environmental problem the world genuinely fixed — CFCs were phased out and the layer is measurably healing

geography.grade10.earthquakes-causes-mea.subject: geography
geography.grade10.earthquakes-causes-mea.question: The epicentre of an earthquake is:
options: The point within the crust where the rupture begins
The point on the earth's surface directly above the focus
The deepest point reached by seismic waves

geography.grade10.earthquakes-causes-mea.subject: geography
geography.grade10.earthquakes-causes-mea.question: Elastic rebound describes how:
options: Rock bends and stores strain energy until friction is overcome, then snaps back, releasing that energy as vibrations
Magma pushes the crust upward until it cracks
Ocean waves strike the coast and shake the land
The earth's magnetic field reverses and jolts the crust

geography.grade10.earthquakes-causes-mea.subject: geography
geography.grade10.earthquakes-causes-mea.question: Shallow-focus earthquakes are the most destructive because:
options: They release more total energy than deep ones
The energy is released close to the surface, so less of it is absorbed before the shaking reaches buildings

geography.grade10.earthquakes-causes-mea.subject: geography
geography.grade10.earthquakes-causes-mea.question: Most earth tremors felt in Gauteng and the Free State goldfields are:
options: Caused by the East African Rift
Induced by deep mining rather than by plate tectonics

geography.grade10.earthquakes-causes-mea.subject: geography
geography.grade10.earthquakes-causes-mea.question: Which seismic wave arrives FIRST and can travel through solids, liquids and gases?

geography.grade10.earthquakes-causes-mea.subject: geography
geography.grade10.earthquakes-causes-mea.question: Which wave causes MOST of the damage in an earthquake?
options: The P-wave, because it is fastest
The surface wave, because it has the largest amplitude and swings the ground furthest
The S-wave, because it cannot pass through liquid
None — damage is caused by the fault itself

geography.grade10.earthquakes-causes-mea.subject: geography
geography.grade10.earthquakes-causes-mea.question: The time gap between the P-wave and S-wave arrivals at a station tells you:
options: The depth of the focus in kilometres
The DISTANCE from that station to the epicentre

geography.grade10.earthquakes-causes-mea.subject: geography
geography.grade10.earthquakes-causes-mea.question: Three recording stations are needed to locate an epicentre because:
options: Each station measures a different wave type
One station cannot record surface waves
One station gives only a distance — a circle of possible positions — and three circles intersect at a single point

geography.grade10.earthquakes-causes-mea.subject: geography
geography.grade10.earthquakes-causes-mea.question: The Richter scale measures:
options: Magnitude — the energy released at the focus, giving one value per earthquake
Intensity — the damage observed at each place

geography.grade10.earthquakes-causes-mea.subject: geography
geography.grade10.earthquakes-causes-mea.question: Compared with a magnitude 5 earthquake, a magnitude 7 earthquake releases approximately:
options: 1 000 times the energy, with 100 times the ground movement
100 times the energy, with 1 000 times the ground movement

geography.grade10.earthquakes-causes-mea.subject: geography
geography.grade10.earthquakes-causes-mea.question: Why does one earthquake produce MANY Mercalli values?
options: Because different countries use different scales
Because the magnitude changes as the waves travel
Because intensity records observed effects, which vary with distance, ground conditions and building quality

geography.grade10.earthquakes-causes-mea.subject: geography
geography.grade10.earthquakes-causes-mea.question: Two towns the same distance from the epicentre record different Mercalli intensities. The most likely reason is:
options: One town measured the P-wave and the other the S-wave
The Richter magnitude differed between them
One town is built on loose sediment that amplifies shaking, the other on solid bedrock

geography.grade10.earthquakes-causes-mea.subject: geography
geography.grade10.earthquakes-causes-mea.question: Which of these is a SECONDARY effect of an earthquake?
options: Liquefaction, in which saturated loose sediment loses strength and buildings tilt and sink
Ground rupture along the fault line
The initial shaking of the ground
The release of energy at the focus

geography.grade10.earthquakes-causes-mea.subject: geography
geography.grade10.earthquakes-causes-mea.question: A tsunami is generated when:
options: Strong winds blow across a warm ocean
An undersea earthquake displaces the sea bed vertically, lifting the whole water column above it
A volcano erupts on land near the coast
Two rivers meet at a delta

geography.grade10.earthquakes-causes-mea.subject: geography
geography.grade10.earthquakes-causes-mea.question: The MAIN reason death tolls differ hugely between earthquakes of similar magnitude is:
options: Differences in the type of seismic wave produced
Differences in the time of year
Differences in vulnerability — building quality and enforcement, density, wealth, preparedness and ground conditions
Differences in the Richter scale used

geography.grade10.earthquakes-causes-mea.subject: geography
geography.grade10.earthquakes-causes-mea.question: Base isolators fitted under a building work by:
options: Making the building heavier so it cannot move
Absorbing the sound of the earthquake
Letting the ground move while the building above stays comparatively still

geography.grade10.earthquakes-causes-mea.subject: geography
geography.grade10.earthquakes-causes-mea.question: In the bent-ruler comparison, the moment the ruler snaps represents:
options: The arrival of the surface wave
The focus — where the fault finally slips and stored energy is released

geography.grade10.earthquakes-causes-mea.subject: geography
geography.grade10.earthquakes-causes-mea.question: If the rupture happens three kilometres beneath a soccer field, the epicentre is:
options: Wherever the shaking is felt last
The middle of the soccer field, on the surface directly above the focus

geography.grade10.earthquakes-causes-mea.subject: geography
geography.grade10.earthquakes-causes-mea.question: Why are people kept out of damaged buildings after the main shock?
options: Because the Richter value has not yet been calculated
Because surface waves keep travelling for weeks
Because aftershocks continue for days or months and can finish off structures the main shock only cracked

geography.grade10.earthquakes-causes-mea.subject: geography
geography.grade10.earthquakes-causes-mea.question: The lightning-and-thunder comparison explains:
options: Why the gap between the P-wave and S-wave arrivals grows with distance from the epicentre
Why deep earthquakes are less damaging
How the Richter scale is calculated

geography.grade10.earthquakes-causes-mea.subject: geography
geography.grade10.earthquakes-causes-mea.question: An S-wave is best pictured as:
options: A bump running down a stretched spring
A ripple running along a flicked skipping rope — sideways shaking
A rolling swell along the ground surface
A sound wave in the air

geography.grade10.earthquakes-causes-mea.subject: geography
geography.grade10.earthquakes-causes-mea.question: A station records a very SHORT gap between the P and S arrivals. This means the station is:

geography.grade10.earthquakes-causes-mea.subject: geography
geography.grade10.earthquakes-causes-mea.question: Triangulation locates an epicentre by:
options: Measuring the magnitude at three depths
Comparing Mercalli values in three towns
Drawing a distance circle around each of three stations and finding the single point where they intersect

geography.grade10.earthquakes-causes-mea.subject: geography
geography.grade10.earthquakes-causes-mea.question: In the stadium sound-system comparison, the Mercalli scale is like:
options: How loud it actually sounded where you were standing
The size of the amplifier at the source

geography.grade10.earthquakes-causes-mea.subject: geography
geography.grade10.earthquakes-causes-mea.question: Which statement about earthquake prediction is CORRECT?
options: Seismologists can name the exact date of the next major earthquake
High-risk zones and long-term probabilities can be identified, but no one can name a date, so preparedness matters more than prediction
Animal behaviour gives reliable warning a week ahead
Earthquakes cannot be studied at all before they happen

geography.grade10.earthquakes-causes-mea.subject: geography
geography.grade10.earthquakes-causes-mea.question: The recommended personal action during strong shaking is:
options: Stand in an open doorway on the top floor
Drop, take cover under something solid, and hold on
Use the lift to reach ground level

geography.grade10.earthquakes-causes-mea.subject: geography
geography.grade10.earthquakes-causes-mea.question: "Earthquakes do not kill people; falling buildings do" is used in the lesson to make the point that:
options: Magnitude does not matter at all
Deaths depend largely on construction quality, enforcement of codes, ground conditions and preparedness

geography.grade10.floods-causes-and-hydr.subject: geography
geography.grade10.floods-causes-and-hydr.question: Fifty millimetres of rain in one hour is more dangerous than the same fifty over a week because:
options: Intense rain overwhelms the ground's ability to absorb it, so most becomes immediate runoff
Rain gauges cannot measure hourly rain

geography.grade10.floods-causes-and-hydr.subject: geography
geography.grade10.floods-causes-and-hydr.question: A cut-off low causes major floods because it:
options: Breaks away from the upper westerlies and stalls, wringing rain over the same region for days

geography.grade10.floods-causes-and-hydr.subject: geography
geography.grade10.floods-causes-and-hydr.question: Antecedent moisture matters because a saturated catchment:
options: Turns almost all further rain directly into runoff
Absorbs more rain than a dry one

geography.grade10.floods-causes-and-hydr.subject: geography
geography.grade10.floods-causes-and-hydr.question: A compact, round catchment tends to produce higher flood peaks than a long narrow one because:
options: It receives more rainfall in total
All its water arrives at one point at nearly the same time, stacking the flow

geography.grade10.floods-causes-and-hydr.subject: geography
geography.grade10.floods-causes-and-hydr.question: Urbanisation increases flooding chiefly because:
options: City rivers are narrower than rural ones
Urban trees drink too much water
Tar, rooftops and paving seal the ground, and stormwater drains deliver runoff to rivers fast

geography.grade10.floods-causes-and-hydr.subject: geography
geography.grade10.floods-causes-and-hydr.question: Destroying a wetland worsens floods because a wetland:
options: Is a natural sponge that stores floodwater and releases it slowly

geography.grade10.floods-causes-and-hydr.subject: geography
geography.grade10.floods-causes-and-hydr.question: Deforestation and overgrazing add a second injury beyond faster runoff:
options: They lower the water table permanently
Eroded silt settles in channels and dams, raising riverbeds and shrinking flood capacity

geography.grade10.floods-causes-and-hydr.subject: geography
geography.grade10.floods-causes-and-hydr.question: Flood risk in South Africa is distributed by inequality means:
options: Those with the least choice — informal settlements — occupy the most dangerous flood-prone land
Insurance covers all flood damage equally

geography.grade10.floods-causes-and-hydr.subject: geography
geography.grade10.floods-causes-and-hydr.question: On a flood hydrograph, the axes show:
options: Time on the horizontal axis and discharge in cumecs on the vertical axis

geography.grade10.floods-causes-and-hydr.subject: geography
geography.grade10.floods-causes-and-hydr.question: Base flow is:
options: The river's everyday flow, fed by groundwater seeping into the channel
The lowest point of the flood peak

geography.grade10.floods-causes-and-hydr.subject: geography
geography.grade10.floods-causes-and-hydr.question: Lag time is the interval between:
options: The start and end of rainfall
Base flow and the rising limb
The heaviest rainfall and peak discharge

geography.grade10.floods-causes-and-hydr.subject: geography
geography.grade10.floods-causes-and-hydr.question: The falling limb descends more gently than the rising limb climbed because:
options: The last water arrives by slower routes — through the soil and from the furthest parts of the catchment
Measuring stations record falling water badly

geography.grade10.floods-causes-and-hydr.subject: geography
geography.grade10.floods-causes-and-hydr.question: Compared with a rural vegetated catchment in the same storm, an urbanised catchment's hydrograph shows:
options: A longer lag and lower peak
A shorter lag, a higher narrower peak and steeper limbs
A higher base flow between storms

geography.grade10.floods-causes-and-hydr.subject: geography
geography.grade10.floods-causes-and-hydr.question: The rural sponge catchment keeps a persistent base flow between storms because:
options: Infiltrated water recharges groundwater, which keeps feeding the channel

geography.grade10.floods-causes-and-hydr.subject: geography
geography.grade10.floods-causes-and-hydr.question: The Laingsburg flood of January 1981 was a flash flood because:
options: A cut-off low dumped over 400 mm in about two days onto bare rocky catchments, giving almost no lag time
It lasted several weeks across many provinces
It was caused by a dam failure
It happened at the coast during a cyclone

geography.grade10.floods-causes-and-hydr.subject: geography
geography.grade10.floods-causes-and-hydr.question: A regional flood, like KwaZulu-Natal in April 2022, differs from a flash flood by:
options: Being caused only by burst pipes
Building over one to several days across a wide area, slower to arrive but vast in extent and duration
Peaking within minutes in a single valley

geography.grade10.floods-causes-and-hydr.subject: geography
geography.grade10.floods-causes-and-hydr.question: In the yard experiment, the corrugated iron sheet represents:
options: Surfaces that reject infiltration — rock, baked or saturated ground, and the paved city

geography.grade10.floods-causes-and-hydr.subject: geography
geography.grade10.floods-causes-and-hydr.question: A full sponge IS a sheet of iron means:
options: Wetlands turn to rock over time
A saturated catchment sheds the next storm as if it were sealed

geography.grade10.floods-causes-and-hydr.subject: geography
geography.grade10.floods-causes-and-hydr.question: Intensity beats total means:
options: The biggest storms always have the most water
A hard hour of rain that outpaces the ground's drinking speed floods where the same water as all-day drizzle would soak away

geography.grade10.floods-causes-and-hydr.subject: geography
geography.grade10.floods-causes-and-hydr.question: Real rivers still flow in the dry season because:
options: Base flow — groundwater seeping steadily into the channel — sustains them
Dew collects in the channel overnight

geography.grade10.floods-causes-and-hydr.subject: geography
geography.grade10.floods-causes-and-hydr.question: The river does not rise the moment the rain starts because:
options: Water needs time to travel from the hills to the gauge — the lag time
The gauge only reads once a day
Rivers rise before the rain arrives

geography.grade10.floods-causes-and-hydr.subject: geography
geography.grade10.floods-causes-and-hydr.question: The three questions for interpreting any hydrograph are:
options: How wide, how deep, how muddy
How high the peak, how soon after the rain, how steep the climb
How long, how cold, how fast
Which river, which town, which month

geography.grade10.floods-causes-and-hydr.subject: geography
geography.grade10.floods-causes-and-hydr.question: After a storm, base flow settles slightly higher than before because:
options: Stormwater drains keep discharging for weeks
The recharged soil now feeds the channel more generously

geography.grade10.floods-causes-and-hydr.subject: geography
geography.grade10.floods-causes-and-hydr.question: At Laingsburg in 1981, the catchment answered like a corrugated roof because:
options: The town had paved its entire catchment
Bare rock and baked Karoo soil could absorb almost nothing of the extreme rain
The Buffels River was dammed upstream

geography.grade10.floods-causes-and-hydr.subject: geography
geography.grade10.floods-causes-and-hydr.question: In the April 2022 eThekwini floods, the deaths were concentrated in:
options: Informal settlements on steep slopes and low riverside land

geography.grade10.floods-causes-and-hydr.subject: geography
geography.grade10.floods-causes-and-hydr.question: The pair of floods illustrates the two flood characters as:
options: Laingsburg the spike-hydrograph flash flood; eThekwini the broad, sustained regional flood
Both were flash floods lasting minutes
eThekwini the flash flood; Laingsburg the regional flood

geography.grade10.floods-causes-and-hydr.subject: geography
geography.grade10.floods-causes-and-hydr.question: The remedies read off the hydrograph all aim to:
options: Shorten the lag and raise the peak
Stop rain from falling on catchments
Lengthen lag time and lower the peak — sponges restored, floodplains respected, drains maintained, warnings issued

geography.grade10.folds-faults-and-the-l.subject: geography
geography.grade10.folds-faults-and-the-l.question: Compression, tension and shearing are associated respectively with which plate boundaries?

geography.grade10.folds-faults-and-the-l.subject: geography
geography.grade10.folds-faults-and-the-l.question: Rock deep in the crust tends to FOLD rather than fault because:
options: It is always made of granite
Heat and confining pressure make it behave plastically, so it deforms without fracturing
There is no force acting at depth

geography.grade10.folds-faults-and-the-l.subject: geography
geography.grade10.folds-faults-and-the-l.question: The correct order in which rock responds to increasing stress is:
options: Elastic deformation, plastic deformation, fracture and displacement

geography.grade10.folds-faults-and-the-l.subject: geography
geography.grade10.folds-faults-and-the-l.question: Which condition makes fracturing (faulting) MORE likely than folding?
options: Very slow application of force over millions of years
Sudden application of force to cold, brittle surface rock

geography.grade10.folds-faults-and-the-l.subject: geography
geography.grade10.folds-faults-and-the-l.question: An anticline is:
options: A downfold, or trough, in the strata
An upfold, or arch, with limbs dipping away on both sides and the oldest rocks at its core
A fracture along which rock has moved
A block of crust dropped between two faults

geography.grade10.folds-faults-and-the-l.subject: geography
geography.grade10.folds-faults-and-the-l.question: Arrange these folds in order of INCREASING compression:

geography.grade10.folds-faults-and-the-l.subject: geography
geography.grade10.folds-faults-and-the-l.question: Inversion of relief occurs because:
options: Synclines are always made of softer rock
Rivers only ever flow along anticlines
Rock stretched over an anticline crest cracks and erodes faster, while compressed syncline rock resists, so the arch may become a valley and the trough a ridge

geography.grade10.folds-faults-and-the-l.subject: geography
geography.grade10.folds-faults-and-the-l.question: The sloping sides of a fold are called its:

geography.grade10.folds-faults-and-the-l.subject: geography
geography.grade10.folds-faults-and-the-l.question: What distinguishes a fault from an ordinary crack or joint in rock?
options: Rock has actually MOVED along a fault
A fault is filled with lava
A fault occurs only in sedimentary rock

geography.grade10.folds-faults-and-the-l.subject: geography
geography.grade10.folds-faults-and-the-l.question: In a NORMAL fault:
options: Compression drives the hanging wall up over the footwall
Movement is purely horizontal with no throw
Tension causes the hanging wall to slide DOWN relative to the footwall, leaving a fault scarp
Two plates slide past each other creating a trench

geography.grade10.folds-faults-and-the-l.subject: geography
geography.grade10.folds-faults-and-the-l.question: A block of crust that DROPS between two parallel normal faults is called a:
options: Horst, seen as a block mountain
Graben, seen at the surface as a rift valley

geography.grade10.folds-faults-and-the-l.subject: geography
geography.grade10.folds-faults-and-the-l.question: The vertical displacement along a fault plane is the throw. The horizontal displacement is the:

geography.grade10.folds-faults-and-the-l.subject: geography
geography.grade10.folds-faults-and-the-l.question: The Cape Fold Mountains were formed:
options: By volcanic eruptions about 5 million years ago
By compression roughly 250 to 280 million years ago, while Gondwana was being assembled
By tension along the East African Rift
By glacial erosion during the last ice age

geography.grade10.folds-faults-and-the-l.subject: geography
geography.grade10.folds-faults-and-the-l.question: The characteristic landscape pattern of the Cape Fold Mountains is:
options: Isolated flat-topped blocks with steep straight sides
Long, narrow, parallel ranges separated by long, narrow valleys
A staircase of step faults descending to the sea

geography.grade10.folds-faults-and-the-l.subject: geography
geography.grade10.folds-faults-and-the-l.question: Why are the valleys between the Cape ranges so intensively farmed?
options: They are sheltered, have deep soils washed down from the ridges, and are watered by rivers rising in the mountains
They are the only flat land in South Africa
They receive no rainfall at all, which suits vines

geography.grade10.folds-faults-and-the-l.subject: geography
geography.grade10.folds-faults-and-the-l.question: The recommended order for describing any structure in an answer is:
options: The force, the response of the rock, the shape produced, the resulting landform

geography.grade10.folds-faults-and-the-l.subject: geography
geography.grade10.folds-faults-and-the-l.question: Pushing a rug across a floor until it rides up into ridges illustrates:

geography.grade10.folds-faults-and-the-l.subject: geography
geography.grade10.folds-faults-and-the-l.question: The chocolate comparison — sagging when pressed slowly, shattering when hit — illustrates that:
options: Rock type is the only thing that matters
The RATE at which force is applied helps decide whether rock bends or breaks

geography.grade10.folds-faults-and-the-l.subject: geography
geography.grade10.folds-faults-and-the-l.question: Which rock is MOST likely to bend rather than snap?
options: Layered sandstone and shale deep in the crust

geography.grade10.folds-faults-and-the-l.subject: geography
geography.grade10.folds-faults-and-the-l.question: A syncline is best pictured as:
options: A trough or smile shape, with the layers sagging to a low point

geography.grade10.folds-faults-and-the-l.subject: geography
geography.grade10.folds-faults-and-the-l.question: Bending a stack of newspaper cracks the OUTSIDE of the bend. In rock, this explains why:
options: Faults never form in folded rock
The crest of an anticline is stretched, cracked and attacked hardest by weathering and erosion
Folds cannot occur in sedimentary rock

geography.grade10.folds-faults-and-the-l.subject: geography
geography.grade10.folds-faults-and-the-l.question: A fold that has been pushed over so far that it lies almost flat is called:

geography.grade10.folds-faults-and-the-l.subject: geography
geography.grade10.folds-faults-and-the-l.question: Inversion of relief means that in the finished landscape:
options: The anticline may form a valley and the syncline may stand up as a ridge
The rock layers turn upside down

geography.grade10.folds-faults-and-the-l.subject: geography
geography.grade10.folds-faults-and-the-l.question: Standing on the floor of a rift valley, you would see:
options: A rounded, curved mountain crest on all sides
Flat ground in front of you with a long straight cliff wall on either side, and often a deep lake between them
A circular crater with a lava plug
A staircase of terraces climbing to a single summit

geography.grade10.folds-faults-and-the-l.subject: geography
geography.grade10.folds-faults-and-the-l.question: A block mountain (horst) is recognised in the landscape by:
options: Curved, wavy crests running in parallel ranges
A cone shape with a crater at the summit
Steep straight sides and a flat top, as though cut with a knife

geography.grade10.folds-faults-and-the-l.subject: geography
geography.grade10.folds-faults-and-the-l.question: Many parallel faults each dropping the land a little further produce:
options: Step faulting — a landscape descending like a staircase

geography.grade10.folds-faults-and-the-l.subject: geography
geography.grade10.folds-faults-and-the-l.question: Driving from Worcester through the Hex River Valley — mountains left, mountains right, a fertile valley of vineyards between, repeating for a hundred kilometres — you are looking at:
options: Folding, from compression during the building of Gondwana
Step faulting along a transform boundary

geography.grade10.free-basic-water-and-s.subject: geography
geography.grade10.free-basic-water-and-s.question: The free basic water policy entitles every poor household each month to:
options: 6 000 litres — six kilolitres — of clean water free of charge

geography.grade10.free-basic-water-and-s.subject: geography
geography.grade10.free-basic-water-and-s.question: The six kilolitre figure is calculated from:
options: The average size of a municipal dam
25 litres per person per day for a household of eight
150 litres per person per day for a family of four

geography.grade10.free-basic-water-and-s.subject: geography
geography.grade10.free-basic-water-and-s.question: The rising block tariff is double-edged because it:
options: Charges everyone the same rate per litre
Makes all water free in drought years
Protects the poor in the cheap first blocks while charging heavy users rates that discourage waste

geography.grade10.free-basic-water-and-s.subject: geography
geography.grade10.free-basic-water-and-s.question: Access on paper is not water in the hand means:
options: A household counted as having access may share a distant standpipe or depend on broken infrastructure
The constitution does not mention water
Households must apply in writing for water

geography.grade10.free-basic-water-and-s.subject: geography
geography.grade10.free-basic-water-and-s.question: Serving dispersed rural settlements costs far more per household than serving a suburb because:
options: Small clusters of homes scattered across huge, often mountainous areas need long pipes for few users

geography.grade10.free-basic-water-and-s.subject: geography
geography.grade10.free-basic-water-and-s.question: When rural schemes break down, the burden falls heavily on women and children, who:
options: Walk kilometres carrying water containers, at a cost in school hours, safety and health
Are always supplied first by tankers

geography.grade10.free-basic-water-and-s.subject: geography
geography.grade10.free-basic-water-and-s.question: Non-revenue water is:
options: Treated water lost to leaks, faulty meters or use that is never billed — a third or more of municipal water nationally

geography.grade10.free-basic-water-and-s.subject: geography
geography.grade10.free-basic-water-and-s.question: Informal settlements are especially hard to serve because they:
options: Grow faster than pipes can follow, often on unplanned land such as floodplains or steep ground
Are always far from any city
Use more water per household than suburbs

geography.grade10.free-basic-water-and-s.subject: geography
geography.grade10.free-basic-water-and-s.question: The Lesotho Highlands Water Project works by gravity because:
options: The Vaal flows uphill into Lesotho
Its pumps are powered by coal
The Lesotho highlands catch the region's heaviest precipitation AND stand higher than Gauteng, so tunnel water flows down to the Vaal system

geography.grade10.free-basic-water-and-s.subject: geography
geography.grade10.free-basic-water-and-s.question: Lesotho's side of the bargain includes:
options: Royalties that rank among its largest revenue sources, plus hydro-electric power
A share of South Africa's gold mines

geography.grade10.free-basic-water-and-s.subject: geography
geography.grade10.free-basic-water-and-s.question: The Tugela-Vaal scheme differs from the Lesotho scheme because it:
options: Must pump water UP the escarpment into Sterkfontein Dam, fighting gravity at great cost

geography.grade10.free-basic-water-and-s.subject: geography
geography.grade10.free-basic-water-and-s.question: The correct order of municipal water purification is:
options: Screening, coagulation and flocculation, sedimentation, filtration, disinfection

geography.grade10.free-basic-water-and-s.subject: geography
geography.grade10.free-basic-water-and-s.question: Sustainable water use means:
options: Using as much water as the dams currently hold
Meeting today's needs without crippling tomorrow's supply — using no faster than the system replenishes

geography.grade10.free-basic-water-and-s.subject: geography
geography.grade10.free-basic-water-and-s.question: Working for Water is celebrated as a double win because it:
options: Employs thousands to clear thirsty alien plants, returning runoff to rivers while creating jobs

geography.grade10.free-basic-water-and-s.subject: geography
geography.grade10.free-basic-water-and-s.question: Greywater, which individuals can reuse on gardens, is:
options: Gently used water from basins, baths and washing machines

geography.grade10.free-basic-water-and-s.subject: geography
geography.grade10.free-basic-water-and-s.question: During the 2018 Day Zero crisis, Cape Town's consumption:
options: Was roughly halved — from about a thousand million litres a day toward five hundred million — through saving measures
Fell only because rain returned immediately

geography.grade10.free-basic-water-and-s.subject: geography
geography.grade10.free-basic-water-and-s.question: Twenty-five litres per person per day is best understood as:
options: A floor covering drinking, cooking and a basic wash — a single shower can use more
Enough for a garden and a pool
The amount lost to leaks per person

geography.grade10.free-basic-water-and-s.subject: geography
geography.grade10.free-basic-water-and-s.question: The swimming pool subsidises the standpipe describes:
options: A rule that pools must be shared
Heavy users in expensive tariff blocks funding the free basic blocks of poor households

geography.grade10.free-basic-water-and-s.subject: geography
geography.grade10.free-basic-water-and-s.question: The constitutional anchor of the free basic water policy is:
options: Section 27 — everyone's right of access to sufficient water

geography.grade10.free-basic-water-and-s.subject: geography
geography.grade10.free-basic-water-and-s.question: The two facts that make the Lesotho Highlands scheme work are:
options: Lesotho has more people and more pumps
Lesotho catches the region's heaviest rain and snow, and stands far higher than Johannesburg
Lesotho has desalination plants and a coastline
Lesotho shares the Vaal Dam and the Orange mouth

geography.grade10.free-basic-water-and-s.subject: geography
geography.grade10.free-basic-water-and-s.question: The dams built high in the Maluti mountains for the scheme include:
options: Katse and Mohale, with Polihali being added

geography.grade10.free-basic-water-and-s.subject: geography
geography.grade10.free-basic-water-and-s.question: Gravity is free; fighting gravity is expensive contrasts:
options: The Lesotho tunnels flowing downhill against Tugela-Vaal pumping up the escarpment

geography.grade10.free-basic-water-and-s.subject: geography
geography.grade10.free-basic-water-and-s.question: In the kitchen version of purification, stir in a pinch that makes the fine dirt clump stands for:
options: Coagulation and flocculation with a chemical such as aluminium sulphate

geography.grade10.free-basic-water-and-s.subject: geography
geography.grade10.free-basic-water-and-s.question: Day Zero was:
options: The day Cape Town's dams overflowed
The published date on which Cape Town's municipal taps would be turned off, with residents queuing for a 25-litre daily ration
The start of the Lesotho Highlands project

geography.grade10.free-basic-water-and-s.subject: geography
geography.grade10.free-basic-water-and-s.question: The most important lesson of the Cape Town crisis is that:
options: Only new dams can save a city
The cheapest, fastest new supply is the water people stop wasting — the city halved its use through millions of small decisions
Desalination alone kept the taps open

geography.grade10.free-basic-water-and-s.subject: geography
geography.grade10.free-basic-water-and-s.question: Neither half works alone means:
options: Saving citizens with rotten pipes still lose the water, and perfect pipes with careless households still drain the dams
Rural and urban areas must share dams
The two Lesotho dams must operate together

geography.grade10.free-basic-water-and-s.subject: geography
geography.grade10.free-basic-water-and-s.question: Which belongs on the INDIVIDUAL's half of the sustainability list?
options: Auditing municipal water quality through Blue Drop
Enforcing the National Water Act against polluters
Harvesting roof rainwater, reusing greywater and watering the garden in the cool of evening

geography.grade10.gis-components-and-rem.subject: geography
geography.grade10.gis-components-and-rem.question: A Geographical Information System is best defined as:
options: A satellite that photographs the earth
A paper atlas stored in a library
A computerised system that captures, stores, analyses and displays geographically referenced information
A GPS receiver in a car

geography.grade10.gis-components-and-rem.subject: geography
geography.grade10.gis-components-and-rem.question: A spreadsheet of clinic names becomes geographical information when:
options: Each clinic carries coordinates tying it to a position on the earth's surface
It is emailed to a planner

geography.grade10.gis-components-and-rem.subject: geography
geography.grade10.gis-components-and-rem.question: Overlay analysis means:
options: Printing a map on transparent paper
Stacking georeferenced layers so questions can be answered by combining them — such as finding dense settlement far from clinics
Deleting old layers from the database

geography.grade10.gis-components-and-rem.subject: geography
geography.grade10.gis-components-and-rem.question: For a school stored in a GIS, its position is the spatial data, while its name, learner numbers and language of instruction are:
options: Attribute data linked to the feature

geography.grade10.gis-components-and-rem.subject: geography
geography.grade10.gis-components-and-rem.question: The five components of a GIS are:
options: Hardware, software, data, people and procedures
Satellites, aircraft, drones, balloons and towers
Maps, globes, atlases, photographs and charts
Keyboards, screens, printers, mice and cables

geography.grade10.gis-components-and-rem.subject: geography
geography.grade10.gis-components-and-rem.question: Data is called the most important and most expensive component because:
options: Computers cannot store very much of it
It must be bought from other countries
Without accurate, up-to-date georeferenced data, even the best hardware and software produce misleading results

geography.grade10.gis-components-and-rem.subject: geography
geography.grade10.gis-components-and-rem.question: The procedures component of a GIS covers:
