options: The electrical wiring of the computers
The rules for checking data, updating layers and verifying accuracy

geography.grade10.gis-components-and-rem.subject: geography
geography.grade10.gis-components-and-rem.question: Census results from Statistics South Africa enter GIS work as:
options: Data feeding the layers used for planning

geography.grade10.gis-components-and-rem.subject: geography
geography.grade10.gis-components-and-rem.question: Remote sensing is:
options: Measuring rainfall with gauges on the ground
Gathering information about the earth's surface from a distance, without physical contact, using sensors on satellites or aircraft
Using a compass to find direction

geography.grade10.gis-components-and-rem.subject: geography
geography.grade10.gis-components-and-rem.question: Sensors can reveal things invisible to the human eye because they:
options: Zoom in more than any camera
Read wavelengths such as infrared, in which stressed crops and soil moisture show up

geography.grade10.gis-components-and-rem.subject: geography
geography.grade10.gis-components-and-rem.question: Compared with aerial photographs, satellite images:
options: Cover far larger areas and revisit the same spot on a fixed cycle, building a time series
Show finer detail over smaller areas
Are always free of cloud problems
Are taken from a lower altitude

geography.grade10.gis-components-and-rem.subject: geography
geography.grade10.gis-components-and-rem.question: A key limitation of remote sensing for population studies is that it:
options: Only works in the southern hemisphere
Counts roofs, not names — it cannot ask who lives in a dwelling, so the ground census remains essential

geography.grade10.gis-components-and-rem.subject: geography
geography.grade10.gis-components-and-rem.question: Satellite images help planners serve informal settlements by:
options: Replacing the need for water and clinics
Showing new roof clusters appearing between censuses, which become a GIS layer overlaid with service layers
Predicting the weather for the settlement

geography.grade10.gis-components-and-rem.subject: geography
geography.grade10.gis-components-and-rem.question: Before a census, Statistics South Africa uses aerial and satellite imagery to:
options: Divide the country into small counting areas so no dwelling is missed
Count the population automatically from space

geography.grade10.gis-components-and-rem.subject: geography
geography.grade10.gis-components-and-rem.question: During the April 2022 KwaZulu-Natal floods, before-and-after satellite images were valuable because they:
options: Identified destroyed neighbourhoods and cut roads while the ground was still impassable
Warned residents a year in advance

geography.grade10.gis-components-and-rem.subject: geography
geography.grade10.gis-components-and-rem.question: South Africa's national space agency, which receives satellite data at Hartebeesthoek, is:

geography.grade10.gis-components-and-rem.subject: geography
geography.grade10.gis-components-and-rem.question: In the pizza-search example, the analysis step of the GIS definition is performed when:
options: The phone connects to the internet
The application works out the nearest pizza place and the streets connecting it to you

geography.grade10.gis-components-and-rem.subject: geography
geography.grade10.gis-components-and-rem.question: In the smartphone example, the people component of the GIS is:
options: The user asking the question and choosing the answer
The red pins on the map

geography.grade10.gis-components-and-rem.subject: geography
geography.grade10.gis-components-and-rem.question: Tapping a pin to open a shop's name, menu and rating demonstrates:
options: The link between spatial data — the position — and attribute data — the description

geography.grade10.gis-components-and-rem.subject: geography
geography.grade10.gis-components-and-rem.question: In the transparent-sheets picture, one sheet showing only rivers represents:
options: A single thematic layer, georeferenced to the same ground as the other sheets

geography.grade10.gis-components-and-rem.subject: geography
geography.grade10.gis-components-and-rem.question: Stacking the density, clinic and road sheets reveals an underserved community because:
options: The sheets change colour when stacked
Each sheet answers the question on its own
Dense population shading appears where the clinic layer shows nothing — a combination no single sheet could show

geography.grade10.gis-components-and-rem.subject: geography
geography.grade10.gis-components-and-rem.question: A five-year-old clinic layer is dangerous in a GIS because:
options: The analysis will look convincing while recommending decisions based on outdated reality
Old layers take up too much memory
The computer refuses to load old data
Clinics cannot be mapped after five years

geography.grade10.gis-components-and-rem.subject: geography
geography.grade10.gis-components-and-rem.question: Lining up satellite images of the same place over months and years allows analysts to:
options: Detect change — a shrinking dam, a creeping city edge, a changing coastline
Measure the temperature of the sensor

geography.grade10.gis-components-and-rem.subject: geography
geography.grade10.gis-components-and-rem.question: South Africa's 1 to 10 000 orthophoto maps are built from:
options: Corrected aerial photographs taken from aircraft, detailed enough to show single houses

geography.grade10.gis-components-and-rem.subject: geography
geography.grade10.gis-components-and-rem.question: Healthy crops can be told apart from struggling crops across a whole province because:
options: Healthy plants reflect strongly in infrared, which sensors read but eyes cannot

geography.grade10.gis-components-and-rem.subject: geography
geography.grade10.gis-components-and-rem.question: The lesson's closing point about the satellite and the census enumerator is that:
options: The satellite sees everywhere but the person at the door asks everything — each needs the other
Satellites will soon replace the census entirely
The census only counts urban areas

geography.grade10.heating-of-the-atmosph.subject: geography
geography.grade10.heating-of-the-atmosph.question: Of 100 units of insolation, the approximate split used in the lesson is:
options: 30 reflected back to space, 20 absorbed by the atmosphere, 50 absorbed at the earth's surface
50 reflected, 30 absorbed by the atmosphere, 20 at the surface

geography.grade10.heating-of-the-atmosph.subject: geography
geography.grade10.heating-of-the-atmosph.question: Albedo is:
options: The heat stored in the oceans
The proportion of insolation REFLECTED back to space — high for snow, ice and pale desert soils, low for dark ocean and forest
The rate at which temperature falls with height
The total energy the sun emits

geography.grade10.heating-of-the-atmosph.subject: geography
geography.grade10.heating-of-the-atmosph.question: The earth radiates energy back to space as LONG-WAVE radiation because:
options: The earth is far cooler than the sun, so its emitted radiation is of longer wavelength — and the atmosphere absorbs long-wave well

geography.grade10.heating-of-the-atmosph.subject: geography
geography.grade10.heating-of-the-atmosph.question: Global winds and ocean currents exist chiefly because:
options: The tropics run a permanent energy SURPLUS and the polar regions a permanent DEFICIT, and the imbalance must be transferred

geography.grade10.heating-of-the-atmosph.subject: geography
geography.grade10.heating-of-the-atmosph.question: The transfer of heat HORIZONTALLY by moving air — for example a sea breeze at Muizenberg or a berg wind reaching the coast — is:

geography.grade10.heating-of-the-atmosph.subject: geography
geography.grade10.heating-of-the-atmosph.question: Conduction matters only in the lowest few metres of the atmosphere because:
options: Air is a POOR CONDUCTOR, so molecule-to-molecule transfer reaches no further than the air actually in contact with the ground

geography.grade10.heating-of-the-atmosph.subject: geography
geography.grade10.heating-of-the-atmosph.question: A convection current is established when:
options: Air warmed at the surface expands, becomes less dense and rises, while cooler denser air sinks to replace it

geography.grade10.heating-of-the-atmosph.subject: geography
geography.grade10.heating-of-the-atmosph.question: The single most important consequence in this section is that the atmosphere is heated:
options: Directly by the sun's short-wave radiation
FROM BELOW — insolation passes largely through the air, warms the ground, and the ground then heats the air, which is why temperature falls with height in the troposphere

geography.grade10.heating-of-the-atmosph.subject: geography
geography.grade10.heating-of-the-atmosph.question: The correct order of the greenhouse mechanism is:
options: Short-wave passes through → absorbed by the surface → re-radiated as long-wave → absorbed by greenhouse gases → re-radiated in all directions including back down
Long-wave passes through → absorbed by clouds → reflected to space
Short-wave absorbed by greenhouse gases → radiated to space
Ozone absorbs long-wave → the surface cools

geography.grade10.heating-of-the-atmosph.subject: geography
geography.grade10.heating-of-the-atmosph.question: The NATURAL greenhouse effect is necessary because without it the global average surface temperature would be about:
options: −18 °C instead of about 15 °C — some 33 degrees of habitability

geography.grade10.heating-of-the-atmosph.subject: geography
geography.grade10.heating-of-the-atmosph.question: Which list gives human sources of the ENHANCED greenhouse effect?
options: Volcanic eruptions and ocean currents only
Burning fossil fuels, deforestation, livestock and rice agriculture, landfills, and cement manufacture

geography.grade10.heating-of-the-atmosph.subject: geography
geography.grade10.heating-of-the-atmosph.question: Which is NOT given in the lesson as a consequence of climate change for Africa?
options: Less reliable rainfall and longer droughts in the south and west
Falling maize yields and threatened food security
Malarial mosquitoes moving into higher, cooler areas
A thinning of the ozone layer over the Antarctic

geography.grade10.heating-of-the-atmosph.subject: geography
geography.grade10.heating-of-the-atmosph.question: Temperature falls from equator to poles because at high latitudes the sun's rays:
options: Strike obliquely, so the same beam spreads over a larger area AND travels a longer, more absorbing path through the atmosphere
Are weaker when they leave the sun
Are blocked by the ozone layer

geography.grade10.heating-of-the-atmosph.subject: geography
geography.grade10.heating-of-the-atmosph.question: Johannesburg sits near 1 750 m. Using a lapse rate of 6,5 °C per 1 000 m, the temperature fall due to altitude alone is about:

geography.grade10.heating-of-the-atmosph.subject: geography
geography.grade10.heating-of-the-atmosph.question: The sea moderates coastal temperatures mainly because water:
options: Heats and cools far more slowly than land — it is transparent, mixes by currents and waves, loses heat to evaporation and needs more energy per degree — so coastal places have a SMALL annual temperature range

geography.grade10.heating-of-the-atmosph.subject: geography
geography.grade10.heating-of-the-atmosph.question: The correct pairing of South Africa's currents is:
options: Cold Agulhas on the east, warm Benguela on the west
Warm Benguela on the east, cold Agulhas on the west
Warm AGULHAS flowing south down the east coast, giving Durban warmth, humidity and summer rain; cold BENGUELA flowing north up the west coast, giving Port Nolloth cool, dry, foggy conditions

geography.grade10.heating-of-the-atmosph.subject: geography
geography.grade10.heating-of-the-atmosph.question: In the hundred-rand story, the thirty rand that 'never gets spent' represents:
options: The albedo — energy reflected straight back off cloud tops, dust and bright surfaces

geography.grade10.heating-of-the-atmosph.subject: geography
geography.grade10.heating-of-the-atmosph.question: The 'twist that explains the whole topic' is that the ground:
options: Spends the energy back upward in a DIFFERENT currency — long-wave instead of short-wave — and the atmosphere grabs long-wave greedily on the way out

geography.grade10.heating-of-the-atmosph.subject: geography
geography.grade10.heating-of-the-atmosph.question: Wind is described as 'the planet settling a debt' because:
options: The tropics collect a permanent surplus of energy and the poles a permanent shortfall, so winds and currents carry the surplus to the shortfall

geography.grade10.heating-of-the-atmosph.subject: geography
geography.grade10.heating-of-the-atmosph.question: In the kitchen version, 'standing next to a braai and feeling the heat on your face' is:

geography.grade10.heating-of-the-atmosph.subject: geography
geography.grade10.heating-of-the-atmosph.question: The churning of the pap in the pot stands for convection, and in the atmosphere it explains:
options: Sea fog on the west coast
Hot afternoons on the Highveld building thunderclouds as warm air rises and cooler air sinks to replace it
The reflection of sunlight by snow

geography.grade10.heating-of-the-atmosph.subject: geography
geography.grade10.heating-of-the-atmosph.question: 'The stove is under the pot, not above it' means:
options: The sun is below the horizon at night
The atmosphere is heated from BELOW by the ground, which is why climbers get colder as they climb even though they are getting closer to the sun
The ground is colder than the air

geography.grade10.heating-of-the-atmosph.subject: geography
geography.grade10.heating-of-the-atmosph.question: The four kitchen words for the four heat-transfer processes are:
options: Braai, handle, churn, breeze — radiation, conduction, convection, advection

geography.grade10.heating-of-the-atmosph.subject: geography
geography.grade10.heating-of-the-atmosph.question: The torch analogy explains which factor?
options: LATITUDE — a torch shone straight down gives a small bright circle, a tilted torch smears the same light over a wide dim patch

geography.grade10.heating-of-the-atmosph.subject: geography
geography.grade10.heating-of-the-atmosph.question: 'Water is a slow cooker and land is a frying pan' explains why:
options: The coast never goes to extremes — Durban is mild in July and not brutal in January — while the deep interior swings hard between the seasons

geography.grade10.heating-of-the-atmosph.subject: geography
geography.grade10.heating-of-the-atmosph.question: Cloud is called 'a blanket that works both shifts' because it:
options: Keeps the DAY cooler by blocking sun and the NIGHT warmer by holding heat in, so cloudy places have small daily ranges and clear Karoo skies give scorching days and freezing nights

geography.grade10.heating-of-the-atmosph.subject: geography
geography.grade10.heating-of-the-atmosph.question: In South Africa, the slope that catches most sun and is warmest and driest faces:
options: NORTH — the southern hemisphere is the mirror of the north, which is why orchards are sited there

geography.grade10.humidity-condensation-.subject: geography
geography.grade10.humidity-condensation-.question: Relative humidity is:
options: The vapour actually present expressed as a percentage of the maximum the air could hold AT THAT TEMPERATURE
The mass of vapour in grams per cubic metre
The temperature at which dew forms
The total rainfall for the month

geography.grade10.humidity-condensation-.subject: geography
geography.grade10.humidity-condensation-.question: Air at 20 °C can hold at most 17 g/m³ of water vapour and actually contains 8,5 g/m³. Its relative humidity is:

geography.grade10.humidity-condensation-.subject: geography
geography.grade10.humidity-condensation-.question: That same air is cooled to 10 °C, where the maximum it can hold is about 8,5 g/m³. Its relative humidity is now:
options: 100% — the air is SATURATED; nothing was added, the container simply shrank

geography.grade10.humidity-condensation-.subject: geography
geography.grade10.humidity-condensation-.question: The dew point is best described as:
options: The temperature at which water boils
The mass of vapour in the air
The percentage of the sky covered by cloud
The temperature to which air must be COOLED for it to become saturated — a moisture measurement disguised as a temperature

geography.grade10.humidity-condensation-.subject: geography
geography.grade10.humidity-condensation-.question: Frost rather than dew forms when:
options: The dew point lies BELOW 0 °C, so vapour deposits directly as ice — which is why farmers watch for clear, windless winter nights

geography.grade10.humidity-condensation-.subject: geography
geography.grade10.humidity-condensation-.question: The fog that rolls into Port Nolloth and the west-coast towns is:
options: Radiation fog from a still valley night
ADVECTION fog — moist maritime air moving horizontally over the cold Benguela Current is chilled below its dew point

geography.grade10.humidity-condensation-.subject: geography
geography.grade10.humidity-condensation-.question: Adiabatic cooling means a rising parcel of air cools because:
options: It EXPANDS as the surrounding pressure falls — cooling without heat being removed; 1 °C per 100 m when unsaturated, about 0,5 °C per 100 m once saturated

geography.grade10.humidity-condensation-.subject: geography
geography.grade10.humidity-condensation-.question: Surface temperature 25 °C, surface dew point 15 °C. The condensation level (cloud base) lies at:
options: 1 000 m — the parcel must cool 10 °C at 1 °C per 100 m

geography.grade10.humidity-condensation-.subject: geography
geography.grade10.humidity-condensation-.question: In cloud names, 'nimbus' indicates:
options: The cloud is made of ice

geography.grade10.humidity-condensation-.subject: geography
geography.grade10.humidity-condensation-.question: A thin milky sheet of high cloud producing a halo around the sun or moon is:

geography.grade10.humidity-condensation-.subject: geography
geography.grade10.humidity-condensation-.question: Which cloud brings steady, prolonged rain rather than short showers?

geography.grade10.humidity-condensation-.subject: geography
geography.grade10.humidity-condensation-.question: A cumulonimbus flattens into an anvil at its top because:
options: The wind blows it sideways at random
It rises until it strikes the tropopause, where the temperature inversion above acts as a ceiling and forces it to spread sideways

geography.grade10.humidity-condensation-.subject: geography
geography.grade10.humidity-condensation-.question: All three rainfall types share the same four steps. They differ only in:
options: WHAT FORCES THE AIR TO RISE
The season in which they occur

geography.grade10.humidity-condensation-.subject: geography
geography.grade10.humidity-condensation-.question: The Little Karoo is arid enough for ostrich farming because it:
options: Lies too far north for frontal rain
Sits in the RAIN SHADOW of the Cape mountains — air that has already rained on the seaward slopes descends the leeward side, is compressed, warms, and its relative humidity falls
Is cooled by the Benguela Current

geography.grade10.humidity-condensation-.subject: geography
geography.grade10.humidity-condensation-.question: The late-afternoon thunderstorm of a Gauteng summer is a textbook example of:
options: CONVECTIONAL rainfall — intense surface heating drives strong thermals that build cumulonimbus, breaking as short, heavy, localised storms

geography.grade10.humidity-condensation-.subject: geography
geography.grade10.humidity-condensation-.question: The Western Cape's winter rainfall is delivered by:
options: Moist easterly air rising over the Drakensberg
Warm fronts moving in from the north-east
COLD FRONTS sweeping in from the south-west across the Atlantic, one behind another, roughly between May and August

geography.grade10.humidity-condensation-.subject: geography
geography.grade10.humidity-condensation-.question: In the shopping-bag picture:
options: Warm air is a BIG bag and cold air is a SMALL bag
Warm air is a small bag and cold air is a big bag
Both bags are the same size
The bag size depends on pressure only

geography.grade10.humidity-condensation-.subject: geography
geography.grade10.humidity-condensation-.question: A cold Coke sweats on a summer day because:
options: The air touching the cold metal is chilled below its dew point, so its bag shrinks below what it was carrying and the extra comes out as liquid
Salt in the air attracts water

geography.grade10.humidity-condensation-.subject: geography
geography.grade10.humidity-condensation-.question: The exam habit the section insists on is to:
options: Report the dew point on its own
Report the temperature on its own
Report the GAP between air temperature and dew point — small gap means the bag is nearly full and rain is nearby; big gap means a dry day
Ignore both numbers and read the cloud

geography.grade10.humidity-condensation-.subject: geography
geography.grade10.humidity-condensation-.question: The four building blocks of cloud names mean:
options: Cirro = high and wispy, alto = middle, strato = spread flat, cumulo = heaped
Cirro = low, alto = high, strato = heaped, cumulo = flat
Cirro = raining, alto = dry, strato = windy, cumulo = still

geography.grade10.humidity-condensation-.subject: geography
geography.grade10.humidity-condensation-.question: Fog is described as:
options: STRATUS that came all the way down to the ground

geography.grade10.humidity-condensation-.subject: geography
geography.grade10.humidity-condensation-.question: Fair-weather cumulus clouds all sit on the same invisible shelf because:
options: They are all the same age
That shelf is the CONDENSATION LEVEL — the height at which every parcel in that air mass reaches its dew point

geography.grade10.humidity-condensation-.subject: geography
geography.grade10.humidity-condensation-.question: Cirrus streaming into the Cape sky in winter usually means:
options: The air is very dry at ground level
A front is roughly a day away — high wispy cloud arrives ahead of the system

geography.grade10.humidity-condensation-.subject: geography
geography.grade10.humidity-condensation-.question: 'Push number one — the mountain' produces:
options: RELIEF rainfall, wet on the side facing the wind and dry in the rain shadow behind

geography.grade10.humidity-condensation-.subject: geography
geography.grade10.humidity-condensation-.question: 'Push number two — the hot ground' gives rain that is:
options: Short, violent, loud and very localised — often over your street while the next suburb stays dry

geography.grade10.humidity-condensation-.subject: geography
geography.grade10.humidity-condensation-.question: 'Push number three — the cold bulldozer' works because:
options: Cold air is lighter and rises
Cold air is heavier, so it shoves underneath the warm air and lifts it right off the ground

geography.grade10.humidity-condensation-.subject: geography
geography.grade10.humidity-condensation-.question: The examiner's trick the lesson warns about is:
options: Deciding the rainfall type by HOW HARD it is raining instead of by what did the pushing — and then forgetting to name the region and the season, which are separate marks

geography.grade10.inside-the-earth.subto.subject: geography
geography.grade10.inside-the-earth.subto.question: The boundary between the crust and the mantle, detected because seismic waves suddenly speed up across it, is the:

geography.grade10.inside-the-earth.subto.subject: geography
geography.grade10.inside-the-earth.subto.question: The physical state of the mantle is best described as:
options: SOLID silicate rock, with a plastic zone — the asthenosphere — in its upper part that deforms and flows extremely slowly

geography.grade10.inside-the-earth.subto.subject: geography
geography.grade10.inside-the-earth.subto.question: The inner core is SOLID despite being the hottest part of the earth because:
options: It is made of a different metal
It has cooled from the outside in
The pressure there is so immense that it forces the iron to remain solid — pressure, not temperature alone, determines state

geography.grade10.inside-the-earth.subto.subject: geography
geography.grade10.inside-the-earth.subto.question: The earth's magnetic field is generated by:
options: Circulating molten iron and nickel in the LIQUID OUTER CORE

geography.grade10.inside-the-earth.subto.subject: geography
geography.grade10.inside-the-earth.subto.question: Continental crust (sial) compared with oceanic crust (sima) is:
options: Thicker (30–50 km, up to 70 km), granitic, LESS dense (about 2,7 g/cm³) and far older
The same thickness but different colour

geography.grade10.inside-the-earth.subto.subject: geography
geography.grade10.inside-the-earth.subto.question: No ocean floor anywhere on earth is older than about 200 million years because:
options: Oceanic crust is continuously CREATED at mid-ocean ridges and continuously DESTROYED at subduction zones
Oceans only formed 200 million years ago
Older rock sinks under its own weight

geography.grade10.inside-the-earth.subto.subject: geography
geography.grade10.inside-the-earth.subto.question: Where oceanic and continental crust converge, the oceanic plate subducts because:
options: It is DENSER — subduction is buoyancy, not an arbitrary rule

geography.grade10.inside-the-earth.subto.subject: geography
geography.grade10.inside-the-earth.subto.question: A tectonic plate consists of:
options: The LITHOSPHERE — crust plus the rigid uppermost mantle, about 100 km thick, riding on the plastic asthenosphere

geography.grade10.inside-the-earth.subto.subject: geography
geography.grade10.inside-the-earth.subto.question: S-waves cannot travel through liquid because:
options: A liquid has no rigidity to transmit a sideways shear

geography.grade10.inside-the-earth.subto.subject: geography
geography.grade10.inside-the-earth.subto.question: The complete absence of S-waves beyond about 103° from the epicentre proves that:
options: The OUTER CORE IS LIQUID — it is the silence that proves it

geography.grade10.inside-the-earth.subto.subject: geography
geography.grade10.inside-the-earth.subto.question: The P-wave shadow zone between roughly 103° and 143° arises because P-waves are:
options: REFRACTED — bent sharply where they pass from the solid mantle into the liquid outer core, and the size of the ring gives the depth of the core-mantle boundary

geography.grade10.inside-the-earth.subto.subject: geography
geography.grade10.inside-the-earth.subto.question: Which is a SUPPORTING line of evidence for a metallic core?
options: The thickness of the ocean floor
The whole earth averages about 5,5 g/cm³ while surface rocks average only 2,7 — so the interior must be far denser, pointing to metal

geography.grade10.inside-the-earth.subto.subject: geography
geography.grade10.inside-the-earth.subto.question: Describing any layer of the earth's interior, the fixed order given is:
options: Name, depth range, composition, physical state, one distinguishing feature

geography.grade10.inside-the-earth.subto.subject: geography
geography.grade10.inside-the-earth.subto.question: Which statement corrects the most heavily punished error in this topic?
options: The crust is thicker than the mantle
The mantle is SOLID rock; only the asthenosphere behaves plastically, and even it flows rather than pours — magma exists in localised pockets, not as a global ocean

geography.grade10.inside-the-earth.subto.subject: geography
geography.grade10.inside-the-earth.subto.question: The depth of the core-mantle boundary (the Gutenberg discontinuity) is about:

geography.grade10.inside-the-earth.subto.subject: geography
geography.grade10.inside-the-earth.subto.question: Which pairing is correct?
options: Continental crust: thin, dense, basaltic, young
Oceanic crust: thick, light, granitic, old
Continental crust: thick, light, granitic, old; oceanic crust: thin, dense, basaltic, young

geography.grade10.inside-the-earth.subto.subject: geography
geography.grade10.inside-the-earth.subto.question: In the avocado model, the skin, the green flesh and the pip stand for:

geography.grade10.inside-the-earth.subto.subject: geography
geography.grade10.inside-the-earth.subto.question: The butter comparison — fridge-cold butter versus butter that has sat in a Durban kitchen — is used to explain:
options: That the mantle is solid rock, but in one band near the top it is soft enough to ooze very slowly, which is what lets the plates move

geography.grade10.inside-the-earth.subto.subject: geography
geography.grade10.inside-the-earth.subto.question: Why does the hottest place in the earth not melt?
options: It is made of a metal with a very high melting point only
It is cooled from the outside
It is squeezed so hard by everything above it that the iron cannot spread out into a liquid — pressure beats heat
It is not actually the hottest place

geography.grade10.inside-the-earth.subto.subject: geography
geography.grade10.inside-the-earth.subto.question: In the swimming-pool picture, the thick polystyrene block and the thin steel sheet stand for:

geography.grade10.inside-the-earth.subto.subject: geography
geography.grade10.inside-the-earth.subto.question: When the two are pushed together, the steel sheet slides under the polystyrene because:
options: It is DENSER — and that is subduction, which is why the great ocean trenches sit right against continents

geography.grade10.inside-the-earth.subto.subject: geography
geography.grade10.inside-the-earth.subto.question: The Kaapvaal Craton beneath much of northern South Africa is offered as an example of:
options: One of the oldest surviving pieces of continental crust anywhere on the planet

geography.grade10.inside-the-earth.subto.subject: geography
geography.grade10.inside-the-earth.subto.question: 'Crust is the skin; the plate is the skin with a layer of flesh still attached' means:
options: The plate is thinner than the crust
Plates are made of ocean water
The crust and the plate are the same thing
A plate is the crust PLUS the rigid top slice of the mantle — about a hundred kilometres of solid rock sliding on the soft layer below

geography.grade10.inside-the-earth.subto.subject: geography
geography.grade10.inside-the-earth.subto.question: The 'knock' we use to explore the earth's interior is:
options: An earthquake, with thousands of seismic stations as the ears

geography.grade10.inside-the-earth.subto.subject: geography
geography.grade10.inside-the-earth.subto.question: The rope-and-water comparison explains that:
options: Sideways shaking travels along a rope but not through water, because liquid has no rigidity — which is why S-waves die in the outer core
Both waves stop at the Moho

geography.grade10.inside-the-earth.subto.subject: geography
geography.grade10.inside-the-earth.subto.question: P-waves are said to bend 'the way a straw looks broken where it enters a glass of water'. That bending:
options: Leaves a quiet ring on the surface whose size tells us exactly how deep the core starts

geography.grade10.inside-the-earth.subto.subject: geography
geography.grade10.inside-the-earth.subto.question: Which is NOT one of the three backing clues given?
options: The whole earth weighs far more per bucket than surface rocks do
A compass works, and only sloshing liquid metal can make a magnetic field
Iron meteorites look like the cores of smashed-up planets
Volcanoes erupt liquid rock, proving the mantle is a global ocean of magma

geography.grade10.kinds-of-population-mo.subject: geography
geography.grade10.kinds-of-population-mo.question: A daily commuter is NOT a migrant because:
options: Commuting is too cheap to count
Migration requires a permanent or semi-permanent change of residence, and a commuter returns home

geography.grade10.kinds-of-population-mo.subject: geography
geography.grade10.kinds-of-population-mo.question: A person who leaves Zimbabwe and settles in South Africa is called:
options: An emigrant from Zimbabwe and an immigrant into South Africa

geography.grade10.kinds-of-population-mo.subject: geography
geography.grade10.kinds-of-population-mo.question: A refugee differs from an internally displaced person because a refugee:
options: Has crossed an international border fleeing persecution or conflict

geography.grade10.kinds-of-population-mo.subject: geography
geography.grade10.kinds-of-population-mo.question: Mineworkers spending eleven months on the mines and each December at home, year after year, illustrate:

geography.grade10.kinds-of-population-mo.subject: geography
geography.grade10.kinds-of-population-mo.question: Push factors are:
options: The costs of the journey between two places
The permits needed at a border
The negatives of the place of origin that drive people out

geography.grade10.kinds-of-population-mo.subject: geography
geography.grade10.kinds-of-population-mo.question: Which family of factors dominates world migration?
options: Economic factors — most migrants move toward work and wages

geography.grade10.kinds-of-population-mo.subject: geography
geography.grade10.kinds-of-population-mo.question: Chain migration means:
options: Existing migrant communities at the destination make each next migration easier, strengthening the stream
Migration only happens along railway lines

geography.grade10.kinds-of-population-mo.subject: geography
geography.grade10.kinds-of-population-mo.question: People keep migrating into cities that already have severe unemployment because:
options: They are forced to move there by law
They move on a perceived picture of the destination that is often brighter than its reality

geography.grade10.kinds-of-population-mo.subject: geography
geography.grade10.kinds-of-population-mo.question: The historical roots of the Eastern Cape to Gauteng stream lie in:
options: The discovery of diamonds in the Eastern Cape
A government resettlement programme of the 1990s
The province's position on the coast
The homeland system and the migrant labour system, which confined families to poor land while men worked mine contracts

geography.grade10.kinds-of-population-mo.subject: geography
geography.grade10.kinds-of-population-mo.question: A decisive pull factor lowering obstacles for new Eastern Cape migrants to Gauteng is:
options: Relatives and home-community networks already established there

geography.grade10.kinds-of-population-mo.subject: geography
geography.grade10.kinds-of-population-mo.question: For the rural origin areas, the migration stream causes:
options: Overcrowding of village schools by working adults
Remittances and returning skills as gains, but the loss of working-age adults, leaving children and grandparents

geography.grade10.kinds-of-population-mo.subject: geography
geography.grade10.kinds-of-population-mo.question: For Gauteng as destination, the stream brings:
options: A young workforce and larger economy, but informal settlement growth and overcrowded services

geography.grade10.kinds-of-population-mo.subject: geography
geography.grade10.kinds-of-population-mo.question: The main causes of the Zimbabwean migration stream to South Africa from around 2000 were:
options: Economic collapse with hyperinflation and unemployment, compounded by political fear

geography.grade10.kinds-of-population-mo.subject: geography
geography.grade10.kinds-of-population-mo.question: The Zimbabwean stream is called mixed migration because it contains:
options: Voluntary economic migrants, refugees and asylum seekers, and everything between

geography.grade10.kinds-of-population-mo.subject: geography
geography.grade10.kinds-of-population-mo.question: For origin countries such as Zimbabwe, emigration to South Africa brings:
options: Remittances as a lifeline, but a brain drain of teachers, nurses and skilled workers
The return of all skilled workers
An end to unemployment at home

geography.grade10.kinds-of-population-mo.subject: geography
geography.grade10.kinds-of-population-mo.question: The xenophobic violence of 2008 and 2015 is explained in the lesson as igniting where:
options: Border posts process the most permits
Competition for scarce jobs, housing and services concentrates in the poorest areas

geography.grade10.kinds-of-population-mo.subject: geography
geography.grade10.kinds-of-population-mo.question: The two sorting questions for any migrant's story are:
options: Did they cross a border, and did they choose to move

geography.grade10.kinds-of-population-mo.subject: geography
geography.grade10.kinds-of-population-mo.question: The same journey earns a person two labels — emigrant and immigrant — because:
options: Each label depends on which side of the border is speaking
One label is for documents, the other for the census

geography.grade10.kinds-of-population-mo.subject: geography
geography.grade10.kinds-of-population-mo.question: The two-place life of the historical mine contract system meant:
options: Mineworkers settled permanently at the mines with their families
Families moved to the mines every December
Eleven months in a mine hostel and December at home, repeated for years — oscillating between two homes

geography.grade10.kinds-of-population-mo.subject: geography
geography.grade10.kinds-of-population-mo.question: In the tug-of-war picture, the knots in the rope stand for:
options: The pull factors of the city
Obstacles between origin and destination — fares, distance, borders and leaving family

geography.grade10.kinds-of-population-mo.subject: geography
geography.grade10.kinds-of-population-mo.question: Every cousin already in Johannesburg makes the rope pull harder because:
options: Cousins pay for all expenses forever
Family ahead means a place to sleep and someone who knows where jobs are — so each mover recruits the next

geography.grade10.kinds-of-population-mo.subject: geography
geography.grade10.kinds-of-population-mo.question: Which pairing correctly matches a push with its mirror pull?
options: Failing farm at home — jobs and wages in the city
War at home — drought in the city
Good school at home — no school in the city
Peace at home — persecution in the city

geography.grade10.kinds-of-population-mo.subject: geography
geography.grade10.kinds-of-population-mo.question: For many rural households in origin areas, remittances are:
options: A small bonus at year end
The main income — groceries, school shoes and electricity

geography.grade10.kinds-of-population-mo.subject: geography
geography.grade10.kinds-of-population-mo.question: The both are true at once point about origin villages is that they:
options: Gain remittance money while losing their working-age adults

geography.grade10.kinds-of-population-mo.subject: geography
geography.grade10.kinds-of-population-mo.question: The four boxes answer pattern for migration consequences covers:
options: Origin gains, origin losses, destination gains, destination strains

geography.grade10.kinds-of-population-mo.subject: geography
geography.grade10.kinds-of-population-mo.question: The destination city's gains from migration include:
options: Young, determined workers — nurses, builders, shopkeepers — whose labour and businesses build the economy

geography.grade10.plate-boundaries-and-p.subject: geography
geography.grade10.plate-boundaries-and-p.question: The single supercontinent proposed by Wegener, and its two fragments, were:
options: Gondwana, splitting into Pangaea and Laurasia
Pangaea, splitting into Laurasia in the north and Gondwana in the south
Laurasia, splitting into Pangaea and Gondwana
Panthalassa, splitting into Africa and Asia

geography.grade10.plate-boundaries-and-p.subject: geography
geography.grade10.plate-boundaries-and-p.question: Why is Mesosaurus such strong evidence for continental drift?
options: It was a freshwater reptile that could not cross an ocean, yet its fossils occur in both the Karoo and South America
It was a flying reptile that could migrate between continents
Its fossils are found only in Africa

geography.grade10.plate-boundaries-and-p.subject: geography
geography.grade10.plate-boundaries-and-p.question: The Dwyka tillite in South Africa is climatic evidence for drift because it shows that:
options: The Karoo was once a warm swamp
Sea levels were once much higher
A continental ice sheet once covered land that now has a hot climate, matching glacial deposits on other continents
Volcanic ash once buried the region

geography.grade10.plate-boundaries-and-p.subject: geography
geography.grade10.plate-boundaries-and-p.question: Wegener's theory was rejected for half a century mainly because:
options: His fossil evidence was proved false
The coastlines did not actually fit
Nobody had mapped the ocean floor
He could not explain what force moved the continents

geography.grade10.plate-boundaries-and-p.subject: geography
geography.grade10.plate-boundaries-and-p.question: Convection currents in the mantle are driven by:
options: Heat from radioactive decay and from the earth's formation, making hot rock rise and cooler rock sink
The pull of the moon on the ocean floor

geography.grade10.plate-boundaries-and-p.subject: geography
geography.grade10.plate-boundaries-and-p.question: Which statement about the mantle is CORRECT?
options: It is a global ocean of liquid lava
It is solid rock that flows plastically at a few centimetres a year
It is a gas layer under pressure
It is frozen solid and does not move at all

geography.grade10.plate-boundaries-and-p.subject: geography
geography.grade10.plate-boundaries-and-p.question: Slab pull refers to:
options: New crust sliding off the raised mid-ocean ridge
The weight of a cold, dense sinking plate hauling the rest of the plate behind it

geography.grade10.plate-boundaries-and-p.subject: geography
geography.grade10.plate-boundaries-and-p.question: Magnetic striping on the ocean floor proves sea-floor spreading because the stripes are:
options: Randomly scattered across the whole ocean
Only found next to the continents
Parallel to the ridge and mirrored symmetrically on both sides of it

geography.grade10.plate-boundaries-and-p.subject: geography
geography.grade10.plate-boundaries-and-p.question: Divergent boundaries are also called constructive boundaries because:
options: New crust is created there as magma rises and solidifies

geography.grade10.plate-boundaries-and-p.subject: geography
geography.grade10.plate-boundaries-and-p.question: The East African Rift Valley is best described as:
options: A single deep canyon cut by a river
A broad flat-floored valley walled by fault scarps, holding long deep lakes, with volcanoes along the fractures
A ridge of folded mountains raised by compression
A chain of volcanic islands rising from the sea floor

geography.grade10.plate-boundaries-and-p.subject: geography
geography.grade10.plate-boundaries-and-p.question: At a transform (conservative) boundary you would NOT expect to find:

geography.grade10.plate-boundaries-and-p.subject: geography
geography.grade10.plate-boundaries-and-p.question: Earthquakes at mid-ocean ridges are shallow and moderate because:
options: The ocean water absorbs the energy
The magma is too cold to fracture
The crust there is thin, hot and weak, so it cannot store large amounts of strain

geography.grade10.plate-boundaries-and-p.subject: geography
geography.grade10.plate-boundaries-and-p.question: Oceanic crust subducts beneath continental crust because it is:
options: Denser, at about 3,0 g/cm³ against about 2,7 g/cm³

geography.grade10.plate-boundaries-and-p.subject: geography
geography.grade10.plate-boundaries-and-p.question: The Peru-Chile Trench and the Andes were produced by:
options: The Nazca oceanic plate subducting beneath the South American continental plate
A transform fault sliding past the coast
A mid-ocean ridge splitting the continent

geography.grade10.plate-boundaries-and-p.subject: geography
geography.grade10.plate-boundaries-and-p.question: Continental-continental collision such as India into Eurasia produces:
options: Very high fold mountains and powerful earthquakes, but essentially no volcanoes
New oceanic crust and magnetic striping

geography.grade10.plate-boundaries-and-p.subject: geography
geography.grade10.plate-boundaries-and-p.question: South Africa records few natural earthquakes mainly because:
options: Its rocks are too young to fracture
It has no fault lines of any kind
The Cape Fold Mountains absorb the shaking
It lies near the middle of the African plate, far from any plate boundary

geography.grade10.plate-boundaries-and-p.subject: geography
geography.grade10.plate-boundaries-and-p.question: In the torn-newspaper comparison, the 'sentences running across the tear' stand for:
options: The shape of the coastlines only
Matching fossils, rocks and glacial deposits that continue from one continent onto another
The width of the Atlantic Ocean
The names given to the continents

geography.grade10.plate-boundaries-and-p.subject: geography
geography.grade10.plate-boundaries-and-p.question: Glossopteris supports drift because its seeds were:
options: Carried by ocean currents to every continent
Too heavy to be blown across an ocean, yet the plant grew on five now-separated landmasses

geography.grade10.plate-boundaries-and-p.subject: geography
geography.grade10.plate-boundaries-and-p.question: The Cape Fold Mountains are geological evidence for drift because they:
options: Are the oldest mountains on earth
Run from north to south instead of east to west
Continue, with the same age and folding, in Argentina and Antarctica

geography.grade10.plate-boundaries-and-p.subject: geography
geography.grade10.plate-boundaries-and-p.question: In the pot-on-the-stove comparison, the 'skin of cooled porridge' represents:
options: The lithosphere — crust plus the rigid top of the mantle, about 100 km thick

geography.grade10.plate-boundaries-and-p.question: The 'tablecloth sliding off the table' describes which force?

geography.grade10.plate-boundaries-and-p.subject: geography
geography.grade10.plate-boundaries-and-p.question: The age of the ocean floor supports spreading because it is:
options: Oldest at the ridge and youngest at the continents
Youngest at the ridge, older toward the continents, and nowhere older than about 200 million years

geography.grade10.plate-boundaries-and-p.subject: geography
geography.grade10.plate-boundaries-and-p.question: Roughly how fast do plates move?
options: A few centimetres per year — about as fast as fingernails grow

geography.grade10.plate-boundaries-and-p.subject: geography
geography.grade10.plate-boundaries-and-p.question: Two taxis squeezing past each other side by side illustrates which boundary?

geography.grade10.plate-boundaries-and-p.subject: geography
geography.grade10.plate-boundaries-and-p.question: Where two oceanic plates converge, the landform produced is:
options: A trench with a curved island arc of volcanic islands, as at Japan
A mid-ocean ridge with fissure eruptions
A straight fault with offset streams

geography.grade10.plate-boundaries-and-p.subject: geography
geography.grade10.plate-boundaries-and-p.question: Which boundary neither creates nor destroys crust?

geography.grade10.plate-boundaries-and-p.subject: geography
geography.grade10.plate-boundaries-and-p.question: The Ring of Fire is a belt of volcanoes and earthquakes that traces:
options: The subduction boundaries encircling the Pacific Ocean

geography.grade10.population-distributio.subject: geography
geography.grade10.population-distributio.question: Population distribution refers to:
options: The average number of people per square kilometre
The pattern of where people are spread across an area
The rate at which a population is growing
The number of births per thousand people

geography.grade10.population-distributio.subject: geography
geography.grade10.population-distributio.question: Two districts each have 50 000 people in 1 000 km². In one they are spread evenly; in the other all live in a single town. This shows that:
options: Distribution and density mean the same thing
Density cannot be calculated for either district
Identical density can go with completely different distribution

geography.grade10.population-distributio.subject: geography
geography.grade10.population-distributio.question: Settlement strung out along a river or main road is described as:

geography.grade10.population-distributio.subject: geography
geography.grade10.population-distributio.question: "Sparsely populated" means:
options: Few people spread over a large area
Many people in a small area

geography.grade10.population-distributio.subject: geography
geography.grade10.population-distributio.question: The main weakness of a national population density figure is that:
options: It is an average that conceals huge internal variation, describing no actual place
It cannot be calculated for large countries

geography.grade10.population-distributio.subject: geography
geography.grade10.population-distributio.question: Geographers sometimes divide population by ARABLE land rather than total land because:
options: Arable land is easier to measure
It shows how many people each unit of productive land must support, which total area hides
It always gives a smaller number
Total area is not recorded by governments

geography.grade10.population-distributio.question: Which is the STRONGEST single physical control on where people live?
options: Climate, especially temperature and reliable rainfall

geography.grade10.population-distributio.subject: geography
geography.grade10.population-distributio.question: Equatorial rainforests are sparsely populated mainly because of:
options: Extreme cold and a frozen growing season
A complete absence of fresh water
Leached soils, dense vegetation and disease

geography.grade10.population-distributio.subject: geography
geography.grade10.population-distributio.question: Mineral deposits attract dense population even to unattractive sites because:
options: The resource cannot be moved to the people, so the people must come to it
Mining areas have the best soils
Governments require people to live there

geography.grade10.population-distributio.subject: geography
geography.grade10.population-distributio.question: Some of the densest rural populations on earth are found on floodplains and deltas because of:
options: Deep, fertile alluvial soils that support intensive agriculture

geography.grade10.population-distributio.subject: geography
geography.grade10.population-distributio.question: South Africa's population is much denser in the east than the west chiefly because:
options: The east is closer to the equator
Rainfall declines westward, falling below about 500 mm a year over much of the west

geography.grade10.population-distributio.subject: geography
geography.grade10.population-distributio.question: Gauteng is described as an anomaly in the population pattern because it:
options: Has the highest rainfall in the country
Is the largest province by area
Lies on the coast with the country's best harbour
Has no coast and no navigable river, yet holds the largest concentration of people — because of gold

geography.grade10.population-distributio.subject: geography
geography.grade10.population-distributio.question: High rural population densities in parts of the Eastern Cape and Limpopo are best explained by:
options: Apartheid-era policy that confined the majority population to a small share of the land in the homelands

geography.grade10.population-distributio.subject: geography
geography.grade10.population-distributio.question: The recommended order for answering a question about a population pattern is:
options: Pattern first, then the evidence for it, then the explanation

geography.grade10.population-distributio.subject: geography
geography.grade10.population-distributio.question: Moving forty learners from a classroom into a stadium changes:
options: The density, because the same number of people now occupies far more space

geography.grade10.population-distributio.subject: geography
geography.grade10.population-distributio.question: Gathering the same forty people into one corner of the stadium changes:
options: The density but not the distribution
The distribution but not the density

geography.grade10.population-distributio.subject: geography
geography.grade10.population-distributio.question: A question asking about DISTRIBUTION should be answered with:
options: Words describing the pattern — clustered, linear, dense here, empty there
A single figure in people per square kilometre
The total area in square kilometres

geography.grade10.population-distributio.subject: geography
geography.grade10.population-distributio.question: In dry country, settlement often forms a thin string of dots because:
options: The government builds only along straight lines
Settlement follows the watercourse, since fresh water is the first requirement
The soil is only fertile in strips
Roads are cheaper to build in a line

geography.grade10.population-distributio.subject: geography
geography.grade10.population-distributio.question: Steep mountain areas hold few people mainly because of:
options: Thin soils, difficult access and expensive building

geography.grade10.population-distributio.subject: geography
geography.grade10.population-distributio.question: A natural harbour attracts dense settlement because:
options: Trade collects there, and people collect around trade

geography.grade10.population-distributio.subject: geography
geography.grade10.population-distributio.question: Drawing an imaginary line down the middle of South Africa shows that:
options: The east receives decent rain and holds most of the people, while the west is dry and sparsely settled
The west receives more rain than the east
Population is evenly spread on both sides

geography.grade10.population-distributio.subject: geography
geography.grade10.population-distributio.question: The chain of growth described for Gauteng runs:
options: Gold, mine workers, towns and services, factories making machinery, banks and offices, roads and railways

geography.grade10.population-distributio.subject: geography
geography.grade10.population-distributio.question: Gauteng remains the economic heart of the region even though the gold is largely worked out because:
options: The gold reserves are secretly untouched
Once people, roads and jobs are established in a place, they hold each other there

geography.grade10.population-distributio.subject: geography
geography.grade10.population-distributio.question: Durban, Cape Town and Gqeberha all grew large chiefly because:
options: They are the flattest sites in the country

geography.grade10.population-distributio.subject: geography
geography.grade10.population-distributio.question: The three-point summary of South Africa's population map given in the lesson is:
options: Dense east and empty dry west from rainfall; four city clusters from gold and harbours; crowded rural pockets in the former homelands from history
Even spread; low density; no cities
Coastal only; inland empty; no rural population
Dense west, empty east, and no urban centres

geography.grade10.population-indicators-.subject: geography

Births per hundred families per month
The total number of births in a country

geography.grade10.population-indicators-.subject: geography

Germany has a higher birth rate

Every family needs at least two workers

options: It is the easiest rate to count
It only depends on the number of hospitals
Babies are counted twice in the census
Keeping babies alive requires clean water, nutrition, vaccination, clinics and educated mothers all working together

options: A fall in the birth rate
The mass rollout of antiretroviral treatment for HIV
An increase in the fertility rate

Nobody in the country grows old
The country must have a low birth rate

Males on the left bars, females on the right bars, in five-year age cohorts from youngest at the bottom

A printing error in the graph
A baby boom in that generation
Heavy immigration of that age group

Fertility has fallen below replacement — the population is ageing and will shrink

options: Expansive — Japan; stationary — Niger; constrictive — Sweden

Expansive — Niger; stationary — Sweden or the USA; constrictive — Japan or Germany
Expansive — Italy; stationary — the DRC; constrictive — Mozambique

options: Nobody in that country reaches old age
Life expectancy is an average that infant deaths drag down hard
The country has a low birth rate

geography.grade10.population-indicators-.subject: geography

options: Indicators from poor countries cannot be trusted
Death rates are always lower in rich countries
Never judge on one number alone — ask who is in the population and use several indicators together

That age group refused to be photographed
A baby boom happened in those years

geography.grade10.population-indicators-.subject: geography
geography.grade10.population-indicators-.question: In the oldest rows of most pyramids, the female bars are longer than the male bars because:
options: More girls are born than boys
Old men are not counted in the census
Women outlive men almost everywhere in the world

Old people migrate back to rural areas
The pyramid keeps the same shape forever
Today's huge child cohorts become tomorrow's parents, so growth continues for decades even after fertility falls

geography.grade10.population-indicators-.subject: geography
geography.grade10.population-indicators-.question: Fast-forwarding a constrictive stack thirty years gives:

geography.grade10.population-water-and-s.question: Egypt shows that national density figures can mislead because:

options: The death rate falls with clean water and vaccines while the birth rate stays high
Both birth and death rates rise together
The birth rate rises while the death rate is unchanged
Migration brings millions into the country

geography.grade10.population-water-and-s.question: A population pyramid with a wide base and a narrow top indicates:
options: Low birth rate and an ageing population
A high birth rate, a young fast-growing population and heavy youth dependency
A shrinking population with few children
Equal numbers in every age group

geography.grade10.population-water-and-s.question: Overpopulation is best defined as:

An emigrant from South Africa and an immigrant in Australia

The movement of people between two cities

The empty arid west of the country
The whole of South Africa equally

geography.grade10.population-water-and-s.subject: geography

options: Pump quickly and seal it with concrete
Use it only in summer and drain it in winter
Never drill more than one borehole and never map it
Pump no faster than rain recharges it, and never let pollution seep down into it

geography.grade10.world-population-growt.subject: geography
geography.grade10.world-population-growt.question: The world reached its first one billion people around:

geography.grade10.world-population-growt.subject: geography
geography.grade10.world-population-growt.question: The population explosion of the last two centuries was caused mainly by:
options: A sudden worldwide rise in birth rates
Death rates collapsing — through food, clean water, vaccines and antibiotics — while birth rates stayed high

geography.grade10.world-population-growt.subject: geography
geography.grade10.world-population-growt.question: Population growth described as a J-curve means:
options: A long, almost flat stretch across the centuries, then a bend into a nearly vertical climb
Steady, straight-line growth from the beginning
Rapid early growth followed by centuries of decline
Growth that rises and falls every decade

geography.grade10.world-population-growt.subject: geography
geography.grade10.world-population-growt.question: World population is still rising even though the growth rate has fallen since the late 1960s because:
options: The United Nations miscounts each year
Immigration adds people to the world total
Momentum — the huge cohorts already born keep producing children even as families shrink

geography.grade10.world-population-growt.subject: geography
geography.grade10.world-population-growt.question: A country has 30 births and 10 deaths per thousand people per year. Its natural increase is:

geography.grade10.world-population-growt.subject: geography
geography.grade10.world-population-growt.question: Using the rule of 70, a population growing at 2% a year doubles in about:

geography.grade10.world-population-growt.subject: geography
geography.grade10.world-population-growt.question: Doubling time behaves like compound interest because:
options: Each year's increase adds people who themselves produce the next year's increase
Populations only grow in leap years
The rule of 70 was invented by economists

geography.grade10.world-population-growt.subject: geography
geography.grade10.world-population-growt.question: Which matching of country to growth situation is correct?
options: Niger shrinking; Japan doubling in 20 years; South Africa at 4%
Niger at about 1%; Japan at 3,7%; South Africa shrinking
Niger growing at roughly 3,7%; Japan shrinking as deaths exceed births; South Africa near 1%
All three countries growing at exactly 2%

geography.grade10.world-population-growt.subject: geography
geography.grade10.world-population-growt.question: A region is overpopulated when:
options: Its density exceeds 100 people per square kilometre
Its population exceeds the carrying capacity of its resources and technology
It has more than ten million people
Most of its people live in cities

geography.grade10.world-population-growt.subject: geography
geography.grade10.world-population-growt.question: The Netherlands, with over 500 people per square kilometre, is NOT overpopulated because:
options: Density figures for Europe are unreliable
Its fertile land, technology and strong economy support its people at a high standard of living

geography.grade10.world-population-growt.subject: geography
geography.grade10.world-population-growt.question: Parts of the arid Sahel can be overpopulated at under 20 people per square kilometre because:
options: Rainfall is so scarce and soils so thin that even a sparse population presses beyond what the land can regenerate
The Sahel has the world's highest birth rate
Density is always highest in deserts

geography.grade10.world-population-growt.subject: geography
geography.grade10.world-population-growt.question: Carrying capacity is not fixed. It can be RAISED by:
options: Irrigation, fertiliser and improved seed, which let the same land feed more people

geography.grade10.world-population-growt.subject: geography
geography.grade10.world-population-growt.question: The single most reliable measure ever found for lowering birth rates is:
options: Keeping girls in school longer — educated women marry later, earn incomes and use family planning

geography.grade10.world-population-growt.subject: geography
geography.grade10.world-population-growt.question: Reducing infant mortality lowers birth rates because:
options: Parents stop having insurance children once child survival becomes normal
Fewer surviving children means a smaller population immediately

geography.grade10.world-population-growt.subject: geography
geography.grade10.world-population-growt.question: China's one-child policy is treated as a cautionary case because it:
options: Had no effect on the birth rate at all
Was copied successfully by every other country
Cut births but left an ageing population, a shrinking workforce and a skewed sex ratio
Was only applied in rural areas

geography.grade10.world-population-growt.subject: geography
geography.grade10.world-population-growt.question: Thailand and Kerala matter in this debate because they:
options: Achieved fertility declines comparable to China's through education, healthcare and voluntary family planning
Still have the world's highest fertility rates

geography.grade10.world-population-growt.subject: geography
geography.grade10.world-population-growt.question: In the 24-hour stadium picture of population history, the first billion people are seated:
options: Only by about quarter to midnight — after nearly the whole day

geography.grade10.world-population-growt.subject: geography
geography.grade10.world-population-growt.question: The population explosion happened because:
options: People suddenly started having more babies than ever before
Death slowed down — deaths collapsed while births carried on as before for a generation or two

geography.grade10.world-population-growt.subject: geography
geography.grade10.world-population-growt.question: The queue outside the stadium getting shorter every year represents:
options: The falling growth rate, as families everywhere shrink

geography.grade10.world-population-growt.subject: geography
geography.grade10.world-population-growt.question: In the lifeboat picture, the boat's rating for 20 people represents:
options: The carrying capacity — the number the resources can support decently
The number of people currently aboard

geography.grade10.world-population-growt.subject: geography
geography.grade10.world-population-growt.question: Crowded is not the same as overloaded means:
options: Density and overpopulation are identical measures
A dense place with strong resources can be fine, while a sparse place with weak resources can be overpopulated

geography.grade10.world-population-growt.subject: geography
geography.grade10.world-population-growt.question: A region becoming overpopulated without a single person being added happens when:
options: Young people return from the cities
The resource base shrinks — through drought, erosion or exhausted wells — so the boat gets smaller beneath the same crowd

geography.grade10.world-population-growt.subject: geography
geography.grade10.world-population-growt.question: Which of these is a sign of strain from overpopulation named in the lesson?
options: Falling school enrolment as classrooms empty
Family plots splitting smaller each generation while settlements outgrow pipes and power lines

geography.grade10.world-population-growt.subject: geography
geography.grade10.world-population-growt.question: The chain from the school gate to the birth rate runs:
options: Girls finish school, marry later, gain plans and incomes, invest in fewer children's schooling, and use family planning
Schools directly limit family sizes by law

geography.grade10.world-population-growt.subject: geography
geography.grade10.world-population-growt.question: Save more babies slows growth because:
options: It lowers the death rate, which is the same as lowering the birth rate
When child survival becomes normal, parents stop having extra children as insurance
Saved babies emigrate when they grow up

geography.grade10.world-population-growt.subject: geography
geography.grade10.world-population-growt.question: Pensions reduce birth rates because:
options: Pensions are only paid to small families
Where old age is protected by a pension, children are no longer a retirement plan

geography.grade10.world-population-growt.subject: geography
geography.grade10.world-population-growt.question: South Africa's fertility fell from about six children per woman to about 2,3 through:
options: A legal limit on family size
Education, urbanisation, clinic-based family planning and choice — never compulsion

geography.grade11.batholiths-granite-dom.subject: geography
geography.grade11.batholiths-granite-dom.question: A CONCORDANT intrusion is one that:

geography.grade11.batholiths-granite-dom.subject: geography
geography.grade11.batholiths-granite-dom.question: A batholith is:
options: A thin horizontal sheet between strata
An enormous, deep-seated, discordant granite mass, tens to hundreds of kilometres across, with no known floor
A vertical wall in a crack

geography.grade11.batholiths-granite-dom.subject: geography
geography.grade11.batholiths-granite-dom.question: The laccolith and lopolith differ in that:
options: The laccolith is discordant and the lopolith concordant
The lopolith arches the roof upward
The laccolith ARCHES the overlying strata up into a mushroom blister, while the heavy lopolith SAGS the strata beneath it into a saucer

geography.grade11.batholiths-granite-dom.subject: geography
geography.grade11.batholiths-granite-dom.question: The world's largest lopolith, source of most of the planet's platinum, is:

geography.grade11.batholiths-granite-dom.subject: geography
geography.grade11.batholiths-granite-dom.question: A buried intrusion becomes a landform through:

geography.grade11.batholiths-granite-dom.question: A resistant dyke exposed in softer country rock forms:
options: A long, narrow, WALL-like ridge marching straight across country

geography.grade11.batholiths-granite-dom.subject: geography
geography.grade11.batholiths-granite-dom.question: An exposed resistant sill typically appears as:
options: A vertical wall cutting across valleys
A horizontal cliff band at one level, a hard cap on a mesa, or the lip of a waterfall

geography.grade11.batholiths-granite-dom.subject: geography
geography.grade11.batholiths-granite-dom.question: On a map, a dyke betrays itself as:
options: A contour-hugging cliff line at constant height
A dead-straight narrow ridge that ignores the drainage pattern

geography.grade11.batholiths-granite-dom.subject: geography
geography.grade11.batholiths-granite-dom.question: Pressure release, or unloading, happens when:
options: Erosion strips the overburden, the pressure on the deep granite drops, and the rock expands slightly
Rain adds weight to the granite

geography.grade11.batholiths-granite-dom.subject: geography
geography.grade11.batholiths-granite-dom.question: Sheet joints are:
options: Curved cracks PARALLEL to the land surface, wrapped around the granite like onion layers, formed by expansion
Cracks made by plant roots only

geography.grade11.batholiths-granite-dom.subject: geography
geography.grade11.batholiths-granite-dom.question: Exfoliation makes a granite dome MORE rounded because:
options: Each curved sheet that peels away exposes a fresh, smoother curved surface beneath — the dome renews its own shape
Rivers carve it into a circle

geography.grade11.batholiths-granite-dom.subject: geography
geography.grade11.batholiths-granite-dom.question: Textbook examples of granite dome scenery include:
options: The Three Sisters and the Fish River Canyon
Paarl Mountain's domes and the whalebacked hills of the Matopos

geography.grade11.batholiths-granite-dom.question: In the two-stage theory of tor formation, the FIRST stage is:

Boulders rolling downhill into a pile

geography.grade11.batholiths-granite-dom.question: The tor becomes visible when:
options: Erosion strips away the soft grus, leaving the hard corestones freestanding in their original stacked positions
People pile the boulders for landmarks

geography.grade11.batholiths-granite-dom.subject: geography
geography.grade11.batholiths-granite-dom.question: The joint-spacing rule says:
options: Close joints give domes, wide joints give tors
Joint spacing has no effect on landforms
Joints only occur in sedimentary rock
WIDELY spaced joints leave huge blocks that weather into domes, while CLOSELY spaced joints give small blocks that become corestones and tors

geography.grade11.batholiths-granite-dom.question: The buried wall and the buried shelf are:

geography.grade11.batholiths-granite-dom.question: The expanding granite cracks:
options: In curved shells parallel to the surface, layered like an onion
Not at all — granite cannot crack

geography.grade11.batholiths-granite-dom.subject: geography
geography.grade11.batholiths-granite-dom.question: Exfoliation polishes the mountain into a dome rather than rubble because:

Wind carries the fragments away instantly
Curved shells can only shed into curves — each peeled slab leaves a smoother, rounder surface beneath

A stack of survivors LEFT BEHIND when erosion stripped the rotten grus from around the corestones
Boulders carried and dumped by a river

options: The migration of the pressure belts
The rising of air at the equator
The Coriolis deflection of winds over the rotating earth
The friction between wind and ground

options: The two cities share one cloud system
Cape Town's mountains only work in winter
The Agulhas current reverses in winter
The whole circulation migrates north: the ITCZ leaves the plateau dry while the westerlies' fronts reach the Cape

geography.grade11.climate-geomorphology-.question: Tors form when:
options: Rivers pile boulders in their beds
Water rots jointed granite at the block corners underground, and erosion removes the grit leaving rounded cores stacked
Wind carves layered sandstone into towers

geography.grade11.climate-geomorphology-.question: Granite landscapes never form steps or terraces because:
options: Granite is too soft to hold a step
They are protected by cap rock
Steps only form under ice sheets
Massive rock has no layers, so erosion works on one structureless body

options: Water or human interference such as undercutting and stripped vegetation

Asymmetry — contours packed on the scarp side and widely spaced on the dip side
A single contour looping the summit

geography.grade11.coal-and-thermal-elect.subject: geography

All rivers flow away from the escarpment

options: True hydro-electric sources adding net energy
Giant batteries — pumping water uphill with cheap off-peak power and releasing it through turbines at peak, consuming more energy than they produce

geography.grade11.coal-and-thermal-elect.subject: geography
geography.grade11.coal-and-thermal-elect.question: South Africa's electricity mix is approximately:

Evenly split among coal, nuclear and renewables
Roughly 80 per cent coal, with slivers for nuclear (Koeberg), hydro, pumped storage and growing renewables

geography.grade11.coal-and-thermal-elect.subject: geography
geography.grade11.coal-and-thermal-elect.question: The energy chain in a coal station runs:
options: Chemical energy to heat to kinetic energy to electrical energy — coal, steam, spin, spark
Electrical to kinetic to heat to chemical
Heat to chemical to electrical to kinetic
Kinetic to heat to chemical to electrical

Powder burns fast and completely in the furnace
It reduces the ash produced to zero

geography.grade11.coal-and-thermal-elect.question: Dry-cooled stations like Kendal and Matimba are a South African speciality because:

It is the cheapest kind of solar power
It only operates during peak hours

A coal station converted to nuclear in 2000

geography.grade11.coal-and-thermal-elect.question: The concentration of nuclear fuel is captured by:
options: One tonne of uranium equalling one tonne of coal
A fingertip-sized uranium pellet holding the energy of about a tonne of coal
Uranium burning hotter than coal in the same furnace

geography.grade11.coal-and-thermal-elect.subject: geography
geography.grade11.coal-and-thermal-elect.question: Nuclear's main disadvantages include:
options: Carbon emissions during operation and ash disposal
The highest construction costs and longest build times in the energy world, waste needing isolation for thousands of years, and rare but enormous accident risk

geography.grade11.coal-and-thermal-elect.subject: geography
geography.grade11.coal-and-thermal-elect.question: The lesson's conclusion on conventional-only supply is:
options: Coal alone can carry the century
Nuclear alone should replace coal immediately
Hydro can be expanded to dominate the mix
Conventional sources alone cannot carry long-term needs — coal's constraints are structural and nuclear is slow and costly — so the realistic path is a mix

geography.grade11.coal-and-thermal-elect.subject: geography
geography.grade11.coal-and-thermal-elect.question: In the kettle picture, the generator is:
options: A spinning magnet inside coils of wire — motion becoming electricity
The furnace that burns the coal

geography.grade11.coal-and-thermal-elect.subject: geography
geography.grade11.coal-and-thermal-elect.question: The white clouds above the funnel-shaped towers are:
options: Water vapour from cooling the used steam — the actual smoke leaves by the tall thin stacks

geography.grade11.coal-and-thermal-elect.subject: geography
geography.grade11.coal-and-thermal-elect.question: 'Send the electricity travelling, not the coal' explains:
options: Why coal exports go through Richards Bay
Why stations huddle on the coalfields while high-voltage lines carry power to distant Gauteng
Why stations are built near cities

geography.grade11.coal-and-thermal-elect.subject: geography
geography.grade11.coal-and-thermal-elect.question: 'One truck in three' refers to:
options: The share of coal lost in transport
The portion of trucks carrying ash
Coal reserves lasting three more decades
Only about a third of coal's chemical energy leaving as electricity — the rest is heat lost to the sky

geography.grade11.coal-and-thermal-elect.subject: geography
geography.grade11.coal-and-thermal-elect.question: The receipts drawer for coal contains:
options: Historically cheap power that built industry, steady baseload, about ninety thousand mining jobs, coal towns and Richards Bay exports

geography.grade11.coal-and-thermal-elect.subject: geography
geography.grade11.coal-and-thermal-elect.question: The 'nastiest line item' in the bills drawer is:
options: Acid mine drainage — old flooded mines leaking acidic, metal-heavy water toward rivers a century after closing

geography.grade11.coal-and-thermal-elect.subject: geography
geography.grade11.coal-and-thermal-elect.question: The land bill of coal includes:
options: Opencast pits consuming the same Mpumalanga farmland that grows much of the maize crop

geography.grade11.coal-and-thermal-elect.subject: geography
geography.grade11.coal-and-thermal-elect.question: 'Coal built the house AND is quietly burning some of it down' is the reminder that:
options: Any honest answer opens both drawers — real benefits and real, accumulating costs together

geography.grade11.coal-and-thermal-elect.subject: geography
geography.grade11.coal-and-thermal-elect.question: The road signs that turn coal-only into a countdown include:
options: An ageing fleet, banks refusing new coal finance, looming carbon border taxes, water constraints and climate commitments
The closure of Richards Bay terminal

geography.grade11.coal-and-thermal-elect.subject: geography
geography.grade11.coal-and-thermal-elect.question: From the steam onward, a nuclear station is 'just the kettle again' because:
options: Nuclear stations boil water at lower temperatures
Fission heat raises steam that drives a turbine and generator exactly as in any thermal plant
Uranium is burned in the same furnace as coal
Nuclear stations have no cooling systems

geography.grade11.coal-and-thermal-elect.subject: geography
geography.grade11.coal-and-thermal-elect.question: South Africa's nuclear waste is stored:
options: At sea beyond the continental shelf
At Koeberg and at the Vaalputs facility in the Northern Cape

geography.grade11.coal-and-thermal-elect.subject: geography
geography.grade11.coal-and-thermal-elect.question: The exam-safe verdict at the fork is:
options: Choose coal until the reserves run out
Choose nuclear exclusively despite the cost
No single source can carry the future — coal is counting down, nuclear is clean but slow and dear — so the answer is a mix

geography.grade11.cuestas-homoclinal-rid.subject: geography
geography.grade11.cuestas-homoclinal-rid.question: The DIP of a tilted rock layer is:
options: The angle between the layer and the horizontal
The depth of the layer underground
The length of the ridge it forms
