geography.grade11.cuestas-homoclinal-rid.subject: geography
geography.grade11.cuestas-homoclinal-rid.question: The dip slope of a tilted ridge:
options: Cuts across the ends of many layers
FOLLOWS the tilted upper surface of one resistant layer, so its angle matches the dip of the rock
Faces the same way as the scarp slope

geography.grade11.cuestas-homoclinal-rid.subject: geography
geography.grade11.cuestas-homoclinal-rid.question: The scarp slope is steep and often cliffed because it:
options: Runs along a single soft layer
CUTS ACROSS the broken edges of layer after layer, truncating the resistant band near the top

geography.grade11.cuestas-homoclinal-rid.subject: geography
geography.grade11.cuestas-homoclinal-rid.question: Strata become tilted through:
options: Crustal movements — compression and folding, unequal uplift, or the sagging and arching of basins

geography.grade11.cuestas-homoclinal-rid.subject: geography
geography.grade11.cuestas-homoclinal-rid.question: A cuesta forms where the strata dip:
options: Gently, up to about 25 degrees — giving a long gentle dip slope and a short steep scarp slope

geography.grade11.cuestas-homoclinal-rid.subject: geography
geography.grade11.cuestas-homoclinal-rid.question: The Magaliesberg near Pretoria is South Africa's textbook example of a:
options: HOMOCLINAL RIDGE — a resistant quartzite ridge with strata dipping steeply between about 25 and 45 degrees

geography.grade11.cuestas-homoclinal-rid.subject: geography
geography.grade11.cuestas-homoclinal-rid.question: A hogsback is near-symmetrical because:
options: With the layers standing beyond about 45 degrees, BOTH sides cut across strata at similar steep angles — the gentle dip-slope ramp disappears

geography.grade11.cuestas-homoclinal-rid.subject: geography
geography.grade11.cuestas-homoclinal-rid.question: As dip increases from gentle to near-vertical, the ridge:
options: Becomes narrower and its two slopes become more EQUAL, until the asymmetry vanishes

geography.grade11.cuestas-homoclinal-rid.subject: geography
geography.grade11.cuestas-homoclinal-rid.question: In a cuesta basin, the slopes of the concentric ridges are arranged with:
options: Dip slopes facing INWARD toward the centre and scarp slopes facing OUTWARD
Dip slopes facing outward and scarps inward

geography.grade11.cuestas-homoclinal-rid.subject: geography
geography.grade11.cuestas-homoclinal-rid.question: Artesian water occurs in cuesta basins because:
options: Water entering a tilted aquifer at the rim flows down the dip and collects under PRESSURE beneath the centre, so boreholes there may flow unaided
The centre of a basin is always a lake

geography.grade11.cuestas-homoclinal-rid.subject: geography
geography.grade11.cuestas-homoclinal-rid.question: In a cuesta dome, the scarp slopes face:
options: INWARD toward each other across the eroded core, because each layer dips down away from the centre

geography.grade11.cuestas-homoclinal-rid.subject: geography
geography.grade11.cuestas-homoclinal-rid.question: South Africa's world-famous ring structure of upturned strata etched into concentric ridges is:
options: The VREDEFORT DOME south-west of Johannesburg, a World Heritage Site

geography.grade11.cuestas-homoclinal-rid.subject: geography
geography.grade11.cuestas-homoclinal-rid.question: On a contour map, a cuesta or homoclinal ridge shows:
options: Contours tightly crowded on ONE side of the crest and widely spaced on the other

geography.grade11.cuestas-homoclinal-rid.subject: geography
geography.grade11.cuestas-homoclinal-rid.question: Crest at 1 500 m; the 1 300 m contour lies 400 m away on the north side and 2 000 m away on the south. The gradients are:
options: North 1 in 2 and south 1 in 10 — so the north is the scarp and the strata dip south

geography.grade11.cuestas-homoclinal-rid.subject: geography
geography.grade11.cuestas-homoclinal-rid.question: With a vertical scale of 1 cm to 100 m and a horizontal scale of 1:50 000, the vertical exaggeration is:
options: 5 times — vertical scale 1:10 000, and 50 000 divided by 10 000 is 5

geography.grade11.cuestas-homoclinal-rid.subject: geography
geography.grade11.cuestas-homoclinal-rid.question: Human activity in tilted-strata country typically places:
options: Highways straight up the scarp faces
Farms on the gentle dip slopes, roads and towns in the strike valleys, and crossings where rivers have cut poorts through the crest — like the Hartbeespoort gap in the Magaliesberg

geography.grade11.cuestas-homoclinal-rid.subject: geography
geography.grade11.cuestas-homoclinal-rid.question: In the tilted lever-arch file picture, the top cover you run your hand down stands for:
options: The DIP SLOPE — the gentle ramp riding on the surface of one strong layer

geography.grade11.cuestas-homoclinal-rid.subject: geography
geography.grade11.cuestas-homoclinal-rid.question: The high END of the file, showing the cut-off edges of all the pages, stands for:
options: The SCARP SLOPE — the steep face slicing across the ends of the layers

geography.grade11.cuestas-homoclinal-rid.subject: geography
geography.grade11.cuestas-homoclinal-rid.question: The memory line 'dip follows, scarp cuts' means:
options: The dip slope is always steeper
Both slopes follow the same layer
The dip slope runs along ONE layer's surface while the scarp slope cuts across MANY layers' edges

geography.grade11.cuestas-homoclinal-rid.subject: geography
geography.grade11.cuestas-homoclinal-rid.question: The three dial settings, in order of increasing tilt, are:

geography.grade11.cuestas-homoclinal-rid.subject: geography
geography.grade11.cuestas-homoclinal-rid.question: The 'wheelchair ramp with a cliff at the back' describes:
options: A CUESTA — gentle dip slope, short steep scarp, dip up to about 25 degrees

geography.grade11.cuestas-homoclinal-rid.subject: geography
geography.grade11.cuestas-homoclinal-rid.question: At the hedgehog setting, past about 45 degrees, the ramp disappears because:
options: The ridge sinks below the plain
With layers standing nearly upright, both sides cut across page-edges and both are steep — no side follows a layer surface gently anymore

geography.grade11.cuestas-homoclinal-rid.subject: geography
geography.grade11.cuestas-homoclinal-rid.question: The one-sentence trend for the essay is:
options: The steeper the dip, the wider and flatter the ridge
Dip has no effect on ridge shape
The steeper the dip, the narrower the ridge and the more equal its two slopes, until the difference vanishes near vertical

geography.grade11.cuestas-homoclinal-rid.subject: geography
geography.grade11.cuestas-homoclinal-rid.question: The nested soup bowls stand for a cuesta basin, in which:
options: Gentle dip slopes face INWARD to the centre and scarp rims face OUTWARD

geography.grade11.cuestas-homoclinal-rid.subject: geography
geography.grade11.cuestas-homoclinal-rid.question: Drilling a borehole near the CENTRE of a cuesta basin can yield:
options: ARTESIAN water that rises on its own, because water entering the tilted layer at the rim collects under pressure below the middle

geography.grade11.cuestas-homoclinal-rid.subject: geography
geography.grade11.cuestas-homoclinal-rid.question: The upside-down blister pile stands for:
options: A CUESTA DOME — dip slopes facing outward, scarps facing inward across the eroded core, like the Vredefort Dome

geography.grade11.cuestas-homoclinal-rid.subject: geography
geography.grade11.cuestas-homoclinal-rid.question: The highway, railway and dam all squeeze through the same gap in the Magaliesberg because:
options: The crest is the flattest ground
The valleys are too wide for roads
Traffic can cross the resistant ridge only where a river has already sawn a poort through it — human routes obey the rock

geography.grade11.development-aid-and-it.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-aid-and-it.question: Development aid is defined as:
options: The transfer of money, goods, technology or expertise from richer countries and institutions to poorer ones, on terms softer than the market's
Remittances sent home by migrant workers

geography.grade11.development-aid-and-it.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-aid-and-it.question: Aid pooled through the World Bank, UN agencies or the African Development Bank is called:

geography.grade11.development-aid-and-it.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-aid-and-it.question: Development co-operation differs from traditional aid language because:
options: It involves larger amounts of money
It frames a partnership with obligations on both sides — recipients set priorities and account for results, donors align with the recipient's own plans

geography.grade11.development-aid-and-it.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-aid-and-it.question: South Africa 'sits on both sides of the table' because it:
options: Receives aid — notably health funding — while extending assistance within Africa through the African Renaissance Fund and trilateral projects

geography.grade11.development-aid-and-it.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-aid-and-it.question: Technical aid's characteristic strength is that:
options: A skill keeps working after the money is spent once — engineers, agronomists and trainers leave permanent capacity behind
It arrives faster than any other type

geography.grade11.development-aid-and-it.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-aid-and-it.question: Procurement tying means:
options: Aid must be repaid with interest
The recipient must spend the aid on the donor's own goods and firms, recycling much of the money back to the donor and inflating costs
The recipient chooses any supplier by tender

geography.grade11.development-aid-and-it.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-aid-and-it.question: The structural adjustment programmes of the 1980s and 1990s are cited as the hard case of:
options: Policy conditionality — loans requiring spending cuts, privatisation and open markets, which in many African countries gutted health and education budgets

geography.grade11.development-aid-and-it.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-aid-and-it.question: Judging emergency food aid for failing to industrialise a country is called a category error because:
options: Food aid always industrialises countries eventually
Short-term relief stops the bleeding while long-term development aid builds the hospital — they answer different problems

geography.grade11.development-aid-and-it.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-aid-and-it.question: Aid's single most complete triumph is:
options: The eradication of smallpox through an aid-funded global vaccination campaign

geography.grade11.development-aid-and-it.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-aid-and-it.question: PEPFAR and Global Fund financing mattered to South Africa because:
options: They funded the national road network
They helped carry the world's largest antiretroviral programme, and life expectancy climbed back from the low fifties to above sixty
They replaced the national health budget entirely
They funded only research, never treatment

geography.grade11.development-aid-and-it.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-aid-and-it.question: Aid 'catalysing' investment means:
options: A grant that de-risks a port or power plant can unlock private investment many times its size

geography.grade11.development-aid-and-it.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-aid-and-it.question: The honest generalisation across aid's successes is that aid works best when:
options: It is as large as possible
It is spread across many small unrelated projects
It targets specific, measurable problems, aligns with the recipient's own priorities, and is sustained long enough to finish the job

geography.grade11.development-aid-and-it.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-aid-and-it.question: Aid dependency develops when:
options: Aid finances a large share of a government's budget year after year, tilting accountability toward donors and weakening the drive to build a tax base
A country repays its loans early

geography.grade11.development-aid-and-it.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-aid-and-it.question: Food aid outside genuine emergencies can distort development by:
options: Undercutting local farmers until they stop planting — solving this year's hunger by creating next year's

geography.grade11.development-aid-and-it.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-aid-and-it.question: The 1980s-90s debt crisis showed aid 'flowing backwards' because:
options: Many African countries paid more in debt service than they spent on health and education combined

geography.grade11.development-aid-and-it.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-aid-and-it.question: The scaffolding verdict on aid holds that:
options: Aid should be permanent for all countries
Aid never helps under any conditions
Scaffolding is more important than the building
Aid is essential during construction but must be designed to come down as the building stands — a tool, not a permanent economic strategy

geography.grade11.development-aid-and-it.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-aid-and-it.question: In the proverb picture, the 'fish' is:
options: Humanitarian aid — the food parcel, rescue boat and blankets, judged by speed and reach

geography.grade11.development-aid-and-it.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-aid-and-it.question: 'During the flood, a lesson is useless and a boat is everything' teaches that:
options: Timing decides which aid is right — emergencies need relief, and development needs skills
Boats are a form of technical aid

geography.grade11.development-aid-and-it.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-aid-and-it.question: The beached boats — local fishermen unable to compete with free fish — represent:
options: Dependency and market distortion — permanent free aid pushing local producers out until the town waits on the truck

geography.grade11.development-aid-and-it.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-aid-and-it.question: The neighbour insisting you buy roof sheets from his shop at his prices stands for:
options: Procurement tying — aid money cycling back to donor companies while costs inflate

geography.grade11.development-aid-and-it.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-aid-and-it.question: The neighbour demanding a say in your household budget stands for:
options: Policy conditionality — money flowing only if prescribed policies are adopted, as in the structural adjustment era

geography.grade11.development-aid-and-it.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-aid-and-it.question: Naming donors' mixed motives — influence, trade, security alongside solidarity — is described as:
options: An insult to be avoided in essays
Analysis, not insult — the analytical edge the essay question rewards
Proof that all aid is harmful

geography.grade11.development-aid-and-it.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-aid-and-it.question: The 'co-operation upgrade' to the gift-with-strings works by:
options: Removing all conditions from every grant
Letting the donor design the renovation alone
The household setting its own plan, the neighbour contributing to that plan, and both signing accountability agreements — obligations both ways

geography.grade11.development-aid-and-it.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-aid-and-it.question: Items that belong on the triumphs pan of the scale include:
options: Smallpox eradication, South Africa's ARV programme, steep falls in malaria deaths, and rapid flood relief

geography.grade11.development-aid-and-it.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-aid-and-it.question: Items that belong on the failures pan include:
options: Food dumping beaching local farmers, debt eating health budgets, tied money returning to donors, and dependency on donor funding

geography.grade11.development-aid-and-it.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-aid-and-it.question: 'Nobody calls scaffolding a house' argues that:
options: Aid supports construction but is not itself development, and if it stays up forever something has gone wrong with the building
Construction is the only true aid

geography.grade11.development-aid-and-it.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-aid-and-it.question: The exam-winning conclusion on aid is that it:
options: Works when it targets a specific, finishable job, follows the recipient's own plan, and is designed from day one to become unnecessary

geography.grade11.development-issues-and.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-issues-and.question: The contrast between the mineral-rich, poor DRC and resource-bare, rich Singapore shows that:
options: Resources are not destiny — what matters is whether they are converted into broad development or captured by a few, the failure called the resource curse

geography.grade11.development-issues-and.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-issues-and.question: Education is called the master key among development factors because:
options: It is the cheapest service to provide
Without skills, investment finds no workers and technology finds no users — every success story invested in education first
It replaces the need for energy and resources
It is the only factor governments control

geography.grade11.development-issues-and.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-issues-and.question: Colonial railway lines frustrate development today because they were built:
options: From mine to port rather than town to town, serving extraction instead of internal connection

geography.grade11.development-issues-and.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-issues-and.question: The word the examiner wants for how the development factors operate is:
options: Sequential — each factor acts alone in turn
Interrelated — drought pulls education, education pulls skills, skills pull investment, and the chain loops back

geography.grade11.development-issues-and.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-issues-and.question: The apartheid spatial legacy still shapes development because:
options: Forced removals and homeland policy placed millions far from jobs on the worst land, and that geography outlives the laws that drew it
The homelands were given the best farmland
Commuting costs are equal across the country

geography.grade11.development-issues-and.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-issues-and.question: The pair of figures defining South Africa's core social challenge is:
options: A Gini coefficient near 0,63 and unemployment above 30 per cent — over 40 per cent among youth
Life expectancy of 80 and full employment
A Gini of 0,3 and unemployment of 5 per cent

geography.grade11.development-issues-and.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-issues-and.question: Load-shedding counts as a development issue, not merely an inconvenience, because:
options: It closes the spaza's fridge, the clinic's cold chain and the factory's shift, and deters job-creating investment

geography.grade11.development-issues-and.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-issues-and.question: The balanced assessment CAPS expects of post-1994 South Africa is:
options: Only the economy matters in the assessment
Enormous gains in services and social grants set against stubborn unemployment, inequality and institutional strain — both halves true

geography.grade11.development-issues-and.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-issues-and.question: The core principles of community-based development are:
options: Participation, respect for local knowledge, appropriate technology, skills transfer and community ownership
Speed, scale, central planning and imported expertise

geography.grade11.development-issues-and.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-issues-and.question: Working for Water delivers development and environment gains together by:
options: Building large dams in every catchment
Paying local teams to clear thirsty alien vegetation, returning water to streams while providing wages and training

geography.grade11.development-issues-and.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-issues-and.question: Upgrading informal settlements in place is preferred to relocation because:
options: Relocation is more expensive in every case
Relocation breaks the job connections and social networks that keep poor households afloat

geography.grade11.development-issues-and.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-issues-and.question: The honest limitation of community-based development is that:
options: It always fails within a year
Projects are small relative to national need, can be captured by local elites, and complement rather than replace state-scale delivery

geography.grade11.development-issues-and.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-issues-and.question: Acid mine drainage is the problem of:
options: Acidic, metal-laden water from abandoned Witwatersrand shafts seeping toward rivers — a bill arriving decades after the profits left
Chemical spills from working platinum mines only

geography.grade11.development-issues-and.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-issues-and.question: Environmental damage is called a 'loan against development' because:
options: Eroded soil, polluted water and degraded land subtract from future production — the damage is repaid with interest, mostly by the poor
Loans are needed to clean it up

geography.grade11.development-issues-and.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-issues-and.question: Poverty itself degrades environments because:
options: Households without electricity strip woodland for fuel and hungry herders overstock fragile range — closing the circle back to deeper poverty

geography.grade11.development-issues-and.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-issues-and.question: Tools that pursue development without environmental destruction include:
options: Ignoring impact assessments to speed up projects
Environmental impact assessments, mine rehabilitation obligations, protected areas earning tourism income, and the renewable energy build

geography.grade11.development-issues-and.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-issues-and.question: The earphone knot stands for:
options: The interrelated causes of poverty — pulling one wire tightens the knot somewhere else

geography.grade11.development-issues-and.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-issues-and.question: In the family story, the eldest child leaving school to herd goats after the drought shows:
options: That herding pays better than matric
The resource wire pulling the education wire — one factor tightening another

geography.grade11.development-issues-and.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-issues-and.question: 'It is never the rocks; it is what a country does with them' summarises:
options: The importance of geology in development
The resource curse — treasure captured by a few funds their fights while everyone else stays poor
The need for more mineral exploration

geography.grade11.development-issues-and.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-issues-and.question: The golden rule of the stoep approach is:
options: People maintain what is theirs — plan it, build it, own it
Big projects always beat small ones

geography.grade11.development-issues-and.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-issues-and.question: The Eastern Cape wool farmers' success came from:
options: Government buying their wool at fixed prices
Pooling small harvests and grading them properly, reaching buyers and prices no lone farmer could

geography.grade11.development-issues-and.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-issues-and.question: Crime fell along Khayelitsha's upgraded walkways because:
options: The walkways were closed at night
Residents co-designed lighting and routes they actually walk — the people who walk the path know where the fear lives

geography.grade11.development-issues-and.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-issues-and.question: The evaluation sentence to keep for community projects is:
options: They should replace all state programmes
They fail more often than they succeed
They work only with foreign funding
Powerful but small — community hands and state muscle are both needed, each doing what it does best

geography.grade11.development-issues-and.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-issues-and.question: Burning the roof beams to stay warm this winter stands for:
options: Development that eats its own environment — a loan from tomorrow repaid with interest

geography.grade11.development-issues-and.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-issues-and.question: The 'cruel twist' about environmental bills is that:
options: They are paid by mining companies first
They land on the poor first — the shack settlement, not the golf estate, sits beside the mine dump and drinks from the brown river
They arrive only after a century

geography.grade11.development-issues-and.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-issues-and.question: Overgrazed slopes washing into dams hurt development twice because:
options: The land loses its soil and the city loses water storage in one motion

geography.grade11.development-issues-and.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-issues-and.question: The sentence that ties the whole term together is:
options: Meet today's needs without stealing from your grandchildren's — development that plans to still be standing when they arrive

geography.grade11.development-resources-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-resources-.question: Economic growth and development differ in that:
options: Growth is more output measured in money; development asks whether lives improve in health, education and choice
Growth only happens in developing countries
Development is measured in GDP and growth in HDI

geography.grade11.development-resources-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-resources-.question: The Gini coefficient measures:
options: The total size of an economy
Inequality of income distribution, from zero at perfect equality toward one
The number of people below a poverty line

geography.grade11.development-resources-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-resources-.question: The Human Development Index combines:
options: A long and healthy life, knowledge, and a decent standard of living
Birth rate, death rate and migration

geography.grade11.development-resources-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-resources-.question: A fair criticism of Rostow's model is that it:
options: Has too few stages to describe any economy
Assumes every country repeats the West's staircase, ignoring colonial history and late-starter disadvantages

geography.grade11.development-resources-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-resources-.question: The terms of trade move against raw-material exporters because:
options: Primary prices swing and drift downward against the steadier, rising prices of manufactured imports
Manufactured goods get cheaper faster than ore
Raw materials cannot be exported legally

geography.grade11.development-resources-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-resources-.question: Beneficiation means:
options: Receiving development aid from a donor
Processing your own raw materials to capture the value added before export

geography.grade11.development-resources-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-resources-.question: Tied or conditional aid is aid that:
options: Is delivered only after a disaster
Comes with strings, such as spending it on the donor's goods or adopting the donor's policies

geography.grade11.development-resources-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-resources-.question: The dependency argument against long-term food aid is that it can:
options: Undercut local farmers' prices and destroy the local production it should be building

geography.grade11.development-resources-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-resources-.question: The energy chain inside a coal-fired power station runs:
options: Coal burned, water boiled to steam, steam spins the turbine, turbine spins the generator
Coal crushed, coal spins the turbine directly, electricity stored in the tower
Steam burned, coal boiled, generator heats the turbine
Coal dissolved in water, current extracted chemically

geography.grade11.development-resources-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-resources-.question: Acid mine drainage is:
options: Rainwater draining off power station roofs
The chemical used to wash coal before burning
Water turned acidic in old mine workings, leaking toward rivers
A method of cooling turbines with recycled water

geography.grade11.development-resources-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-resources-.question: Pumped-storage schemes like Ingula act as:
options: The country's main source of new electricity
Giant batteries — pumping water uphill in quiet hours to release through turbines at peak demand

geography.grade11.development-resources-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-resources-.question: The main technical limitation of solar and wind power is:
options: Their fuel is the most expensive available
They emit more carbon than coal
They can only be built underground
Intermittency — the sun sets and the wind lulls, so they need storage and flexible backup

geography.grade11.development-resources-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-resources-.question: Soil is treated as non-renewable because:
options: It takes centuries to form a few centimetres of topsoil, which one storm on bare ground can remove
It cannot be moved between farms
Plants use it up permanently as they grow
South African law classifies it as a mineral

geography.grade11.development-resources-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-resources-.question: The erosion sequence on abused land runs:
options: Donga, then rills, then sheet erosion, then splash
Gully first, then sheet erosion spreads from it
Raindrop splash, sheet erosion, rills, then gullies or dongas
Rills form only after dongas collapse

geography.grade11.development-resources-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-resources-.question: Ploughing along the contours controls erosion because:
options: It loosens soil so water sinks faster downhill
It doubles the speed of runoff
Contour lines mark where erosion cannot happen
Each furrow lies across the slope and acts as a small dam holding water back

geography.grade11.development-resources-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-resources-.question: In the greener economy, the syllabus assigns responsibilities to:
options: Government, businesses and individuals, each with their own list

geography.grade11.development-resources-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-resources-.question: Judging a country by total GDP is like judging a school by total marks because:
options: The biggest school always wins regardless of how its learners actually perform
Marks and money are the same thing

geography.grade11.development-resources-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-resources-.question: In the rigged shop, the trap for raw-material sellers is that:
options: Raw prices wobble and slide while finished-goods prices march up, so the same ore buys less each year
They may not enter the shop at all
Finished goods are banned from export

geography.grade11.development-resources-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-resources-.question: Aid that builds bakeries beats aid that delivers bread means:
options: Emergency food aid is always wrong
Aid that builds local capacity beats permanent handouts that create dependency
Donors should only fund food industries

geography.grade11.development-resources-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-resources-.question: In the braai picture, baseload is:
options: The steady floor of supply a grid needs, like a fire that burns all night
The maximum the grid can ever carry

geography.grade11.development-resources-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-resources-.question: The Northern Cape suits concentrated solar plants because:
options: It has the country's strongest winds
Its clear dry skies deliver among the best sunshine on the planet, and molten salt storage extends output after dark
It is closest to the coalfields

geography.grade11.development-resources-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-resources-.question: Renewable electricity became cheaper than new coal in South Africa largely because:
options: Competitive bidding rounds pulled private investors into wind and solar and drove prices down

geography.grade11.development-resources-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-resources-.question: The just transition requires that:
options: Coalfield workers and towns are retrained and included in the new energy economy rather than abandoned
Renewables are built only outside coal regions

geography.grade11.development-resources-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-resources-.question: The teaspoon and the bucket describe:
options: Soil forming at a teaspoon a year while one storm on bare ground withdraws decades of it
The ratio of rain to evaporation
The difference between rills and gullies

geography.grade11.development-resources-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-resources-.question: In the bank-account picture, coal and sunshine differ because:
options: Coal is capital — a one-time inheritance being burned — while sun and wind are interest arriving fresh forever
Sunshine is capital and coal is interest

geography.grade11.development-resources-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-resources-.question: Gabions heal a donga by:
options: Poisoning the plants that caused it
Draining the water table beneath it
Sealing it under a concrete channel
Slowing each flood with rock-filled baskets until it drops its soil and the channel silts closed

geography.grade11.development-resources-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.development-resources-.question: The circle of the year connects the topics as:
options: Trade causes floods which cause aid
Soil erosion causes El Niño events
Development needs energy; coal energy warms the climate; harder droughts and storms strip the soil; lost soil starves the farming development depends on
The topics are unrelated and must be studied separately

geography.grade11.droughts-and-desertifi.subject: geography
geography.grade11.droughts-and-desertifi.question: A drought is correctly defined as:
options: An extended period of rainfall well below the NORMAL average for that particular place
Any year with less than 500 mm of rain
A season with no rain at all anywhere

geography.grade11.droughts-and-desertifi.subject: geography
geography.grade11.droughts-and-desertifi.question: The correct order of deepening drought is:

geography.grade11.droughts-and-desertifi.subject: geography
geography.grade11.droughts-and-desertifi.question: Hydrological drought is reached when:
options: Soil moisture first drops below crop needs
The shortage reaches the water system — river flow shrinks, dam levels drop and groundwater tables sink

geography.grade11.droughts-and-desertifi.subject: geography
geography.grade11.droughts-and-desertifi.question: A natural cause that tilts southern Africa toward drought years is:
options: EL NIÑO — warm eastern Pacific water reorganising the circulation, as in the 2015-16 drought

geography.grade11.droughts-and-desertifi.subject: geography
geography.grade11.droughts-and-desertifi.question: Desertification is best described as:
options: Degradation of land in arid and semi-arid regions until it becomes desert-like — not a desert advancing, but productive land dying in patches
The Sahara physically marching southward like an army
The natural existence of deserts at 30 degrees

geography.grade11.droughts-and-desertifi.subject: geography
geography.grade11.droughts-and-desertifi.question: Salinisation is caused by:
options: Too much rain washing salt inland
Poor irrigation in hot climates — evaporating water leaves salt behind in the soil until nothing grows

geography.grade11.droughts-and-desertifi.subject: geography
geography.grade11.droughts-and-desertifi.question: Desertification is a positive feedback loop because:
options: It has positive effects on the land
Lost topsoil means less vegetation returns, which bares more soil, which erodes faster — the process feeds itself

geography.grade11.droughts-and-desertifi.subject: geography
geography.grade11.droughts-and-desertifi.question: The world's warning region for desertification, along the southern edge of the Sahara, is:
options: The SAHEL — degraded by overgrazing, firewood cutting and repeated drought

geography.grade11.droughts-and-desertifi.subject: geography
geography.grade11.droughts-and-desertifi.question: The environmental cascade of drought and desertification begins with:
options: Loss of VEGETATION, which collapses grazing, habitats and biodiversity and exposes the soil

geography.grade11.droughts-and-desertifi.subject: geography
geography.grade11.droughts-and-desertifi.question: During the 2015-16 South African drought:
options: Tens of thousands of cattle died and the maize harvest fell so far that the country had to import maize
Only the Western Cape was affected

geography.grade11.droughts-and-desertifi.subject: geography
geography.grade11.droughts-and-desertifi.question: Drought migration refers to:
options: Livestock moving to new grazing camps
Rural families sending members to cities as farm work and incomes fail, swelling informal settlements

geography.grade11.droughts-and-desertifi.subject: geography
geography.grade11.droughts-and-desertifi.question: Cape Town's Day Zero plan of early 2018 was:
options: The date desalination plants would open
The date the dams would be full again
The published date when household taps would be closed and residents would queue for 25 litres each at collection points

geography.grade11.droughts-and-desertifi.subject: geography
geography.grade11.droughts-and-desertifi.question: Early warning systems help farmers by:
options: Letting them reduce herds while animals still have value and plant drought-resistant crops BEFORE the disaster peaks
Replacing the need for any other strategy
Predicting exact rainfall five years ahead

geography.grade11.droughts-and-desertifi.subject: geography
geography.grade11.droughts-and-desertifi.question: Drip irrigation saves water because it:
options: Delivers water straight to the roots instead of flooding the field and losing water to evaporation

geography.grade11.droughts-and-desertifi.subject: geography
geography.grade11.droughts-and-desertifi.question: Working for Water restores rivers by:
options: Paying teams to clear thirsty alien invasive plants — wattles, pines and eucalypts — creating jobs while freeing water

geography.grade11.droughts-and-desertifi.subject: geography
geography.grade11.droughts-and-desertifi.question: The Great Green Wall initiative is best described as:
options: A concrete barrier against sand dunes
A single unbroken forest planted in one year
Thousands of community land-restoration projects re-greening a mosaic across the Sahel from Senegal to Djibouti

geography.grade11.droughts-and-desertifi.subject: geography
geography.grade11.droughts-and-desertifi.question: The bank account picture defines drought as:
options: A salary that suddenly drops far below what THIS account was built on — rainfall below the local normal
Any small salary — low rainfall anywhere

geography.grade11.droughts-and-desertifi.subject: geography
geography.grade11.droughts-and-desertifi.question: In the four-stage account failure, 'the savings run out' stands for:
options: Hydrological drought — rivers shrinking, dams sliding, boreholes dropping

geography.grade11.droughts-and-desertifi.subject: geography
geography.grade11.droughts-and-desertifi.question: Upington's 250 mm a year is not a drought because:
options: Upington gets water from the sea
250 mm is a high rainfall figure
That is NORMAL for Upington — drought is always measured against the local average

geography.grade11.droughts-and-desertifi.subject: geography
geography.grade11.droughts-and-desertifi.question: The 'recipe' for desertification includes:
options: Too many livestock, ploughing without rest, chopping trees for firewood and careless hot-climate irrigation
Planting windbreaks and resting the veld

geography.grade11.droughts-and-desertifi.subject: geography
geography.grade11.droughts-and-desertifi.question: In the shaved-scalp picture, bald land erodes because:
options: Bald soil absorbs too much water
The baked hard surface makes rain bounce and race away in torrents that rip open dongas and steal the topsoil
Grass roots push the soil away

geography.grade11.droughts-and-desertifi.subject: geography
geography.grade11.droughts-and-desertifi.question: South African areas showing classic desertification damage include:
options: Parts of the Karoo, the Kalahari margins and the crowded former homeland areas of the Eastern Cape

geography.grade11.droughts-and-desertifi.subject: geography
geography.grade11.droughts-and-desertifi.question: The rolling snowball stands for:
options: The self-feeding spiral — less soil, less grass, more bare ground, faster erosion

geography.grade11.droughts-and-desertifi.subject: geography
geography.grade11.droughts-and-desertifi.question: Cape Town pushed Day Zero back mainly by:
options: Halving the city's water use through restrictions, steep tariffs, pressure management and a public campaign
Waiting for the rain and doing nothing

geography.grade11.droughts-and-desertifi.subject: geography
geography.grade11.droughts-and-desertifi.question: The planned Day Zero ration of 25 litres per person per day equals roughly:
options: Two buckets — less than one short shower

geography.grade11.droughts-and-desertifi.subject: geography
geography.grade11.droughts-and-desertifi.question: Savings in agriculture matter most because:
options: Agriculture drinks the majority of South Africa's water, so a small percentage saved there beats a big bathroom saving

geography.grade11.droughts-and-desertifi.subject: geography
geography.grade11.droughts-and-desertifi.question: The three management moves in order are:
options: SEE IT COMING with warnings and GIS, SPEND LESS through demand management, and HEAL THE LAND by resting veld, plugging dongas and clearing alien plants

geography.grade11.energy-management-for-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.energy-management-for-.question: The three pressures making energy management unavoidable for South Africa are:
options: Supply strain proven by load-shedding, climate-and-trade pressure including carbon border taxes, and equity — wasted energy is development lost
Falling coal prices, rising exports and tourism
Population decline, urban shrinkage and deflation
Cheap electricity, abundant water and low demand

geography.grade11.energy-management-for-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.energy-management-for-.question: A greener economy is defined as:
options: An economy based only on agriculture
One that grows while its resource use and emissions shrink — decoupling prosperity from pollution
One that exports only renewable electricity

geography.grade11.energy-management-for-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.energy-management-for-.question: Efficiency is called the invisible power station because:
options: Renewable plants are hard to see
Saving one station's worth of demand is cheaper, faster and cleaner than building one, and emits nothing

geography.grade11.energy-management-for-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.energy-management-for-.question: Carbon border taxes threaten South African exports because:
options: Ships must now burn cleaner fuel
Products made with coal-heavy electricity pay penalties at rich-country borders — the dirty grid becomes a tax on every exported ton

geography.grade11.energy-management-for-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.energy-management-for-.question: The Integrated Resource Plan (IRP) is:
options: The official electricity roadmap setting what retires and what gets built by which year — the document investors, Eskom and municipalities steer by

geography.grade11.energy-management-for-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.energy-management-for-.question: South Africa's carbon tax works by:
options: Making emitters pay per ton of carbon dioxide, nudging industry toward cleaner processes — the first tax of its kind in Africa

geography.grade11.energy-management-for-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.energy-management-for-.question: The 'quiet rules' that save more energy than most headline projects are:
options: Building energy-performance regulations, appliance labelling, and minimum efficiency standards banning the worst products

geography.grade11.energy-management-for-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.energy-management-for-.question: The Just Energy Transition Partnership channels international finance into:
options: Grid building, coal-town retraining and green industry — pledged in the tens of billions of dollars

geography.grade11.energy-management-for-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.energy-management-for-.question: An energy audit is:
options: A metered walk through a firm's operations finding where energy is wasted — leaks, worn motors, uninsulated pipes — with fixes ranked by payback
A tax inspection of electricity bills
A count of the firm's generators

geography.grade11.energy-management-for-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.energy-management-for-.question: Wheeling allows a company to:
options: Transport coal by road instead of rail
Generate power at a sunny site and consume it, via the grid, at another site

geography.grade11.energy-management-for-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.energy-management-for-.question: A product's carbon footprint has become a matter of market access because:
options: Footprints are printed on packaging by law worldwide
European carbon border rules tax the emissions embedded in imports, and banks and investors screen for climate risk

geography.grade11.energy-management-for-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.energy-management-for-.question: Greenwashing is:
options: Marketing an unchanged, polluting operation as eco-friendly — the opposite of measured baseline-target-audit-report management

geography.grade11.energy-management-for-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.energy-management-for-.question: The single hungriest machine in a typical home is:
options: The electric geyser, often around 40 per cent of the bill

geography.grade11.energy-management-for-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.energy-management-for-.question: The geyser efficiency ladder runs:
options: Thermostat to 60 degrees, insulating blanket, timer, and ultimately a solar water heater or heat pump so the sun does the heaviest job
Turn the thermostat to maximum for faster heating
Run the geyser only at the evening peak

geography.grade11.energy-management-for-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.energy-management-for-.question: LEDs are 'the cheap victory' because:
options: They give the same light for about a tenth of the electricity of incandescent bulbs and last years longer
They cool the room while lighting it

geography.grade11.energy-management-for-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.energy-management-for-.question: The 'citizen layer' of individual energy management includes:
options: Shifting use off-peak, turning homes into micro power stations with rooftop PV, and supporting the plans and lines the transition needs

geography.grade11.energy-management-for-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.energy-management-for-.question: Redrawing the energy problem as a leaking bucket shifts attention to:
options: Plugging the holes — waste in buildings, bulbs, geysers and motors — rather than only pouring in more supply

geography.grade11.energy-management-for-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.energy-management-for-.question: The comparison between a new station and plugging holes shows:
options: Both cost the same over ten years
A station costs hundreds of billions and takes a decade, while efficiency costs a fraction, works within months and emits nothing
Stations are faster to build than to insulate

geography.grade11.energy-management-for-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.energy-management-for-.question: The one-line summary of the entire topic is:
options: The kilowatt-hour you never use is the cheapest and cleanest one there is

geography.grade11.energy-management-for-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.energy-management-for-.question: The government spanner is 'the big one' because:
options: Only government can write the rules — the IRP roadmap, auctions, carbon tax, building rules, labels and the just transition money

geography.grade11.energy-management-for-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.energy-management-for-.question: The business spanner 'turns the biggest bolts' because:
options: Firms use most of the country's energy, so audits, rooftop solar and clean supply chains move the largest numbers
Only businesses pay the carbon tax

geography.grade11.energy-management-for-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.energy-management-for-.question: 'Foreign buyers now ask how much smoke is inside your product' refers to:
options: Carbon footprint reporting and border carbon rules turning a dirty grid into a trade problem — cleaning up as strategy, not charity

geography.grade11.energy-management-for-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.energy-management-for-.question: The warning label on the business spanner reads:
options: No greenwashing — painting the logo green while changing nothing fools nobody for long

geography.grade11.energy-management-for-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.energy-management-for-.question: The stadium wave answers the question of individual impact by showing:
options: The evening peak is millions of private choices landing together — one arm cannot make a wave, but the wave is nothing except arms
Sport is the biggest energy user

geography.grade11.energy-management-for-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.energy-management-for-.question: The plays ranked by size start with:
options: The geyser — the hungriest machine — then lighting, kitchen habits, winter sealing, standby and transport

geography.grade11.energy-management-for-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.energy-management-for-.question: 'Heat the person, not the ceiling' recommends:
options: Sealing gaps, insulating, and wearing warm clothing before heating whole rooms

geography.grade11.energy-management-for-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.energy-management-for-.question: The closing summary of the whole topic assigns the roles:
options: Individuals write rules, government turns bolts
Business writes the roadmap, households audit factories
Government acts alone while others watch
Government writes the rules, business turns the big bolts, and sixty million households are the wave — with the unused kilowatt-hour as champion

geography.grade11.frameworks-and-models-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.frameworks-and-models-.question: The Brundtland definition of sustainable development is:
options: Development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs
Development that maximises this decade's GDP
Development funded only by renewable industries
Development that stays within one region

geography.grade11.frameworks-and-models-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.frameworks-and-models-.question: A remote Karoo village is better served by solar panels and a borehole pump than by connection to a distant national mega-plant. This illustrates:
options: Appropriate-scale development — the solution matched to local skills, budgets and needs

geography.grade11.frameworks-and-models-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.frameworks-and-models-.question: The five aspects of development named in the lesson are:
options: Primary, secondary, tertiary, quaternary and quinary
Local, regional, national, continental and global
Economic, social, sustainable, appropriate-scale and spatial
Health, education, income, trade and aid

geography.grade11.frameworks-and-models-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.frameworks-and-models-.question: Social development is described as converting money into lives because:
options: It turns economic gains into education, health care, housing, safe water and the inclusion of women — outcomes rather than output

geography.grade11.frameworks-and-models-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.frameworks-and-models-.question: The backwash effect describes:
options: The periphery's young, skilled people and its capital draining toward the core, leaving the periphery less able to catch up
Investment flowing from core to periphery
The decline of the core as costs rise

geography.grade11.frameworks-and-models-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.frameworks-and-models-.question: Cumulative causation is the model's engine because:
options: Government decrees where factories must locate
Success attracts success — a factory draws suppliers, workers and taxes, funding infrastructure that attracts the next factory
All regions grow at the same rate
Raw materials always stay in the periphery

geography.grade11.frameworks-and-models-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.frameworks-and-models-.question: At the national scale, South Africa's clearest core-periphery pair is:
options: The Western Cape core and Gauteng periphery
Gauteng — about a third of GDP on the smallest provincial footprint — as core, with former homeland districts of the Eastern Cape and Limpopo as periphery
The coast as core and the entire interior as periphery

geography.grade11.frameworks-and-models-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.frameworks-and-models-.question: Spread effects are:
options: The expansion of the core's boundaries
Investment, remittances and demand flowing from core to periphery — the flows planners try to strengthen

geography.grade11.frameworks-and-models-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.frameworks-and-models-.question: The correct order of Rostow's five stages is:
options: Traditional society, preconditions for take-off, take-off, drive to maturity, high mass consumption
Traditional society, take-off, preconditions, consumption, maturity
Preconditions, traditional society, take-off, consumption, maturity

geography.grade11.frameworks-and-models-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.frameworks-and-models-.question: Take-off is marked by:
options: Rapid growth of manufacturing with investment climbing past roughly 10 per cent of national income, so growth becomes self-sustaining

geography.grade11.frameworks-and-models-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.frameworks-and-models-.question: The criticism that connects Rostow's model to colonial history is:
options: Colonies took off before their colonisers
Britain's take-off was fuelled partly by colonies whose own development was deliberately suppressed — the ladder was pulled up behind the climbers
The model was written by a colonial administrator

geography.grade11.frameworks-and-models-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.frameworks-and-models-.question: The model's treatment of high mass consumption is criticised because:
options: No country has ever reached the stage
It crowns consumption as the summit with no stage for sustainability — written before anyone asked whether the planet could host eight billion mass consumers

geography.grade11.frameworks-and-models-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.frameworks-and-models-.question: South Africa's Rostow preconditions arrived with:
options: The mineral revolution — railways and ports built after 1870 to serve diamonds and gold
The founding of the JSE alone

geography.grade11.frameworks-and-models-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.frameworks-and-models-.question: Apartheid is described as core-periphery engineering by law because:
options: The homelands were designed as labour reservoirs — peripheries whose backwash of migrant workers fed the mining core
It moved all industry to the periphery

geography.grade11.frameworks-and-models-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.frameworks-and-models-.question: Post-1994 projects like the Coega industrial development zone and the Maputo corridor are best read as:
options: Attempts to build new cores in the periphery and pump spread effects outward

geography.grade11.frameworks-and-models-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.frameworks-and-models-.question: The essay synthesis comparing the two models is:
options: Core-periphery assumes all regions develop together
Rostow describes a timeline and assumes regions ride it together; core-periphery describes a map and insists they do not — use one for history, the other for geography, and criticise both

geography.grade11.frameworks-and-models-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.frameworks-and-models-.question: The inspector who checks whether we are 'burning the roof beams to warm today's room' stands for:
options: Sustainability — meeting today's needs without robbing future generations of theirs

geography.grade11.frameworks-and-models-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.frameworks-and-models-.question: The village given a giant high-tech water plant it cannot repair received:
options: A monument, not development — the solution failed the fit test of appropriate scale

geography.grade11.frameworks-and-models-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.frameworks-and-models-.question: The fifth inspector, who checks the map, is asking:
options: Whether the country's borders are correct
Whether development is spreading spatially or piling up in one favoured corner
Whether the plan is written down

geography.grade11.frameworks-and-models-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.frameworks-and-models-.question: In the magnet picture, the iron filings sliding inward are:
options: People, capital and resources drawn from the periphery to the core — the backwash

geography.grade11.frameworks-and-models-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.frameworks-and-models-.question: A migrant worker's remittances building a house back home in the Eastern Cape is an example of:
options: A spread effect — value trickling from core to periphery

geography.grade11.frameworks-and-models-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.frameworks-and-models-.question: Government planning described as 'plumbing' means:
options: Building water infrastructure in the core
Trying to widen the spread pipes and narrow the backwash drain — for example bolting a new magnet like Coega onto the periphery

geography.grade11.frameworks-and-models-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.frameworks-and-models-.question: The 'three zoom levels' answer applies core-periphery at:
options: Global (North and South), national (Gauteng and former homelands) and local (office-tower core and township edge)

geography.grade11.frameworks-and-models-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.frameworks-and-models-.question: In the aeroplane picture, the ground crew laying railways, building ports and opening banks represents:

geography.grade11.frameworks-and-models-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.frameworks-and-models-.question: The plane's speed 'generating its own lift' captures:
options: Take-off — growth becoming self-sustaining as manufacturing multiplies and investment passes about 10 per cent of income

geography.grade11.frameworks-and-models-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.frameworks-and-models-.question: 'Some planes were fuelled by siphoning other planes' tanks' is the criticism that:
options: All economies grow at the same speed
Colonial powers took off partly on the resources and suppressed markets of their colonies — a history the model ignores

geography.grade11.frameworks-and-models-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.frameworks-and-models-.question: The South African observation that defeats a one-staircase model is:
options: The economy has no service sector
Take-off happened before the mineral revolution
Apartheid deliberately kept millions of people off the flight for decades, and no stage model has a stage for that

geography.grade11.international-trade-an.subject: geography
geography.grade11.international-trade-an.question: A country exporting raw ore and importing finished machinery has the classic peripheral trade profile because:
options: Most value is added in processing, so it is exporting cheap and importing expensive
Machinery cannot be produced in developing countries

geography.grade11.international-trade-an.subject: geography
geography.grade11.international-trade-an.question: Commodity dependence is described as living on a rollercoaster because:
options: World-market commodity prices swing violently with global supply and demand that no small producer controls — Zambia rises and falls with copper
Commodities can only be sold once

geography.grade11.international-trade-an.subject: geography
geography.grade11.international-trade-an.question: The balance of trade is:
options: The ratio of export prices to import prices
The difference between exports and imports — a surplus when exports exceed imports
The value of goods passing through ports

geography.grade11.international-trade-an.subject: geography
geography.grade11.international-trade-an.question: South Africa's encouraging exception among its major exports is:
options: Vehicles built in Gqeberha, East London, Durban and Pretoria — manufactured, value-added exports

geography.grade11.international-trade-an.subject: geography
geography.grade11.international-trade-an.question: A country's terms of trade deteriorate when:
options: Import prices rise faster than its export prices, so it must export ever more to afford the same imports

geography.grade11.international-trade-an.subject: geography
geography.grade11.international-trade-an.question: Primary exporters face long-run deteriorating terms of trade because:
options: Raw materials become heavier over time
Raw materials face competition and substitution while manufactured goods carry technology, branding and patents that protect their prices
Shipping costs only affect raw materials

geography.grade11.international-trade-an.subject: geography
geography.grade11.international-trade-an.question: The trading relationship that gives South African vehicles and fruit preferential access to the United States market is:
options: The African Continental Free Trade Area

geography.grade11.international-trade-an.subject: geography
geography.grade11.international-trade-an.question: Rich-country farm subsidies are the sore point of protectionism because:
options: They raise food prices in Europe
They apply only to luxury crops
They let European and American produce undercut African farmers in the farmers' own markets

geography.grade11.international-trade-an.subject: geography
geography.grade11.international-trade-an.question: The drivers of globalisation named in the lesson are:
options: Cheaper transport — above all the shipping container — instant communication, and lower trade barriers

geography.grade11.international-trade-an.subject: geography
geography.grade11.international-trade-an.question: A transnational corporation (TNC) is:
options: A company operating across many countries — headquarters in one, factories in others, markets everywhere — such as Toyota or MTN

geography.grade11.international-trade-an.subject: geography
geography.grade11.international-trade-an.question: The 'race to the bottom' refers to:
options: TNCs using their mobility to demand tax breaks and lax regulation, relocating whenever cheaper labour appears elsewhere
Countries competing to devalue their currencies

geography.grade11.international-trade-an.subject: geography
geography.grade11.international-trade-an.question: South Africa's clothing and textile job losses illustrate which cost of globalisation?
options: Local industries being crushed by cheaper imports before they can compete

geography.grade11.international-trade-an.subject: geography
geography.grade11.international-trade-an.question: South Korea's export-led recipe ran:
options: Cheap-labour manufactures first, foreign exchange reinvested in education and infrastructure, then climbing the value ladder from textiles to steel to ships to cars to semiconductors
Import substitution behind closed borders throughout
Agriculture only, followed directly by services

geography.grade11.international-trade-an.subject: geography
geography.grade11.international-trade-an.question: The comparison that measures the Tigers' achievement is:
options: In 1960 South Korea's income per person resembled Ghana's; within two generations it joined the developed world

geography.grade11.international-trade-an.subject: geography
geography.grade11.international-trade-an.question: A structural criticism of export-led development as a universal recipe is:
options: Exports are always less profitable than domestic sales
The strategy requires no state involvement
It needs open, growing world markets — and if every country tries simultaneously, the markets flood

geography.grade11.international-trade-an.subject: geography
geography.grade11.international-trade-an.question: Obstacles South Africa faces that the Tigers did not include:
options: No access to any trade agreements
Distance from major markets, electricity insecurity, skills shortages and rigid input costs

geography.grade11.international-trade-an.subject: geography
geography.grade11.international-trade-an.question: In the street picture, the spaza selling cheap raw goods while buying expensive processed goods represents:
options: Countries exporting raw materials while importing manufactured goods — money trickling one way

geography.grade11.international-trade-an.subject: geography
geography.grade11.international-trade-an.question: The coffee bean earning a few rand raw but hundreds once roasted, branded and served shows:
options: That value added stays where the processing happens, not where the bean grew
That farming is more profitable than retail
That transport is the main cost

geography.grade11.international-trade-an.subject: geography
geography.grade11.international-trade-an.question: South Africa 'plays both parts' on the street because:
options: It imports both raw and processed goods
It refuses to trade in raw materials
It sells raw platinum, coal and iron ore like a spaza, but also exports finished vehicles like a supermarket

geography.grade11.international-trade-an.subject: geography
geography.grade11.international-trade-an.question: When one phone cost one bag of oranges last year but three bags this year, the orange seller's:
options: Terms of trade have deteriorated — more exports buy the same imports
Balance of trade is in surplus

geography.grade11.international-trade-an.subject: geography
geography.grade11.international-trade-an.question: The swap rate drifts against raw sellers because:
options: Anyone can grow oranges but few firms make phones, and the phone-makers hold the patents and brands that protect their prices

geography.grade11.international-trade-an.subject: geography
geography.grade11.international-trade-an.question: The African Continental Free Trade Area is a 'team rule' aimed at:
options: Dropping trade fees between neighbours so Africa can trade with Africa instead of only shipping raw goods north

geography.grade11.international-trade-an.subject: geography
geography.grade11.international-trade-an.question: Fair trade schemes protect the farmer by:
options: Guaranteeing a floor price plus a social premium, so the swap rate cannot collapse under her

geography.grade11.international-trade-an.subject: geography
geography.grade11.international-trade-an.question: The rungs of the Tiger ladder, in order, were:
options: T-shirts, then schools and steel, then ships, then cars, then computer chips

geography.grade11.international-trade-an.subject: geography
geography.grade11.international-trade-an.question: 'The ladder needs someone at the top buying' warns that:
options: Export-led growth depends on open, absorbing rich markets, which cannot take every country's exports at once

geography.grade11.international-trade-an.subject: geography
geography.grade11.international-trade-an.question: 'The bottom rungs are brutal' refers to:
options: The first generation working long hours for low pay so the next can study engineering — the human cost of early export-led growth
The difficulty of learning to sew

geography.grade11.international-trade-an.subject: geography
geography.grade11.international-trade-an.question: South Africa's 'heavy backpack' on the ladder consists of:
options: Load-shedding, distance from major markets and a skills gap — burdens the Tigers did not carry

geography.grade11.kalahari-high-itcz-and.subject: geography
geography.grade11.kalahari-high-itcz-and.question: Converging surface winds produce rain because:
options: The air is forced UP, expands, cools adiabatically, its vapour condenses and cloud and rain follow
The winds cancel each other and the air stops moving

geography.grade11.kalahari-high-itcz-and.subject: geography
geography.grade11.kalahari-high-itcz-and.question: A temperature inversion built by subsidence acts as:
options: A ceiling of warm-above-cold air that stops thermals from rising high enough to form cloud

geography.grade11.kalahari-high-itcz-and.subject: geography
geography.grade11.kalahari-high-itcz-and.question: The Sahara, Kalahari and Namib deserts all sit:
options: Under the permanent SUBSIDENCE of the subtropical high-pressure belts near 30 degrees

geography.grade11.kalahari-high-itcz-and.subject: geography
geography.grade11.kalahari-high-itcz-and.question: The Congo Basin is wet nearly all year because it lies:
options: Next to a cold ocean current
On the polar side of the westerlies
Under permanent equatorial CONVERGENCE, where rising air makes convectional rain almost daily

geography.grade11.kalahari-high-itcz-and.subject: geography
geography.grade11.kalahari-high-itcz-and.question: The ITCZ is best defined as:
options: The low-pressure trough where the south-east and north-east trade winds converge and force air upward on a grand scale
A belt of subsiding air near 30 degrees
The boundary between the westerlies and polar easterlies
A cold ocean current along the equator

geography.grade11.kalahari-high-itcz-and.subject: geography
geography.grade11.kalahari-high-itcz-and.question: In January the ITCZ lies:
options: Over the Sahel at about 15 to 20 degrees north
Across southern Africa — roughly over Angola, Zambia and Zimbabwe — driving the southern summer rains
Exactly on the equator, where it stays all year

geography.grade11.kalahari-high-itcz-and.subject: geography
geography.grade11.kalahari-high-itcz-and.question: A double rainfall maximum near the equator occurs because:
options: Two cold fronts pass each year
The ocean currents reverse twice a year
The migrating ITCZ crosses those latitudes TWICE a year — once moving north and once moving south
El Niño happens twice a year

geography.grade11.kalahari-high-itcz-and.subject: geography
geography.grade11.kalahari-high-itcz-and.question: The ITCZ migrates seasonally because:
options: The Coriolis force reverses with the seasons
The trade winds stop blowing in winter
Ocean tides pull it north and south
It follows the belt of greatest surface heating under the overhead sun, lagging about a month behind it

geography.grade11.kalahari-high-itcz-and.subject: geography
geography.grade11.kalahari-high-itcz-and.question: The Highveld is dry in winter because:
options: The Kalahari High strengthens and its inversion sinks BELOW the escarpment, shutting moist ocean air off the plateau
The ITCZ sits over Gauteng in winter
The Benguela Current warms up in winter
Cold fronts never reach South Africa in winter

geography.grade11.kalahari-high-itcz-and.subject: geography
geography.grade11.kalahari-high-itcz-and.question: In summer the interior receives thunderstorm rain because:
options: The inversion sinks lower in summer
Surface heating weakens the Kalahari High, the inversion lifts ABOVE the escarpment and moist Indian Ocean air floods onto the plateau
The Benguela Current brings moisture from the west
The polar easterlies reach the plateau

geography.grade11.kalahari-high-itcz-and.subject: geography
geography.grade11.kalahari-high-itcz-and.question: The Benguela Current keeps the west coast dry because:
options: It is warm and evaporates too quickly
Its COLD upwelled water chills the air from below, making it stable and nearly moistureless — fog at most, almost never rain
It flows away from the coast

geography.grade11.kalahari-high-itcz-and.subject: geography
geography.grade11.kalahari-high-itcz-and.question: Durban is humid and green at the same latitude as dry Port Nolloth because:
options: Durban is at a lower altitude
Durban lies closer to the equator
The Kalahari High covers only the west coast
The warm Mozambique-Agulhas current heats and moistens the east coast air, making it unstable and rain-ready

geography.grade11.kalahari-high-itcz-and.subject: geography
geography.grade11.kalahari-high-itcz-and.question: On a synoptic chart, a cell labelled H with widely spaced isobars means:
options: An anticyclone — subsiding air, clear settled weather and light winds
A low bringing rain and gales

geography.grade11.kalahari-high-itcz-and.subject: geography
geography.grade11.kalahari-high-itcz-and.question: A cold front is drawn on the chart as:
options: A dashed circle around a high
A line of triangles pointing in the direction the front is MOVING, usually sweeping toward the Cape from the south-west
A row of semicircles pointing backwards
A shaded band along the equator

geography.grade11.kalahari-high-itcz-and.subject: geography
geography.grade11.kalahari-high-itcz-and.question: On a station model, the wind is read from:
options: A shaft with feathers flying FROM the direction the wind comes from, each full feather worth ten knots

geography.grade11.kalahari-high-itcz-and.subject: geography
geography.grade11.kalahari-high-itcz-and.question: In an El Niño year, southern Africa usually experiences:
options: No change in weather at all
BELOW-average summer rainfall — the 2015-16 El Niño brought one of the region's worst droughts

geography.grade11.kalahari-high-itcz-and.subject: geography
geography.grade11.kalahari-high-itcz-and.question: In the kitchen picture, a pot boiling with the lid OFF stands for:
options: Convergence — air rushing in and shooting up, building cloud and rain

geography.grade11.kalahari-high-itcz-and.subject: geography
geography.grade11.kalahari-high-itcz-and.question: The 'lid' pressing down over the Sahara and the Kalahari is:
options: The subsiding air of the subtropical highs, which stops anything from rising and raining
A cold front that never moves

geography.grade11.kalahari-high-itcz-and.subject: geography
geography.grade11.kalahari-high-itcz-and.question: A thermal rising from hot ground stops dead at an inversion because:
options: It runs out of water vapour
It meets a layer of WARMER air above, finds itself cooler and heavier than its surroundings, and can rise no further

geography.grade11.kalahari-high-itcz-and.subject: geography
geography.grade11.kalahari-high-itcz-and.question: The sprinkler on a north-south rail stands for:
options: The ITCZ sliding up and down the continent as it chases the overhead sun, about a month behind

geography.grade11.kalahari-high-itcz-and.subject: geography
geography.grade11.kalahari-high-itcz-and.question: In July the sprinkler is watering:
options: The Sahel on the southern edge of the Sahara, while southern Africa stands in its dry season

geography.grade11.kalahari-high-itcz-and.subject: geography
geography.grade11.kalahari-high-itcz-and.question: A place near the far end of the rail, like Zimbabwe or the Sahel, gets:
options: ONE rainy season, because the migrating belt reaches it only once before turning back

geography.grade11.kalahari-high-itcz-and.subject: geography
geography.grade11.kalahari-high-itcz-and.question: When the sprinkler stops short of a district in a given year, the result is:
options: Drought and a failed harvest — most tropical droughts are simply the rain belt not arriving

geography.grade11.kalahari-high-itcz-and.subject: geography
geography.grade11.kalahari-high-itcz-and.question: The warm bucket and cold bucket stand for:
options: The warm Mozambique-Agulhas current loading east coast air with moisture, and the cold Benguela leaving west coast air dry and stable

geography.grade11.kalahari-high-itcz-and.subject: geography
geography.grade11.kalahari-high-itcz-and.question: The 'lid on a hinge' over the interior describes:
options: A cold front crossing the Cape
The Kalahari High clamping down below the escarpment in winter and lifting above it in summer to let moist air in

geography.grade11.kalahari-high-itcz-and.subject: geography
geography.grade11.kalahari-high-itcz-and.question: On the weather map, H and L translate to:
options: H is the lid — sun and no rain; L is the chimney — cloud and rain

geography.grade11.kalahari-high-itcz-and.subject: geography
geography.grade11.kalahari-high-itcz-and.question: A news report of La Niña translates, for a South African summer, to:
options: Cool Pacific water and usually WETTER summers here — as the flooded summers of 2021 and 2022 showed

geography.grade11.karoo-landscapes-mesas.subject: geography
geography.grade11.karoo-landscapes-mesas.question: Differential erosion means:
options: Soft layers are stripped quickly while hard layers survive and stand proud
All rock layers erode at exactly the same rate
Rivers erode but wind does not

geography.grade11.karoo-landscapes-mesas.subject: geography
geography.grade11.karoo-landscapes-mesas.question: The resistant horizontal sheets in the Karoo are made of:
options: DOLERITE — molten rock that squeezed between the layers about 180 million years ago and cooled into tough sills

geography.grade11.karoo-landscapes-mesas.subject: geography
geography.grade11.karoo-landscapes-mesas.question: A cap rock protects a hill by:
options: Shielding the soft layers beneath it like a hard hat, so the hill keeps a flat top and steep sides
Attracting lightning away from the slopes

geography.grade11.karoo-landscapes-mesas.subject: geography
geography.grade11.karoo-landscapes-mesas.question: The basaltic plateau of Lesotho and the high Drakensberg was built by:
options: Stacked basalt LAVA flows that behave exactly like horizontal strata

geography.grade11.karoo-landscapes-mesas.subject: geography
geography.grade11.karoo-landscapes-mesas.question: A mesa differs from a butte in that a mesa is:
options: WIDER than it is high, with a broad flat cap — a butte is higher than it is wide with a small summit

geography.grade11.karoo-landscapes-mesas.subject: geography
geography.grade11.karoo-landscapes-mesas.question: The Three Sisters near Beaufort West are:
options: Dolerite-capped BUTTES standing in file on the Karoo plain

geography.grade11.karoo-landscapes-mesas.subject: geography
geography.grade11.karoo-landscapes-mesas.question: A conical hill or pointed koppie forms when:
options: A river deposits a cone of sediment
The protective cap is finally breached and stripped, letting the soft layers beneath weather into a cone
Wind piles sand around a bush
