geography.grade11.karoo-landscapes-mesas.subject: geography
geography.grade11.karoo-landscapes-mesas.question: The correct erosional sequence for horizontal strata is:
options: Butte, mesa, plateau, plain, conical hill
Conical hill, butte, mesa, plateau, plain
Plain, conical hill, plateau, mesa, butte
Plateau, mesa, butte, conical hill, plain

geography.grade11.karoo-landscapes-mesas.subject: geography
geography.grade11.karoo-landscapes-mesas.question: In scarp retreat, the eroding cliff:
options: Keeps roughly the same steep angle but ends up positioned further BACK — the slope retreats parallel to itself
Becomes gentler and rounder with time
Grows steadily steeper until it overhangs

geography.grade11.karoo-landscapes-mesas.subject: geography
geography.grade11.karoo-landscapes-mesas.question: Back wasting differs from down wasting because back wasting:
options: Lowers the summit from the top
Wears slopes back SIDEWAYS while they keep their shape, instead of flattening the surface from above

geography.grade11.karoo-landscapes-mesas.subject: geography
geography.grade11.karoo-landscapes-mesas.question: The gently sloping rock floor left at the foot of a retreating scarp is a:

geography.grade11.karoo-landscapes-mesas.subject: geography
geography.grade11.karoo-landscapes-mesas.question: A pediplain is formed when:
options: Pediments from scarps retreating on opposite sides meet and merge into a wide, nearly level erosion plain dotted with surviving koppies

geography.grade11.karoo-landscapes-mesas.subject: geography
geography.grade11.karoo-landscapes-mesas.question: A canyon in horizontal strata has step-like walls because:
options: Hard bands stand out as vertical cliffs while soft bands weather back into slopes
Earthquakes shake the walls loose evenly
All the layers are equally strong

geography.grade11.karoo-landscapes-mesas.subject: geography
geography.grade11.karoo-landscapes-mesas.question: On a contour map, a mesa appears as:
options: Widely spaced contours with no pattern
Closed contours with a WIDE empty summit ringed by tightly crowded contours marking the cliff

geography.grade11.karoo-landscapes-mesas.subject: geography
geography.grade11.karoo-landscapes-mesas.question: With a vertical scale of 1 cm to 20 m and a horizontal scale of 1:50 000, the vertical exaggeration is:
options: 25 times — vertical scale 1:2 000, so 50 000 divided by 2 000

geography.grade11.karoo-landscapes-mesas.subject: geography
geography.grade11.karoo-landscapes-mesas.question: A climb of 200 m over a horizontal distance of 1 000 m is a gradient of:
options: 1 in 5 — height difference over distance in the same units, 200 over 1 000

geography.grade11.karoo-landscapes-mesas.subject: geography
geography.grade11.karoo-landscapes-mesas.question: In the cake picture, the rock-hard icing stands for:
options: The dolerite cap that protects the soft shale sponge beneath it

geography.grade11.karoo-landscapes-mesas.subject: geography
geography.grade11.karoo-landscapes-mesas.question: The children picking at the cake always eat the sponge first because:
options: Soft layers weather and erode faster than hard ones — differential erosion

geography.grade11.karoo-landscapes-mesas.subject: geography
geography.grade11.karoo-landscapes-mesas.question: A dead-flat Karoo skyline tells you:
options: There was never any erosion there
A hard cap layer is still unbroken and on duty up top

geography.grade11.karoo-landscapes-mesas.subject: geography
geography.grade11.karoo-landscapes-mesas.question: In the shape code, table, stool and traffic cone stand for:

geography.grade11.karoo-landscapes-mesas.subject: geography
geography.grade11.karoo-landscapes-mesas.question: The hill turns from stool to traffic cone at the moment when:
options: The dolerite hard hat is finally picked through, leaving the soft rock unprotected to round into a cone

geography.grade11.karoo-landscapes-mesas.subject: geography
geography.grade11.karoo-landscapes-mesas.question: The five-age countdown of the landscape reads:
options: Table-land, table, stool, cone, flat — plateau, mesa, butte, conical hill, plain

geography.grade11.karoo-landscapes-mesas.subject: geography
geography.grade11.karoo-landscapes-mesas.question: The Karoo is world-famous to geographers because:
options: It has the world's highest mountains
It is the only place with rivers
All five generations of the landform family can often be seen standing in a single view

geography.grade11.karoo-landscapes-mesas.subject: geography
geography.grade11.karoo-landscapes-mesas.question: The retreating-soldier picture means Karoo cliffs:
options: Keep their steep face to the end, simply rebuilding it a little further back each time — parallel retreat
Slowly slump into round soft hills
Stay in exactly the same place forever

geography.grade11.karoo-landscapes-mesas.subject: geography
geography.grade11.karoo-landscapes-mesas.question: The winter mechanism that levers blocks off the cliff face is:
options: Water freezing in cracks, swelling and wedging the blocks loose

geography.grade11.karoo-landscapes-mesas.subject: geography
geography.grade11.karoo-landscapes-mesas.question: The cleared floor a retreating army leaves behind stands for:
options: The PEDIMENT — the smooth rock apron left at the foot of a retreating scarp, which merges with others into a pediplain

geography.grade11.karoo-landscapes-mesas.subject: geography
geography.grade11.karoo-landscapes-mesas.question: When a large river attacks horizontal strata it produces:
options: A CANYON cut straight down, with stepped walls — like the Fish River Canyon and the Blyde River Canyon

geography.grade11.mass-movement-types-im.subject: geography
geography.grade11.mass-movement-types-im.question: Mass movement is defined as:
options: The downslope movement of weathered material under GRAVITY, without a transporting agent such as a river, glacier or wind
Any material carried by a river

geography.grade11.mass-movement-types-im.subject: geography
geography.grade11.mass-movement-types-im.question: A slope's resisting forces include:
options: Friction, interlocking particles, dry cohesion and plant ROOTS binding the soil

geography.grade11.mass-movement-types-im.subject: geography
geography.grade11.mass-movement-types-im.question: Saturation destabilises a slope because water:
options: Fills the pores pushing particles apart, adds weight, and LUBRICATES potential slide surfaces

geography.grade11.mass-movement-types-im.subject: geography
geography.grade11.mass-movement-types-im.question: Undercutting by a river, waves or a road cutting is dangerous because it:
options: Removes SUPPORT at the slope's base, exactly where resistance matters most

geography.grade11.mass-movement-types-im.subject: geography
geography.grade11.mass-movement-types-im.question: Evidence of soil creep includes:
options: Tilted fence posts, curved tree trunks, terracettes, and soil piled against the upslope side of walls
A crescent scar and a back-tilted block
A valley filled with set mud
A fresh talus cone below a cliff

geography.grade11.mass-movement-types-im.subject: geography
geography.grade11.mass-movement-types-im.question: Solifluction occurs when:
options: Dry sand avalanches down a dune
The thawed, waterlogged surface layer flows slowly over a FROZEN subsoil, as on the high Drakensberg and Lesotho slopes

geography.grade11.mass-movement-types-im.subject: geography
geography.grade11.mass-movement-types-im.question: A slump differs from a landslide because the slump:
options: Moves along a perfectly flat plane
ROTATES along a curved, spoon-shaped surface, leaving a crescent scar and a tilted-back block

geography.grade11.mass-movement-types-im.subject: geography
geography.grade11.mass-movement-types-im.question: The fastest, wettest and deadliest of the six movements is the:
options: MUD FLOW — saturated debris behaving as a fluid, racing down valleys and setting like concrete

geography.grade11.mass-movement-types-im.subject: geography
geography.grade11.mass-movement-types-im.question: Environmental impacts of mass movement include:
options: Slopes stripped to bedrock, topsoil buried, and rivers choked with sediment that smothers aquatic life and silts dams

geography.grade11.mass-movement-types-im.subject: geography
geography.grade11.mass-movement-types-im.question: In the April 2022 KwaZulu-Natal disaster:
options: Over 300 mm of rain fell in 24 hours, hillsides failed in hundreds of places, and more than 400 people died

geography.grade11.mass-movement-types-im.subject: geography
geography.grade11.mass-movement-types-im.question: Poverty multiplies mass movement risk because:
options: Poor communities live only on flat land
Informal settlement is pushed onto steep, unstable slopes with cut platforms, leaking water and no engineering
Rainfall is heavier over poor areas

geography.grade11.mass-movement-types-im.subject: geography
geography.grade11.mass-movement-types-im.question: Chapman's Peak Drive is a recurring example of:
options: ROCK FALL hazard on a mountain road, forcing major protective engineering

geography.grade11.mass-movement-types-im.subject: geography
geography.grade11.mass-movement-types-im.question: Gabions are:
options: Wire baskets packed with rock, used to hold the toe of a slope where support was removed

geography.grade11.mass-movement-types-im.subject: geography
geography.grade11.mass-movement-types-im.question: Managing water on a slope includes:
options: Discharging stormwater onto the slope face
Cut-off drains above the slope, subsurface drains bleeding water out, and fixing leaking pipes
Watering the slope in dry weather

geography.grade11.mass-movement-types-im.subject: geography
geography.grade11.mass-movement-types-im.question: Vegetation protects a slope because:
options: It shades the rock from sunlight only
It attracts animals that compact the soil
Roots BIND the soil, plants intercept rain, and transpiration dries the slope

geography.grade11.mass-movement-types-im.subject: geography
geography.grade11.mass-movement-types-im.question: Planning-level strategies include:
options: Building clinics on the steepest slopes
Ignoring hazard maps to save money
GIS hazard mapping, keeping housing off high-risk slopes, rainfall-triggered evacuation warnings and community education on warning signs

geography.grade11.mass-movement-types-im.subject: geography
geography.grade11.mass-movement-types-im.question: The tug-of-war picture puts gravity against:
options: Friction, particle grip and plant roots stitching the soil like threads in fabric

geography.grade11.mass-movement-types-im.subject: geography
geography.grade11.mass-movement-types-im.question: The sandcastle shows water's double role because:
options: DAMP sand glues grains together, but a poured bucket forces grains apart and slumps the castle into soup
Dry sand builds the best castles

geography.grade11.mass-movement-types-im.subject: geography
geography.grade11.mass-movement-types-im.question: Cutting a platform, stripping grass and leaking pipe water onto one hillside means:
options: People have weakened the slope in three ways at once — less support, no roots, more water
Only earthquakes can now move the slope

geography.grade11.mass-movement-types-im.subject: geography
geography.grade11.mass-movement-types-im.question: The six gears from slowest to fastest are:
options: Creep, solifluction, landslide, slump, rock fall, mud flow
Mud flow, rock fall, slump, landslide, solifluction, creep
Creep, rock fall, mud flow, slump, landslide, solifluction
Landslide, creep, slump, mud flow, solifluction, rock fall

geography.grade11.mass-movement-types-im.subject: geography
geography.grade11.mass-movement-types-im.question: Tree trunks curved like bananas on a hillside are paperwork for:
options: SOIL CREEP — the trees keep growing upright while their bases slip slowly downhill

geography.grade11.mass-movement-types-im.subject: geography
geography.grade11.mass-movement-types-im.question: The loaded tow truck losing its bakkie off the flatbed pictures:
options: A LANDSLIDE — one coherent mass letting go and sliding along a plane, usually after soaking rain

geography.grade11.mass-movement-types-im.subject: geography
geography.grade11.mass-movement-types-im.question: The ladder's overall trend is:
options: All six move at the same speed
Speed UP, water UP — from slow dry creep to the fast fluid mud flow

geography.grade11.mass-movement-types-im.subject: geography
geography.grade11.mass-movement-types-im.question: The sentence that shows understanding of the 2022 Durban disaster is:
options: Same rain, unequal risk — the poorest households stood on the steepest, least engineered slopes when the hills gave way
The rain fell only on informal settlements
Mass movement cannot happen in cities
The disaster had no human dimension

geography.grade11.mass-movement-types-im.subject: geography
geography.grade11.mass-movement-types-im.question: Chapman's Peak Drive's half-tunnel works by:
options: Letting falling rock FLY OVER the road and into the sea

geography.grade11.mass-movement-types-im.subject: geography
geography.grade11.mass-movement-types-im.question: The four fight-back moves are:
options: ENGINEER the slope, DRAIN the water, PLANT the surface, PLAN where people live

geography.grade11.mass-movement-types-im.subject: geography
geography.grade11.mass-movement-types-im.question: Community warning signs of a slope preparing to fail include:
options: Fresh cracks, leaning poles, doors that suddenly jam, and water seeping from a previously dry hillside

geography.grade11.pressure-belts-and-glo.subject: geography
geography.grade11.pressure-belts-and-glo.question: Warm air at the surface produces:
options: LOW pressure — the air expands, becomes less dense and rises, so fewer molecules press on the surface
HIGH pressure, because warm air is heavier
High pressure aloft and high pressure at the surface

geography.grade11.pressure-belts-and-glo.subject: geography
geography.grade11.pressure-belts-and-glo.question: Tightly packed isobars on a synoptic chart indicate:
options: A steep pressure gradient and therefore strong wind

geography.grade11.pressure-belts-and-glo.subject: geography
geography.grade11.pressure-belts-and-glo.question: Why does a high-pressure cell bring clear, dry, settled weather?
options: Air SUBSIDES, is compressed and warms adiabatically, so relative humidity falls and cloud evaporates

geography.grade11.pressure-belts-and-glo.subject: geography
geography.grade11.pressure-belts-and-glo.question: The 16 cardinal points are spaced how far apart, and what is the bearing of a south-easter?
options: 22,5 degrees apart, since 360 ÷ 16 = 22,5; a south-easter blows from 135 degrees

geography.grade11.pressure-belts-and-glo.subject: geography
geography.grade11.pressure-belts-and-glo.question: The subtropical high-pressure belts at about 30 degrees north and south are formed by:
options: Air that rose at the equator, travelled poleward aloft, cooled, grew dense and subsided — which is why the world's great deserts ring this latitude

geography.grade11.pressure-belts-and-glo.subject: geography
geography.grade11.pressure-belts-and-glo.question: The three semi-permanent anticyclones affecting southern Africa are:
options: The South Atlantic High, the South Indian High, and the continental or Kalahari High
The ITCZ, the polar front and the doldrums

geography.grade11.pressure-belts-and-glo.subject: geography
geography.grade11.pressure-belts-and-glo.question: Cape Town receives its rain in winter because:
options: The ITCZ moves south over the Cape in June
The Kalahari High moves over the Cape
The belts migrate about five degrees north in winter, bringing the westerlies and their cold fronts over the south-western Cape
Cold ocean water evaporates faster in winter

geography.grade11.pressure-belts-and-glo.subject: geography
geography.grade11.pressure-belts-and-glo.question: The sub-polar low-pressure belt near 60 degrees is significant for South Africa because:
options: It marks the equatorial rain belt
It is where warm westerlies meet cold polar air along the polar front and rise — the birthplace of the mid-latitude cyclones whose cold fronts cross the Cape

geography.grade11.pressure-belts-and-glo.subject: geography
geography.grade11.pressure-belts-and-glo.question: The Hadley cell is described as the strongest of the three because:
options: Heat drives it directly — air rises at the equatorial low, moves poleward aloft, subsides at 30 degrees and returns as the trade winds
It is closest to the jet stream
It is turned by its two neighbouring cells
It covers the largest latitude range

geography.grade11.pressure-belts-and-glo.subject: geography
geography.grade11.pressure-belts-and-glo.question: In the Southern Hemisphere, the Coriolis force deflects moving air:
options: To the right, and it is strongest at the equator
To the LEFT; it is zero at the equator, greatest at the poles, and changes direction without changing speed

geography.grade11.pressure-belts-and-glo.subject: geography
geography.grade11.pressure-belts-and-glo.question: Geostrophic flow occurs when:
options: Wind blows directly across isobars into the low
Above about a kilometre, friction disappears and the pressure gradient force and Coriolis force balance, so wind blows PARALLEL to straight isobars
The pressure gradient force disappears entirely

geography.grade11.pressure-belts-and-glo.subject: geography
geography.grade11.pressure-belts-and-glo.question: Buys Ballot's Law applied in the Southern Hemisphere states that:
options: With your back to the wind, low pressure is on your left
Wind always blows from low to high pressure
With your back to the wind, low pressure lies on your RIGHT — so lows circulate clockwise and highs anticlockwise

geography.grade11.pressure-belts-and-glo.subject: geography
geography.grade11.pressure-belts-and-glo.question: Air leaving the plateau edge at 1 800 m and 12 degrees Celsius descends to sea level as a berg wind. Its arrival temperature is:
options: 30 degrees Celsius — it warms 1 degree per 100 m, so 1 800 ÷ 100 × 1 = 18 degrees of warming added to 12

geography.grade11.pressure-belts-and-glo.subject: geography
geography.grade11.pressure-belts-and-glo.question: Continental tropical air over the Kalahari is:
options: Hot and very dry, and it drives South African heatwaves
Cool and humid, bringing east coast rain

geography.grade11.pressure-belts-and-glo.subject: geography
geography.grade11.pressure-belts-and-glo.question: A katabatic (mountain) wind at night explains:
options: Cold dense air draining down-slope and pooling on the valley floor, creating frost hollows and temperature inversions

geography.grade11.pressure-belts-and-glo.subject: geography
geography.grade11.pressure-belts-and-glo.question: The Indian summer monsoon is best explained as:
options: A result of the Coriolis force alone
The migration of the polar front
A sea breeze scaled to a continent — the landmass heats rapidly, a vast thermal low forms, and moist air is drawn in off the ocean as the south-west monsoon

geography.grade11.pressure-belts-and-glo.subject: geography
geography.grade11.pressure-belts-and-glo.question: The freezer door spilling cold air at your ankles stands for:
options: A HIGH — cold air is heavy, sinks, and piles up pressing hard on the surface

geography.grade11.pressure-belts-and-glo.subject: geography
geography.grade11.pressure-belts-and-glo.question: The full-taxi and empty-taxi comparison explains:
options: Wind — air flowing from the crowded high to the empty low, and moving faster when the two are close together (packed isobars)

geography.grade11.pressure-belts-and-glo.subject: geography
geography.grade11.pressure-belts-and-glo.question: The fogging bathroom mirror and the hair dryer stand for:
options: Rising air in a LOW cooling and releasing its moisture as cloud and rain, versus sinking air in a HIGH warming and drying out

geography.grade11.pressure-belts-and-glo.subject: geography
geography.grade11.pressure-belts-and-glo.question: Why do the world's biggest deserts sit in a ring at about 30 degrees?
options: Air that rose at the equator has cooled and grown heavy by 30 degrees, so it sinks — and sinking air is drying air
There are no oceans at that latitude
The trade winds blow all the moisture away
The jet stream heats the ground there

geography.grade11.pressure-belts-and-glo.subject: geography
geography.grade11.pressure-belts-and-glo.question: The 'lazy door' in the three-loop picture is:
options: The Ferrel cell, between about 30 and 60 degrees — it does not turn itself but is pushed by the cells on either side; its surface wind is the westerlies

geography.grade11.pressure-belts-and-glo.subject: geography
geography.grade11.pressure-belts-and-glo.question: Jet streams are:
options: Surface winds in the trade wind belt
Ocean currents beneath the polar front
Thin fast rivers of wind high overhead at the joins between the cells, regularly exceeding 200 kilometres per hour
The rising limb of the Hadley cell

geography.grade11.pressure-belts-and-glo.subject: geography
geography.grade11.pressure-belts-and-glo.question: The sliding of the belts by about five degrees with the overhead sun explains:
options: Why cold fronts reach the Western Cape in winter while wet tropical air pushes into Limpopo and Gauteng in summer — one migration, two rainfall regimes

geography.grade11.pressure-belts-and-glo.subject: geography
geography.grade11.pressure-belts-and-glo.question: The spinning roundabout comparison shows that the Coriolis force:
options: Is not a push on the air at all — the ground turns underneath the moving air, so its path appears bent

geography.grade11.pressure-belts-and-glo.subject: geography
geography.grade11.pressure-belts-and-glo.question: Standing with your back to the wind in South Africa, low pressure is:
options: On your RIGHT — from which it follows that lows spin clockwise and highs anticlockwise down here

geography.grade11.pressure-belts-and-glo.subject: geography
geography.grade11.pressure-belts-and-glo.question: A berg wind is scorching and bone-dry because:
options: It picks up heat from the sea
It carries desert sand that heats the air
Falling air is squashed by heavier air below and heats about 1 degree per 100 m — gaining warmth but no water, so relative humidity collapses

geography.grade11.pressure-belts-and-glo.subject: geography
geography.grade11.pressure-belts-and-glo.question: In the Simplifier's account, a monsoon is:
options: The same thing as a berg wind
A jet stream reaching the surface
An enormous sea breeze that reverses with the SEASON instead of the afternoon — wet air drawn onto the hot summer land, dry air pouring back out over the cold winter land

geography.grade11.slope-elements-and-slo.subject: geography
geography.grade11.slope-elements-and-slo.question: South Africa's three great topographic units are:
options: The interior plateau, the Great Escarpment and the marginal or coastal zone
The Highveld, the Lowveld and the Bushveld only
Three mountain ranges along the coast
The Kalahari, the Karoo and the Cape Flats

geography.grade11.slope-elements-and-slo.subject: geography
geography.grade11.slope-elements-and-slo.question: The interior plateau mostly stands at:
options: Between about 1 200 and 1 800 metres above sea level

geography.grade11.slope-elements-and-slo.subject: geography
geography.grade11.slope-elements-and-slo.question: The Great Escarpment reaches its highest, sharpest section in:
options: The KwaZulu-Natal DRAKENSBERG, rising above 3 000 metres

geography.grade11.slope-elements-and-slo.subject: geography
geography.grade11.slope-elements-and-slo.question: A convex slope is one that:
options: Holds a single constant angle like a plank
Bulges outward, STEEPENING downhill like the shoulder of a dome

geography.grade11.slope-elements-and-slo.subject: geography
geography.grade11.slope-elements-and-slo.question: The four slope elements in order from the top down are:

geography.grade11.slope-elements-and-slo.subject: geography
geography.grade11.slope-elements-and-slo.question: The cliff is called the free face because:
options: It is free of any rock
Rock freed from it by weathering FALLS AWAY immediately instead of lying where it was loosened
Anyone may climb it without paying
It faces away from the wind

geography.grade11.slope-elements-and-slo.subject: geography
geography.grade11.slope-elements-and-slo.question: The talus or debris slope is straight because:
options: It is cut from solid rock
Loose rock settles at its ANGLE OF REPOSE, generally between about 25 and 35 degrees

geography.grade11.slope-elements-and-slo.subject: geography
geography.grade11.slope-elements-and-slo.question: The pediment is:
options: The steepest element of the profile
A gently CONCAVE bedrock surface, usually under about 5 degrees, sweeping from the slope foot to the plain

geography.grade11.slope-elements-and-slo.subject: geography
geography.grade11.slope-elements-and-slo.question: In parallel slope retreat, the profile:
options: Keeps its proportions — cliff steep, talus at repose, pediment gentle — while relocating BACKWARD, widening the pediment
Flattens and rounds until the cliff disappears

geography.grade11.slope-elements-and-slo.subject: geography
geography.grade11.slope-elements-and-slo.question: When opposing slopes retreat away from each other over deep time:
options: Pediments from neighbouring valleys meet and merge into a PEDIPLAIN, leaving koppies and inselbergs as survivors
The talus buries the whole landscape

geography.grade11.slope-elements-and-slo.subject: geography
geography.grade11.slope-elements-and-slo.question: South African conditions favour parallel retreat over slope decline because:
options: Semi-arid climates, resistant caprocks and sparse vegetation keep cliffs sharp while soft material is stripped

geography.grade11.slope-elements-and-slo.subject: geography
geography.grade11.slope-elements-and-slo.question: Human activity is best placed on the slope profile as:
options: Houses on the cliff and crops on the talus
Roads straight up the free face
Everything at the foot of an active talus
Settlement, ploughing and roads on gentle crests and pediments — with rockfall and erosion risk on the cliff and talus zones

geography.grade11.slope-elements-and-slo.subject: geography
geography.grade11.slope-elements-and-slo.question: Spatial resolution is:
options: The size of the ground area represented by ONE PIXEL — finer resolution shows smaller detail
The number of wavelength bands a sensor records
The number of colours on a printed map

geography.grade11.slope-elements-and-slo.subject: geography
geography.grade11.slope-elements-and-slo.question: High spectral resolution matters because:
options: More, narrower wavelength bands let analysts tell apart healthy veld, stressed crops, bare soil and water by their different reflections

geography.grade11.slope-elements-and-slo.subject: geography
geography.grade11.slope-elements-and-slo.question: In vector data, a borehole, a river and a farm are stored respectively as:
options: POINT, LINE and AREA — each with attribute data attached

geography.grade11.slope-elements-and-slo.subject: geography
geography.grade11.slope-elements-and-slo.question: Raster data suits phenomena like altitude and rainfall because:
options: They vary CONTINUOUSLY across the land, which a grid of valued cells captures naturally

geography.grade11.slope-elements-and-slo.subject: geography
geography.grade11.slope-elements-and-slo.question: In the book-on-the-table model, the book's edges stand for:
options: The GREAT ESCARPMENT — the sudden drop from plateau toward the coast

geography.grade11.slope-elements-and-slo.subject: geography
geography.grade11.slope-elements-and-slo.question: The Tugela river illustrates the staircase by:
options: Plunging nearly 950 metres off the Drakensberg rim in one of the world's tallest waterfalls
Flowing along the top of the escarpment forever

geography.grade11.slope-elements-and-slo.subject: geography
geography.grade11.slope-elements-and-slo.question: The shoulder, the soup spoon and the plank teach the slope shapes:
options: CONVEX — steepening over the roll; CONCAVE — flattening to the bottom; RECTILINEAR — one constant angle

geography.grade11.slope-elements-and-slo.subject: geography
geography.grade11.slope-elements-and-slo.question: In the production-line picture, the cliff is the factory because:
options: It is where solid rock is broken off and dropped to the slope below
It is the flattest part of the hill

geography.grade11.slope-elements-and-slo.subject: geography
geography.grade11.slope-elements-and-slo.question: A pile of builder's sand always settles at the same slope because:
options: Loose material can rest no steeper than its ANGLE OF REPOSE — extra material slides until the resting angle returns
Gravity is weaker on small piles

geography.grade11.slope-elements-and-slo.subject: geography
geography.grade11.slope-elements-and-slo.question: The chant for the four elements runs:
options: Crest concave, cliff gentle, talus curved, pediment vertical
Crest straight, cliff straight, talus straight, pediment straight
Crest convex, cliff vertical, talus straight, pediment concave
Crest vertical, cliff convex, talus concave, pediment straight

geography.grade11.slope-elements-and-slo.subject: geography
geography.grade11.slope-elements-and-slo.question: A hill in soft-rock country with no resistant band will lack:
options: The CLIFF and its talus — leaving a smooth profile of scalp and apron

geography.grade11.slope-elements-and-slo.subject: geography
geography.grade11.slope-elements-and-slo.question: The 'walking hill' image captures the fact that:
options: The whole profile shifts BACKWARD with its proportions intact — cliff sheer, chute at its angle, apron gentle — as retreat proceeds
Hills physically slide across the plain
The profile softens into a dome as it ages
The pediment moves up the hill

geography.grade11.slope-elements-and-slo.subject: geography
geography.grade11.slope-elements-and-slo.question: Run parallel retreat for tens of millions of years and the result is:
options: Merged aprons forming a PEDIPLAIN with surviving koppies standing on it — the Karoo picture

geography.grade11.slope-elements-and-slo.subject: geography
geography.grade11.slope-elements-and-slo.question: In the Lego-against-graph-paper picture:
options: Lego is raster and graph paper is vector
VECTOR is the Lego — crisp points, lines and areas with attribute tables; RASTER is the graph paper — a grid of valued cells

geography.grade11.slope-elements-and-slo.subject: geography
geography.grade11.slope-elements-and-slo.question: Feeding a raster elevation model into a GIS lets an analyst:
options: Change the height of the mountains
Make rain fall on the pediment
Calculate the steepness of every hillside in a province in seconds — the map a soil conservation officer or road engineer needs

geography.grade11.soil-erosion-in-south-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.soil-erosion-in-south-.question: Soil is treated as a non-renewable resource because:
options: A few centimetres of topsoil take centuries to form under African conditions, while a single storm on bare ground can strip more than that in an afternoon
It contains minerals that never regenerate
It cannot be transported between farms
Parent rock is scarce in South Africa

geography.grade11.soil-erosion-in-south-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.soil-erosion-in-south-.question: Nearly all soil fertility lives in:
options: The dark, humus-rich topsoil, whose humus stores nutrients and moisture and binds particles into stable crumbs

geography.grade11.soil-erosion-in-south-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.soil-erosion-in-south-.question: South Africa's arable endowment is approximately:
options: Half the country arable, a quarter high-potential
12% arable, with barely 3% truly high-potential land

geography.grade11.soil-erosion-in-south-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.soil-erosion-in-south-.question: Vegetation is called the soil's bodyguard because:
options: It shades the soil from sunlight damage
It attracts rainfall to the area
It keeps animals away from fields
Leaves break the force of falling rain, roots bind the crumbs, and litter feeds the humus that holds soil together

geography.grade11.soil-erosion-in-south-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.soil-erosion-in-south-.question: The escalating sequence of water erosion is:
options: Splash, sheet, rill, then gully — dongas being the end state

geography.grade11.soil-erosion-in-south-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.soil-erosion-in-south-.question: The examiner's nuance about physical causes is that:
options: Physical agents mostly finish what land use starts — bare ground is the precondition, and bare ground is usually made
They are stronger than all human causes combined
They ceased after the Dust Bowl

geography.grade11.soil-erosion-in-south-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.soil-erosion-in-south-.question: The past human cause whose scars remain in the Eastern Cape's dongas is:
options: Apartheid's homeland system concentrating too many people and animals on too little land, forcing overuse

geography.grade11.soil-erosion-in-south-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.soil-erosion-in-south-.question: Trampling by cattle contributes to erosion because:
options: Trampled paths attract wind erosion only
Compacted paths stop water soaking in, so it runs off — cattle tracks to water points often become the starter channels for gullies

geography.grade11.soil-erosion-in-south-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.soil-erosion-in-south-.question: The textbook South African case of dam siltation is:
options: The Welbedacht Dam on the Caledon River, which lost most of its capacity within decades of construction
The Gariep Dam doubling its capacity
The Vaal Dam silting completely by 1950

geography.grade11.soil-erosion-in-south-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.soil-erosion-in-south-.question: A river running brown after a storm is evidence of erosion because:
options: The colour is topsoil in transit — fertile land washing toward the sea
It shows the river is flooding
Brown water means acid mine drainage

geography.grade11.soil-erosion-in-south-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.soil-erosion-in-south-.question: An effect of erosion on people, distinct from environmental effects, is:
options: Falling yields and shrinking farm incomes, rising food prices, collapsing rural livelihoods and costly fertiliser substituting for lost fertility

geography.grade11.soil-erosion-in-south-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.soil-erosion-in-south-.question: Erosion is called a slow-motion disaster because:
options: It occurs only over geological time
Storms move slowly across the country
No single storm makes headlines, but the cumulative loss undermines food security, water security and rural livelihoods simultaneously

geography.grade11.soil-erosion-in-south-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.soil-erosion-in-south-.question: Contour ploughing prevents erosion because:
options: Furrows run along the slope's contours, so each ridge dams runoff instead of channelling it downhill
It turns the soil more deeply than normal ploughing
It removes the need for fallow periods

geography.grade11.soil-erosion-in-south-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.soil-erosion-in-south-.question: Gabions control existing gullies by:
options: Acting as rock-packed wire barriers across the channel that slow water and trap sediment, letting the gully floor rise and re-vegetate

geography.grade11.soil-erosion-in-south-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.soil-erosion-in-south-.question: Spatial resolution and spectral resolution refer respectively to:
options: The ground size of one pixel, and which wavelength bands the sensor records — infrared exposing bare or stressed ground

geography.grade11.soil-erosion-in-south-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.soil-erosion-in-south-.question: In a GIS, a borehole, a river and a catchment are stored respectively as:

geography.grade11.soil-erosion-in-south-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.soil-erosion-in-south-.question: 'Deposits by teaspoon, withdrawals by bucket' summarises:
options: Soil forming over centuries while one storm on bare ground can remove decades of accumulation
The cost of fertiliser against the cost of seed
The difference between topsoil and subsoil

geography.grade11.soil-erosion-in-south-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.soil-erosion-in-south-.question: The 'one plate in ten' picture describes:
options: Only about one-tenth of South Africa's land being arable, with a sliver of that high-potential — the plate sixty million people eat from
The share of farmland under irrigation
The portion of harvest lost to pests

geography.grade11.soil-erosion-in-south-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.soil-erosion-in-south-.question: 'Every cause of erosion becomes one story: something fired the bodyguard' means:
options: Erosion is caused mainly by police absence
Nearly every cause works by removing the protective vegetation whose leaves, roots and litter defend the soil
Animals guard soil better than plants

geography.grade11.soil-erosion-in-south-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.soil-erosion-in-south-.question: The five acts of the donga plot, in order, are:
options: Overgrazing bares a patch; raindrops splash soil loose; sheetwash steals the surface; rills form; rills join and deepen into a donga
Donga; rills; sheetwash; splash; bare patch

geography.grade11.soil-erosion-in-south-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.soil-erosion-in-south-.question: Many dongas 'begin life as a footpath' because:
options: Footpaths are dug below ground level
Daily trampling compacts the path hard so water cannot soak in, making it the first drain that concentrates runoff
Paths are always on the steepest slopes
Walkers carry soil away on their shoes

geography.grade11.soil-erosion-in-south-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.soil-erosion-in-south-.question: Wind erosion 'lifts the fine, fertile grains first', which matters because:
options: The soil left behind is the infertile coarse fraction — the field keeps its bulk but loses its fertility, as the Dust Bowl showed

geography.grade11.soil-erosion-in-south-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.soil-erosion-in-south-.question: History enters South Africa's erosion plot because:
options: The Dust Bowl occurred in the Karoo
Apartheid crowded people and cattle onto the smallest, poorest land, building overuse into the map — hence the deepest dongas in former homeland districts

geography.grade11.soil-erosion-in-south-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.soil-erosion-in-south-.question: The 'winter blanket' for fields between seasons is:
options: Mulch, stubble and cover crops keeping the ground from ever lying bare

geography.grade11.soil-erosion-in-south-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.soil-erosion-in-south-.question: Gabions work like 'speed bumps' because:
options: They stop cattle crossing the donga
Each storm's water stumbles over them, drops its load of soil, and the canyon floor slowly rises until grass can hold it
They redirect water onto the road

geography.grade11.soil-erosion-in-south-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.soil-erosion-in-south-.question: Running 'only as many animals as the grass can feed' applies the concept of:
options: The veld's carrying capacity, combined with rotational resting of camps

geography.grade11.soil-erosion-in-south-.subject: geography
geography.grade11.soil-erosion-in-south-.question: Bare ground 'betrays itself from orbit' because:
options: Bare soil is always lighter in colour
Soil emits radio signals when dry
Healthy vegetation reflects infrared strongly, so infrared bands reveal bare or stressed ground — spectral resolution at work

geography.grade11.solar-wind-and-renewab.subject: geography
geography.grade11.solar-wind-and-renewab.question: The two defining properties of non-conventional energy sources are:
options: The fuel is free — sunshine and wind arrive without mining or importing — but the flows are intermittent, needing storage, backup or a smart mix
They are expensive to fuel but steady to run
They require imported fuel and produce no waste
They work only at small household scale

geography.grade11.solar-wind-and-renewab.subject: geography
geography.grade11.solar-wind-and-renewab.question: The evidence for South Africa's exceptional solar endowment is:
options: Rainfall above 1 000 millimetres over the interior
More than 2 500 sunshine hours per year over most of the interior, with the Northern Cape among the world's premium solar territories
The country's position on the equator

geography.grade11.solar-wind-and-renewab.subject: geography
geography.grade11.solar-wind-and-renewab.question: The REIPPPP is:
options: A carbon tax on coal exports
The competitive bidding programme under which private developers build wind and solar farms and sell power to the grid on long contracts
A rooftop solar subsidy for households

geography.grade11.solar-wind-and-renewab.subject: geography
geography.grade11.solar-wind-and-renewab.question: The 'quiet economic reversal' behind this topic is that:
options: REIPPPP auctions drove prices down until new wind and solar became cheaper per kilowatt-hour than new coal

geography.grade11.solar-wind-and-renewab.subject: geography
geography.grade11.solar-wind-and-renewab.question: The core difference between PV and CSP is:
options: PV converts sunlight directly to electricity in semiconductor cells with no moving parts, while CSP focuses mirrors to heat a fluid and drive a steam turbine
PV works only in deserts while CSP works anywhere
CSP is a household technology and PV is utility-scale only
PV requires water cooling and CSP does not

geography.grade11.solar-wind-and-renewab.subject: geography
geography.grade11.solar-wind-and-renewab.question: CSP's decisive gift over PV is:
options: Storage — insulated tanks of hot molten salt keep generating steam for hours after sunset, answering intermittency directly

geography.grade11.solar-wind-and-renewab.subject: geography
geography.grade11.solar-wind-and-renewab.question: Redstone, near Postmasburg in the Northern Cape, is notable for:
options: Being a CSP tower plant with twelve hours of molten-salt storage, built to serve the evening peak

geography.grade11.solar-wind-and-renewab.subject: geography
geography.grade11.solar-wind-and-renewab.question: A world example pairing for solar is:
options: Denmark for CSP and Morocco for offshore panels
China dominating panel manufacturing and installed capacity, and Morocco's Noor complex at Ouarzazate as Africa's CSP giant

geography.grade11.solar-wind-and-renewab.subject: geography
geography.grade11.solar-wind-and-renewab.question: Wind power rises with the cube of wind speed, which means:
options: Doubling the wind gives eight times the power — why towers reach past a hundred metres into faster, steadier air
Doubling the wind doubles the power
Blade length is irrelevant to output

geography.grade11.solar-wind-and-renewab.subject: geography
geography.grade11.solar-wind-and-renewab.question: South Africa's leading wind province, with the Jeffreys Bay and Cookhouse farms, is:

geography.grade11.solar-wind-and-renewab.subject: geography
geography.grade11.solar-wind-and-renewab.question: Denmark's significance in wind energy is that it:
options: Hosts the world's largest single farm
Generates roughly half its electricity from wind and exports its turbine industry — proof a small country can lead a global technology

geography.grade11.solar-wind-and-renewab.subject: geography
geography.grade11.solar-wind-and-renewab.question: Wind's honest cost column includes:
options: High fuel prices and water use
Intermittency, visual and noise objections, bird and bat collisions requiring careful siting, and the need for backup in still air

geography.grade11.solar-wind-and-renewab.subject: geography
geography.grade11.solar-wind-and-renewab.question: The economic positives of the renewable build include:
options: Cheapest new power restraining tariffs, hundreds of billions in investment, rural jobs and community revenue in provinces like the Northern Cape, and a green manufacturing ladder
Guaranteed employment for all coal miners

geography.grade11.solar-wind-and-renewab.subject: geography
geography.grade11.solar-wind-and-renewab.question: The phrase 'just transition' exists because:
options: Renewables need no workers at all
Coal employs about ninety thousand miners concentrated in Mpumalanga towns, and the shift redistributes work across provinces and skills — requiring retraining, pensions and new industry
Transitions must happen within one year

geography.grade11.solar-wind-and-renewab.subject: geography
geography.grade11.solar-wind-and-renewab.question: The binding physical constraint on South Africa's renewable pace is now:
options: The grid — the best sun and wind lie far from Gauteng's demand and the transmission lines are full

geography.grade11.solar-wind-and-renewab.subject: geography
geography.grade11.solar-wind-and-renewab.question: The lesson's defensible conclusion on the non-conventional future is:
options: The resource is too weak to matter
Coal will regain its share by 2040
The question is not resource — ours is world-class — but delivery: grid, storage, policy and a just transition; the argument is only about speed

geography.grade11.solar-wind-and-renewab.subject: geography
geography.grade11.solar-wind-and-renewab.question: The free filling station picture captures:
options: Sunshine and wind costing nothing, with nearly all cost in building the harvesting equipment — paid once, harvesting for decades

geography.grade11.solar-wind-and-renewab.subject: geography
geography.grade11.solar-wind-and-renewab.question: 'Free but moody, against costly but steady' summarises:
options: The trade-off between intermittent renewables and fuel-hungry but steady coal — the whole modern energy argument in five words
The difference between PV and CSP

geography.grade11.solar-wind-and-renewab.subject: geography
geography.grade11.solar-wind-and-renewab.question: Germany's relevance to South Africa's solar debate is that it:
options: Has better sun than the Northern Cape
Built a world-leading solar industry with roughly half our sunshine — proving the race is about pumps, not fuel
Buys most of South Africa's electricity

geography.grade11.solar-wind-and-renewab.subject: geography
geography.grade11.solar-wind-and-renewab.question: The PV panel's one-line secret is:
options: Sunlight to electricity with no moving parts — silent, strongest at noon, asleep by dusk

geography.grade11.solar-wind-and-renewab.subject: geography
geography.grade11.solar-wind-and-renewab.question: CSP's 'thermos' superpower means:
options: Hot molten salt stored in insulated tanks keeps making steam for hours — supper-time electricity from lunchtime sun
The plant needs no sunlight at all

geography.grade11.solar-wind-and-renewab.subject: geography
geography.grade11.solar-wind-and-renewab.question: Wind turbines and farming coexist because:
options: Farms are always abandoned before construction
Sheep graze under the turbines while farmers collect rent and communities hold revenue shares
Turbines are built only on barren rock

geography.grade11.solar-wind-and-renewab.subject: geography
geography.grade11.solar-wind-and-renewab.question: The correct place pairings are:
options: Redstone in Gauteng; Cookhouse in Limpopo
Noor in Denmark; Caledon in China
PV mega-farms around Upington and De Aar; CSP at Khi, KaXu, Xina and Redstone in the Northern Cape; wind at Jeffreys Bay, Cookhouse and Caledon on the coastal belt

geography.grade11.solar-wind-and-renewab.subject: geography
geography.grade11.solar-wind-and-renewab.question: Fumble one — 'the extension cord' — refers to:
options: Full transmission lines between the Northern and Eastern Cape's resources and Gauteng's demand, making new lines the real bottleneck
The cost of undersea cables to Europe
Solar panels needing longer cables than coal

geography.grade11.solar-wind-and-renewab.subject: geography
geography.grade11.solar-wind-and-renewab.question: The 'night shift' is covered by:
options: Running coal stations harder at night forever
A designed mix — CSP's hot salt, batteries, pumped storage, and coastal wind that often blows while solar sleeps

geography.grade11.solar-wind-and-renewab.subject: geography
geography.grade11.solar-wind-and-renewab.question: Passing the baton 'justly' means:
options: Retraining, pensions, new industry and international transition finance for coal towns like Emalahleni and Secunda

geography.grade11.solar-wind-and-renewab.subject: geography
geography.grade11.solar-wind-and-renewab.question: The finish-line verdict on the non-conventional future is:
options: Both direction and speed are unknowable
The environment loses under any scenario
The direction is not in doubt — sun and wind win on environment and increasingly on economics — only the speed is argued, and it depends on wires, storage and justice

geography.grade11.the-concept-of-develop.subject: geography
geography.grade11.the-concept-of-develop.question: Why is economic growth described as necessary but not sufficient for development?
options: Growth enlarges the economy's output, but development requires that the new wealth actually improves lives — health, education, services — and growth can pool in few hands instead
Growth and development are two words for the same thing
Development happens only when growth stops
Growth measures quality of life directly

geography.grade11.the-concept-of-develop.subject: geography
geography.grade11.the-concept-of-develop.question: A miner earns a good salary but works in a dangerous shaft and breathes coal dust. The correct description is:
options: High quality of life, low standard of living
A reasonable standard of living but a poor quality of life, because quality of life includes health, safety and environment beyond income
Both high, since salary determines everything

geography.grade11.the-concept-of-develop.subject: geography
geography.grade11.the-concept-of-develop.question: South Korea, Brazil and Mexico — countries whose manufacturing surged within living memory — are labelled:

geography.grade11.the-concept-of-develop.subject: geography
geography.grade11.the-concept-of-develop.question: The CAPS definition of development is best summarised as:
options: The growth of a country's total output
The process of building more factories
The process of improving people's quality of life — wealth together with health, education, safety, freedom and dignity

geography.grade11.the-concept-of-develop.subject: geography
geography.grade11.the-concept-of-develop.question: A Toyota plant operating in Durban counts inside:
options: South Africa's GDP but Japan's GNP, because GDP counts production within borders while GNP counts production by a country's citizens and companies anywhere
South Africa's GNP but Japan's GDP

geography.grade11.the-concept-of-develop.subject: geography
geography.grade11.the-concept-of-develop.question: Why is GDP per capita a fairer comparison tool than total GDP?
options: It removes inflation from the figures
Dividing by population gives output per person, so a small rich country is no longer out-ranked by a large poor one simply because of population size
It includes the Gini coefficient automatically

geography.grade11.the-concept-of-develop.subject: geography
geography.grade11.the-concept-of-develop.question: The Gini coefficient runs on a scale where:
options: 0 means one person earns everything and 1 means perfect equality
0 means everyone earns the same and 1 means one person earns everything

geography.grade11.the-concept-of-develop.subject: geography
geography.grade11.the-concept-of-develop.question: South Africa's Gini coefficient of about 0,63 tells us:
options: The country is poorer than its neighbours
Income is distributed extremely unequally — a respectable average income coexists with deep poverty, which per capita figures alone cannot show

geography.grade11.the-concept-of-develop.subject: geography
geography.grade11.the-concept-of-develop.question: Infant mortality is called the most sensitive development indicator because:
options: Keeping babies alive demands everything working at once — maternal care, immunisation, sanitation and income — so the number reflects the whole system
Babies are counted more accurately than adults
It is the only indicator measured yearly

geography.grade11.the-concept-of-develop.subject: geography
geography.grade11.the-concept-of-develop.question: The three dimensions combined in the Human Development Index are:
options: Health (life expectancy), education (years of schooling) and income (GNI per capita)
GDP, GNP and the Gini coefficient

geography.grade11.the-concept-of-develop.subject: geography
geography.grade11.the-concept-of-develop.question: South Africa's HDI of about 0,71 trails its income ranking mainly because:
options: Schooling years are the lowest in Africa
The health dimension — life expectancy in the mid-sixties — drags the combined score down despite relatively strong income and schooling

geography.grade11.the-concept-of-develop.subject: geography
geography.grade11.the-concept-of-develop.question: The HDI's designed advantage over GDP-based measures is that:
options: A country cannot buy a good score with money alone, so the index exposes the gap between wealth and wellbeing that GDP hides

geography.grade11.the-concept-of-develop.subject: geography
geography.grade11.the-concept-of-develop.question: The Brandt line of 1980:
options: Split the world into a rich North and poor South, dipping to include Australia and New Zealand — a useful first sketch that has since blurred as countries like South Korea rose
Still describes the world with perfect accuracy

geography.grade11.the-concept-of-develop.subject: geography
geography.grade11.the-concept-of-develop.question: Describing development as a continuum means:
options: Countries alternate between rich and poor each decade
Countries are strung along a line from lowest to highest development with every position filled, rather than clustering into two camps
Only two categories of country exist

geography.grade11.the-concept-of-develop.subject: geography
geography.grade11.the-concept-of-develop.question: Sandton and Diepsloot sharing one metro demonstrates that:
options: The Brandt line runs through Johannesburg
Development differences run within countries as sharply as between them, which is why the Gini coefficient matters

geography.grade11.the-concept-of-develop.subject: geography
geography.grade11.the-concept-of-develop.question: The balanced examination answer on South Africa's development status is:
options: A fully developed MEDC because of the JSE
A developing country — an NIC — with pockets of MEDC prosperity and pockets of LEDC deprivation, supported by evidence on income, HDI, unemployment and inequality

geography.grade11.the-concept-of-develop.subject: geography
geography.grade11.the-concept-of-develop.question: In the two-streets picture, development is:
options: The work of moving the second street toward the first — medicine, taps, teachers and safety, not only money
Building a wall between the streets
Moving people from the second street to the first
Raising the first street's incomes further

geography.grade11.the-concept-of-develop.subject: geography
geography.grade11.the-concept-of-develop.question: The man with a good salary living beside a burning mine dump shows:
options: That salaries determine quality of life
A standard of living without the matching quality of life, because quality of life includes health, safety and clean air
That mine dumps raise property values

geography.grade11.the-concept-of-develop.subject: geography
geography.grade11.the-concept-of-develop.question: The factory that doubles output while every extra rand leaves town illustrates:
options: Growth without development — the engine revving without the wheels turning

geography.grade11.the-concept-of-develop.subject: geography
geography.grade11.the-concept-of-develop.question: In the soccer scoreboard picture, dividing total goals by the number of teams stands for:
options: Calculating GDP per capita — output per person — so big populations stop distorting the comparison

geography.grade11.the-concept-of-develop.subject: geography
geography.grade11.the-concept-of-develop.question: Goals scored inside your own stadium by anyone, versus goals scored by your registered players anywhere, stands for:
options: GDP — production within borders — versus GNP, production by a country's citizens and companies wherever they operate
Standard of living versus quality of life

geography.grade11.the-concept-of-develop.subject: geography
geography.grade11.the-concept-of-develop.question: One team winning 10-nil while forty-nine teams lose, yet the club average looking healthy, is the analogy for:
options: South Africa's inequality — a decent average income beside a Gini coefficient of about 0,63

geography.grade11.the-concept-of-develop.subject: geography
geography.grade11.the-concept-of-develop.question: The paired sentence worth carrying into the exam is:
options: The Gini measures the cake's size; GDP measures the slices
Both measures describe the cake's ingredients
The average tells you the size of the cake per person; the Gini coefficient tells you how the cake is sliced

geography.grade11.the-concept-of-develop.subject: geography
geography.grade11.the-concept-of-develop.question: The three subjects on the HDI report card are:
options: Health via life expectancy, education via schooling years, and income per person

geography.grade11.the-concept-of-develop.subject: geography
geography.grade11.the-concept-of-develop.question: Why can a country not 'cram one subject' to top the HDI class?
options: The subjects are marked by different agencies
The index deliberately averages three dimensions, so wealth cannot buy a top score while health or education lag — which is how it catches rich-but-unwell countries
The income subject is excluded for rich countries
Only education counts in the final mark

geography.grade11.the-concept-of-develop.subject: geography
geography.grade11.the-concept-of-develop.question: A falling infant mortality rate signals genuine development because:
options: Keeping a baby alive needs clinics, vaccines, clean water and income all working at the same time, so the falling number means the whole system is improving

geography.grade11.the-concept-of-develop.subject: geography
geography.grade11.the-concept-of-develop.question: On the ladder picture of world development, South Africa stands:
options: On the top rung with Norway
On the bottom rung with Niger
Mid-ladder — a developing country with one foot on a high rung and one on a low one, defended with evidence

geography.grade11.unequal-heating-energy.subject: geography
geography.grade11.unequal-heating-energy.question: Insolation reaches the top of the atmosphere at roughly the same rate everywhere. Why then do the tropics receive far more heating per square metre?
options: The angle of incidence is high near the equator, so the same beam lands on a small area, while oblique polar rays spread the same energy over a much larger area
The sun is physically closer to the equator

geography.grade11.unequal-heating-energy.subject: geography
geography.grade11.unequal-heating-energy.question: The 'path length' penalty at high latitudes means that:
options: Rays travel further from the sun to the poles
Oblique rays slant through a far greater thickness of atmosphere, so more energy is scattered, reflected and absorbed before reaching the surface
Polar air is thicker than tropical air
The poles receive no radiation in winter

geography.grade11.unequal-heating-energy.subject: geography
geography.grade11.unequal-heating-energy.question: Approximate albedo values quoted in the lesson are:
options: Fresh snow and ice roughly 80–90%, open ocean under 10%

geography.grade11.unequal-heating-energy.subject: geography
geography.grade11.unequal-heating-energy.question: Of the insolation arriving at the top of the atmosphere, the lesson's budget gives roughly:
options: 10% reflected, 10% absorbed by the atmosphere, 80% at the surface
Half reflected and half absorbed by the atmosphere
About 30% reflected to space, about 20% absorbed by the atmosphere, about half absorbed at the surface

geography.grade11.unequal-heating-energy.subject: geography
geography.grade11.unequal-heating-energy.question: The earth's axis is tilted:
options: 23,5 degrees from the vertical, and holds that lean in a fixed direction all year (parallelism)
66,5 degrees from the vertical, changing direction each season
It is not tilted; the orbit is tilted

geography.grade11.unequal-heating-energy.subject: geography
geography.grade11.unequal-heating-energy.question: On about 22 December the overhead sun is at:
options: The Tropic of Capricorn, 23,5 degrees south — South Africa's summer solstice, longest day
The Tropic of Cancer, 23,5 degrees north

geography.grade11.unequal-heating-energy.subject: geography
geography.grade11.unequal-heating-energy.question: Cape Town lies at 34 degrees south. Its midday solar altitude on 21 June (declination 23,5 degrees north) is:

geography.grade11.unequal-heating-energy.subject: geography
geography.grade11.unequal-heating-energy.question: A learner writes that we have winter because the earth is further from the sun. Why does this lose the mark?
options: The earth's orbit is a perfect circle
The earth is furthest from the sun in December
The earth is actually CLOSEST to the sun in early January, during our summer and Europe's winter — seasons are caused by the axial tilt, not distance

geography.grade11.unequal-heating-energy.subject: geography
geography.grade11.unequal-heating-energy.question: Feeling warmth on your face while standing near coals without touching them demonstrates:
options: Radiation — energy transferred as electromagnetic waves, needing no medium

geography.grade11.unequal-heating-energy.subject: geography
geography.grade11.unequal-heating-energy.question: Why is conduction a poor explanation for heating anywhere above the lowest few centimetres of the atmosphere?
options: Air is a poor conductor, so molecule-to-molecule transfer is confined to air in direct contact with a hot surface such as Kalahari sand

geography.grade11.unequal-heating-energy.subject: geography
geography.grade11.unequal-heating-energy.question: The afternoon sea breeze pushing cool marine air into Durban is an example of:
options: Advection — the horizontal transfer of heat by moving air or water

geography.grade11.unequal-heating-energy.subject: geography
geography.grade11.unequal-heating-energy.question: Latent heat is described as the 'quiet giant' because:
options: Evaporating a kilogram of water absorbs about 2,5 megajoules with no temperature rise; the energy travels inside the vapour and is released far away and high up when condensation occurs

geography.grade11.unequal-heating-energy.subject: geography
geography.grade11.unequal-heating-energy.question: The energy SURPLUS zone lies approximately:
options: Between 40 degrees north and 40 degrees south, where absorbed shortwave exceeds longwave lost to space
Poleward of 60 degrees in each hemisphere

geography.grade11.unequal-heating-energy.subject: geography
geography.grade11.unequal-heating-energy.question: The strongest evidence that energy MUST be transported poleward is:
options: The equator-to-pole temperature difference stays broadly stable from decade to decade instead of the tropics heating and the poles cooling without limit

geography.grade11.unequal-heating-energy.subject: geography
geography.grade11.unequal-heating-energy.question: The split of poleward heat transfer between the two carriers is roughly:
options: Atmosphere about three-quarters, oceans about one-quarter

geography.grade11.unequal-heating-energy.subject: geography
geography.grade11.unequal-heating-energy.question: South Africa's two coastal currents illustrate the correction because:
options: The warm Agulhas Current carries tropical heat south along the east coast while the cold Benguela Current draws polar water north along the west coast

geography.grade11.unequal-heating-energy.subject: geography
geography.grade11.unequal-heating-energy.question: Tilting the torch turns the tight bright circle into a big dim oval because:
options: The same amount of light is shared over a much larger area of wall — exactly what happens to sunlight at high latitudes
The torch battery weakens when tilted
The wall reflects more light when tilted
Tilting makes the light travel further from the battery

geography.grade11.unequal-heating-energy.subject: geography
geography.grade11.unequal-heating-energy.question: The 'crowded taxi rank' comparison explains:
options: Path length — slanting sunlight pushes through far more air, losing energy to scattering, reflection and absorption the whole way

geography.grade11.unequal-heating-energy.subject: geography
geography.grade11.unequal-heating-energy.question: The black bakkie and white bakkie comparison stands for:
options: Albedo — bright ice and snow bounce most sunlight away, while the dark ocean absorbs almost all of it

geography.grade11.unequal-heating-energy.subject: geography
geography.grade11.unequal-heating-energy.question: In the leaning-ball demonstration, the rule 'never straighten it and never turn the lean around' represents:
options: Parallelism of the earth's axis — the lean stays fixed in direction all year, which is what produces the seasons
The rotation of the earth on its axis
The elliptical shape of the orbit
The tilt slowly reversing each season

geography.grade11.unequal-heating-energy.subject: geography
geography.grade11.unequal-heating-energy.question: Cape Town's midday sun swings from about 79,5 degrees in December to about 32,5 degrees in June. The full effect on heating is:
options: A 47-degree drop in sun height PLUS about four and a half hours less daylight — weaker energy delivered for fewer hours
A 47-degree drop, but daylight stays the same

geography.grade11.unequal-heating-energy.subject: geography
geography.grade11.unequal-heating-energy.question: Around 21 March and 23 September:
options: The sun is overhead at the Tropic of Cancer
The southern hemisphere has its longest day
The lamp shines square on the ball's middle — the sun is overhead at the equator and day and night are equal everywhere
The earth is closest to the sun

geography.grade11.unequal-heating-energy.subject: geography
geography.grade11.unequal-heating-energy.question: The strongest proof that distance does NOT cause the seasons is:
options: The orbit is a perfect circle
The earth spins once a day
We are closest to the sun in early January, which is our summer but Europe's deep winter — one distance cannot make both

geography.grade11.unequal-heating-energy.subject: geography
geography.grade11.unequal-heating-energy.question: Picking up the metal grid handle left on the fire and burning your fingers demonstrates:
options: Conduction — heat passing by direct touch, molecule to molecule

geography.grade11.unequal-heating-energy.subject: geography
geography.grade11.unequal-heating-energy.question: The shimmer rising straight up off the coals, scaled up to Highveld size, produces:
options: Convection — warm air rising until it condenses into cumulonimbus and delivers the late-afternoon thunderstorm

geography.grade11.unequal-heating-energy.subject: geography
geography.grade11.unequal-heating-energy.question: Feeling cold when a breeze passes over your sweaty skin illustrates:
options: Latent heat — turning water into vapour steals heat from your skin and carries it away invisibly

geography.grade11.unequal-heating-energy.subject: geography
geography.grade11.unequal-heating-energy.question: In the spaza-shop picture of the energy balance:
options: The poles have the surplus and the tropics the deficit
The tropics are the shop with surplus bread, the poles the shop with a deficit, and the winds carry about three loaves in four while ocean currents carry the rest

geography.grade12.agriculture-maize-and-.subject: geography
geography.grade12.agriculture-maize-and-.question: Agriculture's contribution to South Africa's GDP is approximately:

geography.grade12.agriculture-maize-and-.subject: geography
geography.grade12.agriculture-maize-and-.question: The "linkages" argument for agriculture's importance points to:
options: Its supply of raw materials to agro-processing — mills, canneries, refineries, abattoirs
Its control of the taxi industry

geography.grade12.agriculture-maize-and-.subject: geography
geography.grade12.agriculture-maize-and-.question: Which product belongs primarily to South Africa's EXPORT market list?

geography.grade12.agriculture-maize-and-.subject: geography
geography.grade12.agriculture-maize-and-.question: Agriculture slows rural depopulation because it:
options: Pays the highest wages in the economy
Anchors rural settlement and provides jobs where alternatives barely exist

geography.grade12.agriculture-maize-and-.subject: geography
geography.grade12.agriculture-maize-and-.question: Which feature belongs to LARGE-SCALE commercial farming?
options: Heavy capital investment and production for market and export

geography.grade12.agriculture-maize-and-.subject: geography
geography.grade12.agriculture-maize-and-.question: Small-scale farmers on communal land struggle to obtain bank loans because:
options: Communal land cannot easily be used as collateral
Banks do not lend to farmers at all
They have too much machinery already

geography.grade12.agriculture-maize-and-.subject: geography
geography.grade12.agriculture-maize-and-.question: The five clean comparison lines for the two farming systems are:
options: Farm size, capital and technology, labour source, market orientation, land tenure
Province, language, crop colour, season, distance

geography.grade12.agriculture-maize-and-.subject: geography

options: The mole — a fixed pack of 6,02 × 10²³ particles

physical_sciences.grade10.the-mole-conce.subject: physical_sciences
physical_sciences.grade10.the-mole-conce.question: Why is the periodic table called the price list, written in grams per pack?
options: It lists the cost of chemicals in rands
It lists how many packs of each element exist
The number printed for an element is the mass in grams of one mole of it
It tells you the volume of one mole

physical_sciences.grade10.the-mole-conce.subject: physical_sciences
physical_sciences.grade10.the-mole-conce.question: Why may weighing stand in for counting particles?
options: Because all particles weigh the same
Because one mole always holds the same number of particles, so a known mass fixes a known count
Because balances can detect single molecules
Because grams and particles are the same unit

physical_sciences.grade10.the-mole-conce.subject: physical_sciences
physical_sciences.grade10.the-mole-conce.question: Reading CO2 'like an invoice' — one carbon, two oxygens — gives a molar mass of:

physical_sciences.grade10.the-mole-conce.subject: physical_sciences
physical_sciences.grade10.the-mole-conce.question: Why must 8,8 g of CO2 come to 0,2 mol before you touch a calculator?
options: Because every gas question gives 0,2 mol
Because 8,8 g is one fifth of the 44 g that one mole weighs, so it is a fifth of a pack
Because moles are always less than 1

physical_sciences.grade10.the-mole-conce.subject: physical_sciences
physical_sciences.grade10.the-mole-conce.question: Going from moles OUT to molecules you multiply, because:
options: Particles are the tiny, numerous thing, so the count must come out enormous

physical_sciences.grade10.the-mole-conce.subject: physical_sciences
physical_sciences.grade10.the-mole-conce.question: 0,2 mol of carbon dioxide contains:

physical_sciences.grade10.the-mole-conce.subject: physical_sciences
physical_sciences.grade10.the-mole-conce.question: Why does one mole of any gas fill the same volume at the same temperature and pressure?
options: Because all gases have the same molar mass
Because a gas is mostly empty space — the spacing between particles sets the volume, not the size of each particle
Because gas molecules are all identical in size

physical_sciences.grade10.the-mole-conce.subject: physical_sciences
physical_sciences.grade10.the-mole-conce.question: At STP, 0,2 mol of carbon dioxide occupies:
options: 4,48 dm³ — about two large cooldrink bottles

physical_sciences.grade10.the-mole-conce.subject: physical_sciences
physical_sciences.grade10.the-mole-conce.question: In the taxi-rank picture of the mole map, riding OUT of the rank always means:
options: Multiplying — by the molar mass, by Avogadro's number, or by 22,4 dm³/mol

physical_sciences.grade10.the-mole-conce.subject: physical_sciences
physical_sciences.grade10.the-mole-conce.question: When is the 22,4 dm³/mol shortcut NOT allowed?
options: When the substance is a liquid or a solid, or the gas is not at STP
When the gas is carbon dioxide
When the mass is under 10 g
When the question asks for molecules

physical_sciences.grade10.the-periodic-t.subject: physical_sciences
physical_sciences.grade10.the-periodic-t.question: The modern periodic table arranges the elements in order of increasing:

physical_sciences.grade10.the-periodic-t.subject: physical_sciences
physical_sciences.grade10.the-periodic-t.question: The period number of an element equals its number of:

physical_sciences.grade10.the-periodic-t.subject: physical_sciences
physical_sciences.grade10.the-periodic-t.question: Elements in the same group behave similarly because they have the same number of:
options: Valence electrons — electrons in the outermost level

physical_sciences.grade10.the-periodic-t.subject: physical_sciences
physical_sciences.grade10.the-periodic-t.question: An element with configuration 1s two, 2s two, 2p six, 3s two, 3p five sits in:
options: Period 3, group 17 — three occupied levels, seven valence electrons: chlorine

physical_sciences.grade10.the-periodic-t.subject: physical_sciences
physical_sciences.grade10.the-periodic-t.question: Relative to the staircase line, the three kingdoms sit:
options: Metals upper right; non-metals left; metalloids at the bottom
Metals to the left; non-metals to the upper right; metalloids along the staircase
Non-metals to the left; metals upper right; metalloids in group 18

physical_sciences.grade10.the-periodic-t.subject: physical_sciences
physical_sciences.grade10.the-periodic-t.question: Metals conduct electricity well because:
options: Their structure holds a sea of mobile electrons

physical_sciences.grade10.the-periodic-t.subject: physical_sciences
physical_sciences.grade10.the-periodic-t.question: The ion habits of the two sides of the staircase are:
options: Metals lose electrons to form cations; non-metals gain electrons to form anions
Metals gain electrons; non-metals lose them

physical_sciences.grade10.the-periodic-t.subject: physical_sciences
physical_sciences.grade10.the-periodic-t.question: Silicon is essential to electronics because, as a metalloid, it is:
options: A semiconductor — conducting between metal and insulator, and controllably so

physical_sciences.grade10.the-periodic-t.subject: physical_sciences
physical_sciences.grade10.the-periodic-t.question: Across a period from left to right, atomic radius:
options: Decreases — more protons pull on the same outer level, reeling it inward

physical_sciences.grade10.the-periodic-t.subject: physical_sciences
physical_sciences.grade10.the-periodic-t.question: Ionisation energy is the energy needed to:
options: Add an electron to an atom
Remove an electron from an atom — it rises across a period and falls down a group

physical_sciences.grade10.the-periodic-t.subject: physical_sciences
physical_sciences.grade10.the-periodic-t.question: Down a group, ionisation energy decreases because the outer electron is:
options: Further from the nucleus and screened by more inner levels

physical_sciences.grade10.the-periodic-t.subject: physical_sciences
physical_sciences.grade10.the-periodic-t.question: The most electronegative element, at the table's top right, is:
options: Fluorine — the noble gases sit out the trend because they rarely bond

physical_sciences.grade10.the-periodic-t.subject: physical_sciences
physical_sciences.grade10.the-periodic-t.question: Group 1 metals are the most reactive metals because they:
options: Have one cheap-to-lose valence electron, forming plus-one ions

physical_sciences.grade10.the-periodic-t.subject: physical_sciences
physical_sciences.grade10.the-periodic-t.question: Going down group 1, reactivity:
options: Increases — the outer electron sits further out, more screened, and leaves more easily

physical_sciences.grade10.the-periodic-t.subject: physical_sciences
physical_sciences.grade10.the-periodic-t.question: Going down group 17, reactivity:
options: Decreases — fluorine grips new electrons ferociously, iodine only mildly

physical_sciences.grade10.the-periodic-t.subject: physical_sciences
physical_sciences.grade10.the-periodic-t.question: The noble gases of group 18 are unreactive because they:
options: Have full outer levels — nothing to lose, nothing to gain

physical_sciences.grade10.the-periodic-t.subject: physical_sciences
physical_sciences.grade10.the-periodic-t.question: In the street-map picture, the row you live in tells you:

physical_sciences.grade10.the-periodic-t.subject: physical_sciences

physical_sciences.grade10.the-periodic-t.subject: physical_sciences
