options: Row 2, column 2 — two floors, two upstairs: beryllium

physical_sciences.grade10.the-periodic-t.subject: physical_sciences
physical_sciences.grade10.the-periodic-t.question: Walking across a row, the atoms get smaller because each step adds:
options: A proton to the pulling team while the rope length stays the same

physical_sciences.grade10.the-periodic-t.subject: physical_sciences
physical_sciences.grade10.the-periodic-t.question: Walking down a column, the nucleus's grip on the outer electrons weakens because:
options: The rope gets longer — a new level each row — and inner floors muffle the pull

physical_sciences.grade10.the-periodic-t.subject: physical_sciences
physical_sciences.grade10.the-periodic-t.question: Fluorine is the fiercest electron-puller on the table because it combines:
options: A long rope with few pullers
A short rope with a big pulling team — top right of the table
The most neutrons with the fewest protons
A full outer level with no charge

physical_sciences.grade10.the-periodic-t.subject: physical_sciences
physical_sciences.grade10.the-periodic-t.question: Potassium reacts more wildly with water than sodium because its one coin — its valence electron — is:
options: A floor higher, on a longer rope with a weaker grip, so it drops even more easily

physical_sciences.grade10.the-periodic-t.subject: physical_sciences
physical_sciences.grade10.the-periodic-t.question: The mirror rule for reactivity going down the table is:
options: Both givers and collectors strengthen downward
Reactivity never changes within a family
Givers (metals) strengthen downward; collectors (halogens) weaken downward

physical_sciences.grade10.the-periodic-t.subject: physical_sciences
physical_sciences.grade10.the-periodic-t.question: Balloons and old shop signs are filled with noble gases because these gases:
options: Glow on their own in daylight
React with essentially nothing — their outer levels are already full

physical_sciences.grade10.transverse-wav.subject: physical_sciences

options: A single disturbance that moves through a medium
A repeating disturbance that never stops
The number of waves passing a point each second

physical_sciences.grade10.transverse-wav.subject: physical_sciences
physical_sciences.grade10.transverse-wav.question: In a transverse pulse on a rope, the particles of the rope move:

At right angles (perpendicular) to the direction the pulse travels

physical_sciences.grade10.transverse-wav.subject: physical_sciences

options: The pulses bounce off each other and reverse
The rope stays flat forever afterwards
They add algebraically — the rope is momentarily flat — and then both pulses continue on unchanged

physical_sciences.grade10.transverse-wav.subject: physical_sciences

physical_sciences.grade10.transverse-wav.subject: physical_sciences

options: The height of a crest above a trough
The distance between two successive points IN PHASE, such as crest to next crest
The time for one wave to pass a point
The number of crests per second

physical_sciences.grade10.transverse-wav.subject: physical_sciences
physical_sciences.grade10.transverse-wav.question: Two points on a wave are IN PHASE when they:
options: Are both on the rest line
Are one at a crest and one at a trough
Have the same displacement AND are moving in the same direction — separated by a whole number of wavelengths
Have the same amplitude but different wavelengths

physical_sciences.grade10.transverse-wav.subject: physical_sciences
physical_sciences.grade10.transverse-wav.question: Points that are OUT of phase are separated by:
options: An odd number of half wavelengths — half a lambda, one and a half, two and a half

physical_sciences.grade10.transverse-wav.subject: physical_sciences

options: 0,33 s — the period is one divided by the frequency

physical_sciences.grade10.transverse-wav.subject: physical_sciences

From one hump-top to the next hump-top

options: A quarter of a second — frequency and period are the same fact flipped over

physical_sciences.grade10.transverse-wav.subject: physical_sciences

Speed is always three times the frequency
Wavelength and frequency are always equal
The rope stretches as it moves

physical_sciences.grade10.transverse-wav.subject: physical_sciences

options: 60 cm — which is 0,6 m·s⁻¹, the same answer as v = fλ

physical_sciences.grade10.transverse-wav.subject: physical_sciences

options: 0,75 m — two waves per second, so 1,5 ÷ 2

physical_sciences.grade10.transverse-wav.subject: physical_sciences

options: Converting every centimetre to metres and every millisecond to seconds BEFORE multiplying

physical_sciences.grade10.vectors-and-sc.subject: physical_sciences

Vectors can partially or fully cancel depending on their directions

Vectors: displacement, force, velocity; scalars: speed, energy
Vectors: displacement only; scalars: the other four

Draw a circle, measure angles, average them

A vector, because batteries have two terminals
Neither a vector nor a scalar

physical_sciences.grade10.vectors-and-sc.subject: physical_sciences
physical_sciences.grade10.vectors-and-sc.question: A speed on a road sign becomes a velocity when:
options: It is measured in metres per second
It is written with a decimal comma
A direction of travel is attached to it

physical_sciences.grade10.vectors-and-sc.subject: physical_sciences
physical_sciences.grade10.vectors-and-sc.question: You run once around a 400 m block and stop at your own gate. Your distance and displacement are:

options: Displacement is measured in different units
Distance is always the larger number by definition

options: Choose a direction, call it positive, and keep that choice to the final line

options: Because the number should be negative
Because forces are always written in kilonewtons
Because a vector answer needs its direction too — 20 N west

Every formula needs exactly two elements
